## Compliance Module + Modular Feature System: implementation plan authored (2026-09-04)

Requested directly: a multi-session implementation plan for the new Compliance Module (`docs/Compliance_Module_Requirements.md`, 33 sections), explicitly framed as the first of four planned major uplifts (Compliance, a Decisions Record system, Pain Points collection, a better Traceability system) and required to support sessions starting and stopping with context cleared in between. Planning only — no code, migrations, or schema changes in this session.

**Why this is more than "one feature plus a toggle":** the user's own framing — four uplifts, a desire for org-level enable/disable, and a stated future interest in contributor-built custom modules — meant the real deliverable was a generic modular-feature-system architecture that Compliance is the first (and reference) implementation of, not a one-off. The design went through four rounds of correction (recorded in full inside the plan doc's "Design history" section so a future session doesn't relitigate them or simplify the design back toward an already-rejected version):
1. A simple per-org boolean + static registry was rejected as too limited.
2. Two-tier server-entitlement/org-enablement gating plus first-party module packages and Python entry-point backend plugin discovery was rejected on three points: the new server-level role needed to reuse this app's *existing* role-display UI rather than a bespoke section; third-party UI needed to be feasible, not just documented as a future gap; and modules needed to be able to register their own RBAC roles rather than Compliance getting one-off `OrgRole`/`ProjectRole` enum additions.
3. Adding `ServerRole`/`UserServerRole`, a generic module-role mechanism, and an iframe-plus-narrow-postMessage-contract third-party UI design was rejected on one further point: third-party modules must be able to use the app's *actual* shared components (Toast, modals), not a thin isolated message contract.
4. The approved design resolves "isolate untrusted code" against "let it use real shared components" with a two-tier frontend model: Tier A (installed at build time — first-party or a third-party npm package — with direct imports of every real shared component, the tier Compliance itself uses) as the primary path, and Tier B (a remote iframe with a *Host UI Bridge* that renders real host `Toast`/`ConfirmDialog` via RPC rather than reimplementing them) for the genuinely-dynamic, not-installed case.

**The approved plan** is `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, committed to the repo (not this log, and not the ephemeral Claude Code plan-mode file, which isn't visible to a future session) specifically so a cleared-context session can resume cold. It has a "Status / Resume Here" table at the top (0 of 15 phases complete as of this entry) and a "How to Resume a Session" procedure. Phases 0–3 build the module-system infrastructure (server-level RBAC extension via a new `ServerRole`/`UserServerRole` mirroring the existing `OrgRole`/`UserOrgRole` pattern; two-tier entitlement/enablement tables plus `backend/app/modules/` plugin loading via static registration and `importlib.metadata` entry points; a generic module-contributed-RBAC mechanism Compliance uses instead of core enum edits; and the two-tier frontend integration described above). Phases 4–14 build Compliance itself as the reference implementation, each phase cited against the specific `Compliance_Module_Requirements.md` section(s) it satisfies.

**Deliberately out of scope, documented rather than silently dropped** (per this repo's standing "fix or flag, don't silently defer" rule — these are flagged, not skipped): sandboxing/security review of arbitrary third-party *code execution* (the trust boundary is "was deliberately pip-installed/npm-installed into this deployment," the same boundary any language's plugin ecosystem relies on); automatic third-party database migrations (arbitrary third-party SQL against production is its own security-review-shaped question; only first-party modules get real Alembic migrations); and module-role inheritance through org/project groups or project hierarchy (V1 module roles are direct grants only — the core RBAC engine's existing inheritance resolution for `OrgRole`/`ProjectRole` is substantial and extending it generically to module roles deserves its own dedicated review).

**Reused mechanisms confirmed by exploration**, not duplicated: the `DirectoryTable`/`MultiSelectDropdown` combination already used by `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s Users table (every new role-display surface, server or module, must render through this, not a bespoke table); the `Organization.accent_color_hex`-falls-back-to-`ServerSettings` override shape (reused for module entitlement); `services/pats.py`'s scoping model (reused conceptually for the Tier B iframe's short-lived scoped token); the `Requirement`/`RequirementVersion` identity-plus-history shape (reused for Compliance Standard versions); the `FileAsset` + join-table-per-owner-type attachment convention (reused for Evidence); and the existing audit/notification/scheduler/bundle-export services, all cited with file paths inside the plan doc.

### Addendum: module-contributed MCP server tools (2026-09-04, same day)

Identified after the plan above was approved — not a correction, a genuinely new requirement noticed once the module-system shape was settled: modules should also be able to register their own `mcp-server/` tools, not just REST endpoints, RBAC roles, and frontend UI. Added as a new Phase 4 (renumbering the Compliance-specific phases from 4–14 to 5–15; total now 16 phases, 0–15).

`mcp-server/server.py` already has an established, principled pattern worth extending rather than duplicating: every tool is an `@mcp.tool`-decorated function calling a shared `_call_backend` helper that forwards the caller's own bearer token (the server holds no credentials and performs no authorization of its own — `docs/mcp-server.md`'s "Authentication model"); write tools exist only when `MCP_WRITES_ENABLED=true`; and, critically, no tool in either mode can approve, decide, or otherwise change workflow state — a boundary enforced by never exposing the capability as a tool, not by relying on RBAC alone.

Phase 4's design: `ModuleDefinition.mcp_tools` lets a module declare **declarative, single-REST-call tool mappings** (name, HTTP method, path template, param mapping, a `mutates` flag, an `is_approval_action` flag). A new `GET /api/v1/system/modules/mcp-tools` backend endpoint merges these across all implemented modules and **hard-excludes any `is_approval_action: true` entry server-side** — mirroring the existing approval-exclusion principle, but enforced in the manifest builder itself rather than left as an honour-system flag a module could get wrong. `mcp-server` fetches this manifest once at its own startup and registers each entry as a generic proxy tool via FastMCP's programmatic registration API, reusing the existing `_call_backend` helper verbatim; mutating entries only register when `MCP_WRITES_ENABLED` is true, same as today's hand-written write tools.

Two deliberate scope boundaries, flagged rather than silently built, consistent with the rest of this plan: only declarative single-REST-call tools are supported in V1 — genuinely custom tool logic would mean running third-party code inside a process that handles real user bearer tokens, the same trust question already deferred for the backend's own plugin loading; and because the manifest is fetched once at process startup, picking up a new or changed module's tools requires restarting the `mcp-server` container, not a hot-reload — confirmed acceptable by the user, including that this may need its own explicit stage in the deployment pipeline if the mechanism requires it.

Compliance itself (Phases 6–9, renumbered) will declare seven read-only tools (`compliance_list_standards`, `compliance_get_standard_version`, `compliance_list_requirements`, `compliance_get_project_status`, `compliance_list_non_compliant_requirements`, `compliance_list_expiring_evidence`, `compliance_list_pending_approvals`) and explicitly no tool for the approval/sign-off action itself, per the design above.

### Addendum 2: MCP-tools packaging, and a self-found hardening pass on the manifest design (2026-09-04, same day)

Two follow-up questions from the user on the addendum above, both resolved by updating the plan rather than the (still unwritten) code.

**Packaging**: the user asked whether `mcp-server` needs combining into the same container/image as the backend, reasoning that otherwise they didn't see how modules would deploy cleanly via Docker. Investigation found `mcp-server` is currently published as its own independently-deployable image (`ghcr.io/.../reqtrackmanager-mcp-server`) with a documented standalone/remote-client deployment mode (reverse-proxied separately, for clients like Copilot Studio that need a URL independent of the backend's own). A literal same-process merge was offered as an option but would have retired that documented deployment mode. Resolved by re-examining Phase 4's actual mechanism: because module-contributed MCP tools are purely declarative (a JSON manifest fetched over HTTP, proxied through the existing `_call_backend` helper), `mcp-server` never needs a module's Python package installed into its own image at all — the packaging concern doesn't actually apply to this design. `mcp-server/Dockerfile` and its separate image are unchanged; this is revisited only if the already-deferred "custom (non-declarative) MCP tool logic" capability is ever built.

**Security review of the manifest mechanism itself**: the user asked directly whether the dynamic JSON manifest becomes an attack surface. It would have, as originally designed — a self-review found three real gaps and fixed all three in the design before any code was written, per this repo's standing "fix, don't defer" practice:
1. `mutates` and `is_approval_action` were designed as fields a module declares on its own manifest entry — a malicious or buggy module could simply lie (`is_approval_action: false` on a tool that actually performs an approval), defeating the intended protection entirely. Fixed: `mutates` is now derived mechanically from the HTTP method (nothing to misdeclare); `is_approval_action` is now sourced from the real backend route's own metadata (set by that endpoint's own author, reviewed the same way the endpoint is) rather than the module's manifest entry.
2. A declared `path_template` had no constraint tying it to the declaring module's own endpoints — a module could point a tool at any backend path at all, including ones it doesn't own. Fixed: the manifest builder now rejects and logs any entry whose path falls outside that module's own registered router prefix, mechanically enforced rather than trusted from self-declaration.
3. The manifest endpoint was designed to be fetched once at `mcp-server`'s process boot, before any specific user's token exists — meaning either an unauthenticated endpoint (new reconnaissance surface) or an undesigned new service credential. Fixed: the endpoint requires the same bearer-token authentication as every other backend endpoint; `mcp-server` fetches/refreshes it lazily and authenticated, using whichever session's own token first triggers a refresh within a TTL window, cached in-process — never an unauthenticated call.

Documented explicitly as a bounded guarantee, not overclaimed: these fixes are mechanically strong for tools resolving to core/first-party endpoints (we control and review both the endpoint and its metadata). For a third-party module's own endpoints, the guarantee reduces to the same "was deliberately installed" trust boundary Phase 1 already established — which is why Phase 1 was also updated in the same pass to gate third-party module discovery (`importlib.metadata` entry points, `EXTRA_MODULES_PATH`) behind a new deployment-level flag, `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`, default `false`, mirroring `MCP_WRITES_ENABLED`'s existing off-by-default precedent in this codebase. First-party `INSTALLED_MODULES` are unaffected.

**SOC2 planning**: the user separately asked for explicit SOC2 planning across this whole module-system effort, not just a generic per-phase reminder. Read all three directly relevant policy docs in full (`vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md`, `change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md`, `access-control-policy.md`) plus the control matrix (`trust-services-criteria-mapping.md`) rather than assuming their content. Found that `trust-services-criteria-mapping.md`'s CC6.8 ("prevents or detects and acts upon unauthorized/malicious software") is already an open 🔴 gap — no automated dependency/container vulnerability scanning exists — and that this plan's plugin-loading mechanism materially raises the stakes of that already-open gap, which is the concrete reasoning behind `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` defaulting off. Added a new "SOC2 / Security Planning" section to `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` committing Phases 0–2 and Phase 1 to concrete policy-doc edits (a new `access-control-policy.md` subsection documenting the two new RBAC scopes this plan adds — server module role, module-contributed role — including that module roles explicitly don't participate in the existing group/hierarchy inheritance the policy's role-resolution diagram shows for core roles; a new `vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md` clause for installed third-party modules, distinct from a classic subprocessor because it's code running inside the deployment's own trust boundary rather than an external data-processing relationship) rather than leaving "consult the policy" as a vague per-phase reminder.

### Addendum 3: org/project scoping for module MCP tools (2026-09-04, same day)

The user asked two direct questions the plan hadn't actually answered: how does an `mcp-server` module tool behave when the module is disabled for a specific organisation, and how does it behave for a user who belongs to multiple organisations where only some have the module enabled?

The first turned out to need no new design at all: every module tool call names a specific `project_id` or `organization_id`, and the real backend endpoint it proxies to is already gated by `require_module_enabled` for that one resource, 404ing exactly like any other not-found/no-access case `_call_backend` already translates into a clear tool error — the same per-call model every existing tool already relies on.

The second exposed a genuine, previously-unresolved gap: it was never decided whether an org-level module tool (one not scoped to a single project, e.g. listing an organisation's compliance standards) takes an implicit "current org," tries to aggregate across every org the caller belongs to, or requires an explicit org. Checked this app's own existing REST convention directly (`backend/app/routers/orgs.py`'s report-template endpoints, `POST/GET/PUT/DELETE /{organization_id}/report-templates`) rather than guessing — every org-scoped resource in this codebase is addressed as `/{organization_id}/...`, never org-less or aggregate. Resolved by requiring `organization_id` (or `project_id`, for project-scoped tools) as a mandatory parameter on every module tool, mirroring both that REST convention and the existing hand-written tools' own shape (`get_project(project_id)`, `list_requirements(project_id)` always name one specific resource). This also fixed a related error in the addendum's own earlier example: a `path_template` of `/api/v1/modules/compliance/standards/{standard_id}` (no organisation in the path) was inconsistent with the app's actual convention and has been corrected to `/api/v1/orgs/{organization_id}/modules/compliance/standards/{standard_id}`.

Consequence: a user in Org A (module enabled) and Org B (module disabled) calls the same tool with `organization_id=A` and `organization_id=B` and gets correct, independent results from each — no special multi-org logic needed anywhere, since access is always resolved against the one org/project actually named in a given call. An AI wanting to enumerate across a caller's orgs composes this itself (call the existing `list_organizations()` tool, then call module tools per org of interest) rather than `mcp-server` or the manifest mechanism trying to do that aggregation — consistent with V1's declarative-single-REST-call scope boundary, and with how MCP tool composition normally works (client-orchestrated, not server-side). The manifest itself remains deliberately unpersonalized: a module's tools are listed for every session regardless of whether any of that caller's orgs actually have the module enabled, exactly like `list_projects` is listed today for a caller with zero project access anywhere.

`docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s Phase 4 gained an explicit "Org/project scoping" subsection recording this, and every compliance tool declared in Phases 6–9 now shows its required `organization_id`/`project_id` parameter explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

### Files changed

`docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (updated: packaging clarified, Phase 1/4 hardened, new "SOC2 / Security Planning" section added, org/project scoping fixed); `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module plan, Phase 0: server-level RBAC extension (2026-09-04)

First implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` — the module system's foundational RBAC extension: a new `ServerRole` enum, a `UserServerRole` grant table, a `require_server_role` dependency, and `ServerSettings.default_module_entitlement_policy`, plus the frontend role-display consolidation the plan's design history flagged as its single most-corrected point.

**Backend.** `ServerRole` (`app.models.enums`): `SERVER_ADMIN`, `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR`. `User.is_server_admin` is untouched, exactly as the plan specified — `SERVER_ADMIN` exists in the enum for composition/reference only and is never written as a `UserServerRole` row; the new grant endpoint (`POST /system/users/{id}/server-roles`) rejects a `role: "server_admin"` payload with 400, so there is no path to a second, driftable source of truth for that tier. Only `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR` is ever actually granted. `UserServerRole` lives in a new `app/models/server_role.py` module rather than being folded into `models/organization.py` (where `UserOrgRole` lives) — this is genuinely server-wide infrastructure, not an organisation concept, so it gets its own file rather than borrowing org's. Migration `0023_server_roles.py` adds the `server_roles` table and `server_settings.default_module_entitlement_policy` (`ModuleEntitlementPolicy`: `open`/`closed`, default `open`) in one pass, no backfill (additive only, per the plan).

`services/rbac.py::require_server_role(*allowed: ServerRole)` mirrors `require_org_role`'s shape and composes with `is_server_admin` exactly as specified: a genuine server admin always passes regardless of which roles were requested, the same "higher tier implies narrower ones" principle `require_org_role` callers already rely on for `ORG_ADMIN` — and the one Phase 2's `require_module_role` will extend to module-contributed roles. No PAT carve-out was added (unlike `require_server_admin`'s explicit PAT rejection) since nothing reachable through this dependency yet accepts a PAT at all; flagged in the dependency's own docstring to revisit if that changes.

New endpoints in `routers/system.py`: `POST`/`DELETE /system/users/{id}/server-roles[/{role}]` (grant/revoke, `require_server_admin`-only — a narrower role can never grant itself or others a role, mirroring `assign_org_role`'s own `ORG_ADMIN`-only gating for the same reason) and `GET`/`PUT /system/module-entitlement-policy` (`require_server_role(MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR)` — the one settings surface this phase actually gates with the new role rather than requiring full server-admin). `SystemUserOut` gained `is_module_administrator`. Both new mutation paths audit-log via `services/audit.py::log_event` (`entity_type="user_server_role"` / `"system"`), per this repo's standing SOC 2 logging requirement.

**Frontend.** `ServerManagementPage.tsx`'s `AccessReviewTab` roster gained a "Server roles" `MultiSelectDropdown` column (options: Server admin, Module administrator), replacing the old grant/revoke `ActionMenu` items — the exact `DirectoryTable` + `MultiSelectDropdown` combination the plan's design history calls out as the single most-corrected point across four planning rounds, now applied to server roles the same way `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s Users table already applies it to org roles. One deliberate deviation from that precedent, called out in the plan itself: unlike Org Admin's roles column (which toggles directly, no confirmation), toggling either checkbox here still goes through the existing Tier-1 `ConfirmDialog` this tab already used for grant/revoke server admin — granting cross-tenant power warrants the extra step even though granting an org role doesn't. `SERVER_ROLE_LABEL` added to `api/types.ts` alongside the existing `ORG_ROLE_LABEL`/`PROJECT_ROLE_LABEL` maps, per the style guide's label-map rule.

**Incidental fixes found while touching this code (fixed now, not deferred, per this repo's standing rule):**
1. The old `ActionMenu`'s three items (deactivate/reactivate, ban/unban, grant/revoke server admin) were all wrapped in one `{!u.has_org_membership && (...)}` guard — meaning grant/revoke server admin was only ever reachable through this UI for org-less accounts, contradicting this feature's own prior decisions-log entry ("Per-row actions adapt to what's actually valid for that user: Deactivate/Reactivate for org-less accounts, Grant/Revoke server admin for everyone"). Moving grant/revoke into the new column (rendered unconditionally for every row) fixes this as a side effect; the remaining `ActionMenu` (deactivate/ban only) keeps the org-less-only gate, which is correct for those two.
2. The old standalone "Server admin" badge became redundant once the new dropdown's own closed-state summary text started showing the same fact for a checked role — removed rather than left duplicating (a Storybook interaction test caught the resulting ambiguous-text failure immediately, which is what surfaced this).

**Deliberately not built this phase**: no frontend surface for `default_module_entitlement_policy` — the plan's own Phase 0 spec only calls for the Server Roles column, and Phase 1's "Modules" admin UI (which shows entitlement/enablement together) is the natural, non-redundant home for a control over this setting; the backend endpoint exists and is tested via the API now so Phase 1 has something to build against.

**Tests**: `backend/tests/test_module_system_rbac.py` (new) — grant/revoke round-trip, idempotent re-grant, no-op revoke of an ungranted role, `SERVER_ADMIN` rejected via the grant endpoint, org-admin cannot grant (403), a `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR` cannot grant to others (403, escalation-safe), entitlement-policy read/write via `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR` alone, `is_server_admin` composition with no explicit grant, plain member and org-admin-alone both rejected (403) on the policy endpoints. `ServerManagementPage.stories.tsx` updated (existing grant/revoke stories rewritten for the new dropdown flow, `AccessReviewGrantModuleAdministrator` added) rather than left broken — a `getByRole` casing mismatch during the rewrite (`SERVER_ROLE_LABEL` values are sentence-cased, so the generated accessible name is "Grant Server admin to X", matching `OrgAdminPage`'s own equivalent) and the badge-duplication failure above were both caught by actually running `vitest --project=storybook`, not just `tsc`. Full backend pytest suite and full frontend Storybook interaction suite (631 tests) run clean; `ruff check`, `tsc -b`, and `eslint` all clean on every changed file.

**A first full-suite run caught one real drift bug this phase introduced**: `UserServerRole.user_id` had `index=True` omitted from the model even though migration `0023` explicitly creates `ix_server_roles_user_id` on it (copying `ProjectGroupRole`'s pattern for its own FK index but missing the model-side declaration that has to accompany it) — `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py::test_models_and_migrations_have_not_drifted` caught the mismatch immediately. Fixed by adding `index=True` to the model column; re-ran the full suite to confirm the drift test now passes. The same full run's remaining 14 failures (`test_invites_and_external_users.py`, `test_oidc_provisioning.py`, `test_org_export_import.py`) are pre-existing and environmental, not caused by this phase: all are `aiosmtplib.errors.SMTPConnectError: Error connecting to mailhog` — the invite-email flow's SMTP host only resolves inside the `tests/container` Docker network, not from a pytest run against its exposed Postgres port from the host directly. Confirmed via `git stash` (this phase's changes stashed) that one of these same tests fails identically on unmodified code — not a regression.

### Files changed

`backend/app/models/enums.py`, `backend/app/models/server_role.py` (new), `backend/app/models/organization.py`, `backend/app/models/__init__.py`, `backend/alembic/versions/0023_server_roles.py` (new), `backend/app/services/rbac.py`, `backend/app/routers/system.py`, `backend/tests/test_module_system_rbac.py` (new); `frontend/src/api/types.ts`, `frontend/src/pages/ServerManagementPage.tsx`, `frontend/src/pages/ServerManagementPage.stories.tsx`, `frontend/src/i18n/strings.ts`; `docs/soc2/policies/access-control-policy.md` (new Authorization subsection, per the plan's SOC2 planning commitment); `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (Phase 0 marked complete); `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module plan, Phase 1: two-tier module gating + backend plugin loading (2026-09-04)

Second implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, built directly on Phase 0's `ServerRole`/`UserServerRole`/`default_module_entitlement_policy`: the module registry (`backend/app/modules/registry.py`), its two new gating tables (server-tier entitlement, org-tier enablement), the `require_org_module_enabled`/`require_project_module_enabled` RBAC dependencies, org-admin and server-tier management endpoints, and the `app.main` mount loop that will host every future module's router. No first-party module exists yet — this phase is pure infrastructure Phase 5 (Compliance) builds the first real module on top of.

**Backend.** Two new explicit-override-only tables, both unique on `(organization_id, module_key)`: `organization_module_entitlements` (`app.models.module.OrganizationModuleEntitlement`, `entitled: bool`) is the server-tier licensing lever; `organization_modules` (`app.models.module.OrganizationModuleEnablement`, `enabled: bool`) is the org-tier day-to-day switch. Migration `0024_module_registry.py` follows `0023`'s exact raw-SQL, `IF NOT EXISTS`-everywhere style, adding both tables plus their `organization_id` indexes, no backfill (additive only). `Settings` gained `allow_external_modules: bool = False` and `extra_modules_path: str | None = None` (`backend/app/config.py`), documented at the same depth as `oidc_allow_private_network_targets`.

`backend/app/modules/registry.py` (new package) is the merged-registry single source of truth: `ModuleDefinition` (frozen dataclass: `key, name, description, version, default_enabled, implemented, get_router`, plus `roles`/`frontend_manifest`/`mcp_tools` placeholders for Phases 2–4 so the shape won't need a breaking change later); `INSTALLED_MODULES` (static, empty until Phase 5); `_discover_entry_point_modules`/`_discover_path_modules` (third-party sources, per-entry try/except-and-log, never abort the whole discovery); `build_registry(force=)` (process-cached, merges all three sources, installed always wins on a key collision, logs every loaded module at `INFO` with key/version/source); `get_module_registry`/`get_module`; `is_module_entitled`/`is_module_enabled` (the exact "entitled AND (enablement row if present else registry default)" formula from the plan, tolerating a missing `ServerSettings` row the same way `services/branding.py` does). Critically, when `Settings.allow_external_modules` is `False`, `build_registry` does not call either discovery function at all — verified by a test that monkeypatches both to raise and confirms `build_registry(force=True)` doesn't.

`services/rbac.py` gained `require_org_module_enabled(module_key)`/`require_project_module_enabled(module_key)`, structural siblings of `require_org_role`/`require_project_view` (same `check_pat_scope`/`_require_org_active`/`_require_org_2fa` preamble), but returning **404, not 403**, when the module is disabled or the org isn't entitled — matching the plan's explicit requirement that disabled functionality must be indistinguishable from functionality that doesn't exist. `rbac.py` importing `app.modules.registry` (not the reverse) keeps the import graph acyclic, confirmed by a plain `python -c "import app.main"` and the full test suite.

New endpoints: `GET`/`PUT /orgs/{id}/modules[/{module_key}]` (`routers/orgs.py`, `require_org_role(ORG_ADMIN)`, schemas `OrgModuleOut`/`OrgModuleEnablementUpdate` in `schemas/org.py`) — the GET includes non-entitled modules rather than filtering them (the frontend greys them out); the PUT 403s with an explicit message if the org isn't entitled, upserts `OrganizationModuleEnablement`, and audit-logs as `module.enablement_updated`. `GET /system/modules`, `GET`/`PUT /system/orgs/{id}/module-entitlements[/{module_key}]` (`routers/system.py`, `require_server_role(MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR)`, inline `BaseModel` schemas matching that file's own convention) — the PUT upserts `OrganizationModuleEntitlement` and audit-logs as `module.entitlement_updated`; a code comment at the entitlement-revoke path explains why no cascade-delete of a stale enablement row is needed (the AND in `is_module_enabled` already makes it inert). `backend/app/main.py` now builds the registry and mounts every module's `get_router()` in a loop after the existing router includes — mounts nothing today, by design.

**Frontend.** `OrgAdminPage.tsx` gained a new top-level "Modules" resource-menu group: `OrgModule[]` state fetched inside the same try/catch-403-and-hide-section block `advanced`/`sso`/`scim` already use, a `toggleModuleEnabled` function following the immediate-PUT-then-patch-local-state shape `grantOrgRole`/`revokeOrgRole` already established (not the buffered `saveAdvanced` form — a single toggle only ever changes its own row), and a small table reusing the existing shared `ToggleSwitch` component (checked out of `frontend/src/components/` before building anything new, per the style guide) rather than a new checkbox pattern. A non-entitled or not-yet-implemented module renders with its toggle disabled and its own explanatory hint text, never hidden. `OrgModule` added to `api/types.ts`; new `orgAdmin.modules*`/`groupModules` string keys in `i18n/strings.ts`.

**SOC 2 identify → verify → remediate pass** (per the plan's explicit Phase 1 commitment, `change-management-and-secure-development-policy.md`'s practice for security-sensitive changes): **Identified** — plugin loading is a genuinely new code-loading trust boundary: `_discover_entry_point_modules`/`_discover_path_modules` can import and execute arbitrary third-party code discovered via `importlib.metadata`/a filesystem scan, and `docs/soc2/trust-services-criteria-mapping.md`'s CC6.8 gap ("no automated dependency/container vulnerability scanning") already existed before this raised the stakes of it. **Verified** — three concrete mechanisms bound the risk, each covered by a test: (1) `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` defaults `False` and, when off, the discovery functions are never even called (not just filtered), confirmed by `test_allow_external_modules_false_never_calls_discovery_functions` monkeypatching both to raise; (2) `is_module_enabled`'s entitlement-AND-enablement logic means an org admin can never self-enable a module their organisation isn't server-tier entitled to, confirmed by `test_org_admin_cannot_enable_a_non_entitled_module`; (3) `require_org_module_enabled`/`require_project_module_enabled` return 404 rather than 403 on a disabled/non-entitled module, confirmed by four dedicated dependency tests — a caller can't distinguish "disabled" from "never existed," so no information about server-tier entitlement leaks through the error shape. **Remediated/documented** — `docs/soc2/policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md` gained policy point 7 (installed modules are a code-execution-inside-the-boundary risk, distinct from a subprocessor; version-pinning and pre-install due diligence required) and a new Known Gaps entry (no automated vetting of installed modules yet, cross-referencing CC6.8); `trust-services-criteria-mapping.md`'s CC6.8 row gained a note that the `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` gate is a deliberate mitigation layered on the still-open gap, without marking that gap closed.

**Incidental documentation drift found and fixed while updating `docs/solution-architecture.md` for this phase (fixed now, not deferred):** Phase 0's own `server_roles` table/`UserServerRole` model had never been added to that document's identity ER diagram or its exhaustive table list — a real, if narrow, instance of the exact drift class that document's own "Database structure" section already calls out twice from earlier phases. Added alongside this phase's own two new tables rather than left as a second, unrelated gap; total table count corrected 49 → 52 (one for the Phase 0 gap, two for this phase's own tables).

**Tests**: `backend/tests/test_module_registry.py` (new, 24 tests) — all four entitlement/enablement combinations (direct function calls and through `GET /orgs/{id}/modules`); `require_org_module_enabled`/`require_project_module_enabled` 404 behaviour (unregistered module, disabled, not-entitled, and the passing case) via direct dependency invocation against a `_FakeRequest` stand-in (simpler and more targeted than wiring a live fixture router into the shared session-scoped `app` fixture, and avoids mutating that shared app object at all); registry merge logic (entry-point module included/excluded by `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`, installed-always-wins on key collision); the "discovery functions never called when the flag is off" guarantee; org-admin endpoint 403s, the entitlement-blocks-enablement 403, and the audit-log write; server-tier endpoint gating by `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR`/`SERVER_ADMIN` and 404s for unknown org/module. A `fake_module` pytest fixture registers and tears down a fixture `ModuleDefinition` in `INSTALLED_MODULES` per test (rebuilding the registry cache in setup and teardown) so tests remain order-independent per this repo's standing rule. Frontend: `OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx` gained four new stories (`ModulesSectionEmptyState`, `ModulesSectionToggleEntitledModule`, `ModulesSectionNonEntitledModuleIsGreyedOut`, `ModulesSectionNotYetImplementedModuleIsDisabled`) — adding the new `/modules` fetch into `reload()` required updating **two** separate mock `api.get` implementations in that stories file (`mockOrgAdminApis` and the standalone `mockProjectsWorkflowWithOneProject`), the second found only by running the full existing story suite and seeing unhandled-rejection noise from stories that don't use the first mock at all. A new Playwright spec (`tests/playwright/tests/e2e-workflows/org-admin-modules.spec.ts`) covers the section loading and showing the empty state for an org admin — deliberately not a full toggle-interaction test, since the real module registry has zero entries until Phase 5 and fabricating a fake production module package just to test the UI is explicitly against this repo's testing conventions; the spec's own docstring explains this and points at the Storybook stories for the toggle-interaction coverage instead.

Commands actually run, all clean: `ruff check .` (backend, all touched files), `python -c "from app.main import app"` (import/circularity smoke test), `pytest tests/test_module_registry.py` (24 passed) and the full backend suite (784 passed; the same 14 pre-existing `aiosmtplib`/mailhog-hostname-resolution failures Phase 0's entry above already documents as environmental, not caused by either phase — re-confirmed here by re-running those exact tests inside the `tests/container` Docker network, where they pass), `tsc -b` and `eslint .` (frontend, clean), `vitest run --project=storybook` (full suite, 635 passed including the 4 new Modules stories). No mypy/pyright config exists in this repository (`backend/pyproject.toml` has no such section), so no separate type-checker step applies beyond `ruff`'s own type-adjacent lints. No backend model/schema change needed in either seed script (`seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py`): the two new tables are override-only with sensible zero-row defaults, and there are zero implemented modules to demonstrate until Phase 5.

### Files changed

`backend/app/models/module.py` (new), `backend/app/models/__init__.py`, `backend/alembic/versions/0024_module_registry.py` (new), `backend/app/config.py`, `backend/app/modules/__init__.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/registry.py` (new), `backend/app/services/rbac.py`, `backend/app/schemas/org.py`, `backend/app/routers/orgs.py`, `backend/app/routers/system.py`, `backend/app/main.py`, `backend/tests/test_module_registry.py` (new); `frontend/src/api/types.ts`, `frontend/src/pages/OrgAdminPage.tsx`, `frontend/src/pages/OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx`, `frontend/src/i18n/strings.ts`; `tests/playwright/tests/e2e-workflows/org-admin-modules.spec.ts` (new); `docs/solution-architecture.md` (new "Modular Feature System" subsection, ER diagram/table-list updates including the Phase 0 drift fix); `docs/soc2/policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md` (new policy point 7, new Known Gaps entry); `docs/soc2/trust-services-criteria-mapping.md` (CC6.8 mitigation note); `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (Phase 1 marked complete); `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module plan, Phase 2: module-contributed RBAC (2026-09-05)

Third implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, built directly on Phase 0's `ServerRole`/`require_server_role` and Phase 1's registry/gating tables: lets a module declare its own named roles (e.g. a future Compliance module's `compliance_manager`/`compliance_officer`) without extending the core `OrgRole`/`ProjectRole` enums — the plan's own reversal of an earlier draft that would have hardcoded Compliance's roles onto those enums. Reuses `DirectoryTable` + `MultiSelectDropdown` for the frontend surface, per this plan's single most-corrected design-history point (already applied to server roles in Phase 0).

**Backend.** `app.modules.registry.ModuleRoleDefinition` (new frozen dataclass: `role_key, name, description, scope` where `scope: Literal["org", "project"]`) is what a module's `ModuleDefinition.roles` tuple now actually holds — that field's type hint changed from `tuple` to `tuple[ModuleRoleDefinition, ...]`, and its stale "placeholder... left as an empty tuple until Phase 2" docstring sentence was corrected. Two new tables, both in a new `backend/app/models/module_role.py`: `module_role_definitions` (`ModuleRoleDefinitionRow`) is a deliberately **append-only** database mirror of every role the registry has ever declared — `app.modules.registry.sync_module_role_definitions` upserts it on `(module_key, role_key)` at every process start (called from `app.main`'s `lifespan`, right after `run_bootstrap`), matching this plan's own "don't silently drop historical display data" philosophy (cited from Phase 8's evidence-revalidation note) so a grant's display name stays resolvable even if its module is later uninstalled; `user_module_roles` (`UserModuleRole`) is the actual grant table, `organization_id` always set (even for a project-scoped grant, via the project's own organisation) and `project_id` nullable, set only for project-scoped grants. Neither `module_key` nor `role_key` is a foreign key anywhere, for the same "defined in code, not by a database row" reason `OrganizationModuleEntitlement.module_key` already documents. Migration `0025_module_roles.py` follows `0023`/`0024`'s exact raw-SQL, `IF NOT EXISTS`-everywhere style, both tables plus `ix_user_module_roles_user_id`/`ix_user_module_roles_organization_id`, no backfill.

`app.modules.registry.list_enabled_module_roles(db, organization_id, scope)` is the one function every module-role read path funnels through: it yields `(module_key, ModuleRoleDefinition)` for every role of the given scope declared by a module that is *currently effectively enabled* for that organisation — the single place that turns "registered" into "actually offered," reused by both new `GET .../module-roles` endpoints, both new `POST .../module-roles` endpoints' 400 validation, and both `list_org_users`/`get_effective_members`'s own enabled-modules-only filtering of already-held grants.

`services/rbac.py` gained `require_module_role(module_key, role_key)` — a dependency **factory** (called at router-definition time, matching every other `require_*` factory in this file) that resolves the role's declared `scope` immediately by looking it up in the live registry, raising `ValueError` at construction time if the module or role isn't registered (a code-time contract violation, not a request-time 500). The returned dependency is shaped exactly like `require_org_module_enabled`'s/`require_project_module_enabled`'s own inner dependency (same 404-not-403 on a disabled/non-entitled module), then composes: `is_server_admin` always passes; `OrgRole.ORG_ADMIN` (org scope) or `ProjectRole.PROJECT_MANAGER` (project scope) passes with zero grants; otherwise a matching `UserModuleRole` row (`_has_module_role_grant`) is required. This is generic infrastructure with no real caller yet — same position `require_org_module_enabled`/`require_project_module_enabled` were left in after Phase 1 — proven here only against `test_module_contributed_roles.py`'s fixture module.

New endpoints, mirroring `assign_org_role`/`assign_project_role`'s existing idempotent-grant/no-op-revoke/audit-logged shape exactly: `GET /orgs/{id}/module-roles` (`require_org_role(ORG_ADMIN, PROJECT_CREATOR, MEMBER)`, same bar as `list_org_users`), `POST`/`DELETE /orgs/{id}/users/{user_id}/module-roles[/{module_key}/{role_key}]` (`require_org_role(ORG_ADMIN)`); `GET /projects/{id}/module-roles` (`require_project_view_or_manage`), `POST`/`DELETE /projects/{id}/members/{user_id}/module-roles[/{module_key}/{role_key}]` (`require_project_manage`). Both POST endpoints 400 if `(module_key, role_key)` doesn't name a real role of the right scope on a currently-enabled module (via `list_enabled_module_roles`), which is what makes a disabled module's roles ungrantable and catches a typo'd key in one check. `OrgUserOut.module_roles`/`EffectiveMemberOut.module_roles` (both `list[ModuleRoleGrantOut]`) are populated by `list_org_users`/`get_effective_members` respectively, filtered to currently-enabled modules only — a grant for a since-disabled module is simply omitted from the response, never deleted from `user_module_roles`.

**Frontend.** `ModuleRoleDefinition`/`ModuleRoleGrant` added to `api/types.ts`; `OrgUser.module_roles`/`EffectiveMember.module_roles` extended onto the existing types. `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s Users table Roles column `MultiSelectDropdown` now appends one option per org-scoped available module role (fetched alongside `modules` in the same `reload()` block) — `value: "${module_key}:${role_key}"`, `label: "${d.name} (${moduleDisplayNameFor(d.module_key)})"` matching the plan's own worked example ("Compliance Officer (Compliance)"), backed by new `grantModuleRole`/`revokeModuleRole` functions mirroring `grantOrgRole`/`revokeOrgRole`'s exact single-row local-state-patch shape (not a full `reload()`). `ProjectMembersTable.tsx` gained two new props, `availableModuleRoles`/`onToggleModuleRole` — its Role column merges in one option per entry, checked from the member's own `module_roles`, **never subjected to the `purelyDirect`/last-manager disabling logic** the four core-role options get, since module roles are direct-grant-only with no inherited-source state to guard against. Both call sites (`OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s "manage users" modal, `ProjectAdminPage.tsx`'s own Members section) now fetch `GET .../module-roles` and wire the two new props through — the modal fetches it per-project on open (a different project can belong to a different org, hence a different enabled-module set), `ProjectAdminPage.tsx` fetches it once in its own `reload()`.

**Deliberately not built**: no `MODULE_ROLE_LABEL`-style frontend label map — `ModuleRoleDefinition.name`/`description` are already human-readable data returned by the API (set server-side by the module's own author), not a frontend-known closed enum being rendered from a raw wire value, so this repo's label-map rule (CLAUDE.md, style guide Principle 12) doesn't apply the way it does to `OrgRole`/`ProjectRole`; `d.name` is rendered directly. Explicitly confirmed as a deliberate reading of that rule, not a miss.

**Judgment calls the plan's own spec left open, recorded here so a future session doesn't re-derive them:**
- `ModuleRoleGrantOut` (`{module_key, role_key}`) and `ModuleRoleDefinitionOut` (`{module_key, role_key, name, description}`) both landed in `schemas/org.py`, imported into `schemas/project.py` from there — the reverse direction of the existing precedent `orgs.py` already set by importing `MoveDirection` from `schemas/project.py`. No new `schemas/module_role.py` was warranted: Phase 1's own notes already established this codebase only adds a new shared-schemas module when a phase's needs don't fit an existing file's convention, and reusing the existing cross-import precedent covers this.
- The project-scoped read endpoint's gate (`GET /projects/{id}/module-roles`) is `require_project_view_or_manage` — confirmed against that dependency's own docstring and `list_project_groups`'s identical gate, both existing specifically for endpoints exposing role/group *structure* rather than requirement/change-request *content*.
- `ModuleRoleDefinitionRow.description` is `Text`, not a bounded `String(n)` — matching this codebase's existing convention for other free-text description columns (`RequirementAction.description`, `ChangeRequestTask.description`), none of which pick an arbitrary character cap.
- Grant notification: both `assign_org_module_role`/`assign_project_module_role` send a `NotificationType.PERMISSION_GRANTED` notification, mirroring `assign_org_role`/`assign_project_role`'s own notification exactly (title/body adapted to name the module role). The plan flagged this as optional ("if trivial to mirror"); it was, so it's included for parity — a module-role grant is not silently unnotified next to an equivalent core-role grant.
- `ProjectMembersTable.tsx` renders a module-role option's `label` as `d.name` alone (no owning-module-name suffix), unlike `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s parenthetical treatment — the spec's own worked example was for the org-admin surface only; reproducing it here would need a second prop purely for a disambiguation need no module with roles exists yet to exercise. Revisit if a future module's role names collide within one project's dropdown.
- `ProjectMembersTable.tsx`'s existing "Remove all access" action was left untouched — it still only loops the member's core-role `sources`, not their module-role grants. Not called out in the spec; flagged here rather than left undiscoverable, since folding module-role revocation into an already-shipped action would be a behaviour change the spec didn't ask for.

**Tests**: `backend/tests/test_module_contributed_roles.py` (new, 15 tests, separate from `test_module_system_rbac.py` per Phase 0's own stated reasoning for keeping module-system-infrastructure tests out of feature-specific files) — org- and project-scoped grant/revoke idempotency plus audit logging; `require_module_role` composition at both scopes (server admin passes with zero grants, `ORG_ADMIN`/`PROJECT_MANAGER` passes with zero grants, a user holding only the specific grant passes, a plain member/project-member with none of those is refused); `require_module_role` raising `ValueError` at construction for an unknown module or role; 404-not-403 when the module is disabled, even for an org admin/server admin; a disabled module's role disappearing from both `GET .../module-roles` and `list_org_users`'s `module_roles` field while the underlying `UserModuleRole` row still exists (re-enabling brings it back — a filter, not a deletion); 400 on an unknown role key, a wrong-scope role posted to either endpoint, and a disabled module's role; `sync_module_role_definitions` upserting an existing row's `name`/`description` in place (not duplicating) and never deleting a row for a module removed from the live registry. A `fake_module` fixture mirrors `test_module_registry.py`'s own mechanics exactly (mutate `INSTALLED_MODULES` in place, `build_registry(force=True)`, always tear down), registering two fixture roles (one org-scoped, one project-scoped) and calling `sync_module_role_definitions` once so `module_role_definitions` rows exist for it. Extending both stories files' mocked `api.get` implementations to handle the new `/module-roles` paths (in some cases **two** separate mock functions per file, the same class of miss Phase 1's own entry above already flagged) surfaced five unhandled-promise-rejection failures only when the *full* story suite was run, not the individual new stories — fixed by adding the branch to every mock implementation that could reach `reload()`, confirmed clean by re-running each affected file's full suite afterward. ## Compliance module plan, Phase 3: frontend module integration, two-tier (2026-09-05)

Fourth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`: gives `ModuleDefinition.frontend_manifest` its real shape and builds the two-tier frontend integration model the design history's final correction required — "third-party modules should be able to use core components... so their interfaces are consistent with the main UI." Tier A ("installed") is the primary path a first-party or npm-installed module uses, compiled directly into this bundle with full native shared-component reuse; Tier B ("remote") is a sandboxed `<iframe>` plus a Host UI Bridge for a genuinely dynamic, not-installed module, relaying real shared chrome over `postMessage` rather than reimplementing it. No actual module (first-party or third-party) ships in this phase — Compliance itself doesn't land until Phase 5+/12 — so every piece here is proven against fixture modules, the same position Phase 1/2 left their own infrastructure in.

**Backend.** `app.modules.registry.ModuleFrontendManifest` (new frozen dataclass: `tier: Literal["installed", "remote"]`, `nav_label`, `nav_path`, `frame_url: str | None`) is what `ModuleDefinition.frontend_manifest`'s type changed from `object | None` to — `__post_init__` enforces `frame_url` is set if and only if `tier == "remote"`. `app.modules.registry.get_frontend_manifest(module_key)` is the one function every read path funnels through: for a `"remote"` manifest, it cross-checks `frame_url`'s origin against the new `Settings.module_frame_allowed_origins` (env `MODULE_FRAME_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`, comma-separated, empty/`frame-src 'none'` by default — mirrors `cors_origins`' shape for the opposite direction) and returns `None` (logged at `WARNING`) if it falls outside, rather than trusting the module's own declaration — the same "verify mechanically" principle Phase 4's design already commits to for MCP tools, applied here to a different field ahead of that phase landing. `main.py`'s `security_headers_middleware` now builds `Content-Security-Policy: frame-src` from that same setting on every response (`'none'` by default) — a second, independent, browser-enforced backstop alongside the registry-level check.

**Tier B token minting and scoping.** `app.security.create_module_frame_token(module_key, organization_id, user_id, project_id=None)`/`decode_module_frame_token` mint/verify a 15-minute JWT (`purpose: "module_frame"`) scoped to exactly one module/org/(optionally)project/user tuple, mirroring `create_oidc_state_token`'s multi-claim shape. `POST /orgs/{organization_id}/modules/{module_key}/frame-token` (`routers/orgs.py`) and `POST /projects/{project_id}/modules/{module_key}/frame-token` (`routers/projects.py`) mint these, gated by two new `services/rbac.py` dependencies, `require_org_module_enabled_dynamic`/`require_project_module_enabled_dynamic` — plain-function siblings of the existing `require_org_module_enabled(module_key)`/`require_project_module_enabled(module_key)` *factories*, needed because a generic minting endpoint can't fix `module_key` as a closure constant at router-definition time the way a real module's own router does. Both depend on plain `get_current_user`, never a module-frame-accepting one, so an iframe's own already-scoped token can never mint itself a different one.

The harder design question — making the minted token actually "checked by `require_module_enabled`/`require_module_role` exactly like any other request," per the plan's own text — turned on one fact confirmed by reading `deps.py` before writing any code: `_resolve_user_from_token` already rejects any bearer token whose `purpose` isn't `"access"` (the same mechanism that already rejects a replayed 2FA challenge token), so a module-frame token is *already* mechanically unusable against `get_current_user` and therefore every endpoint outside the module-gating dependencies, with no new code needed for that half. A new `deps.get_current_user_or_module_frame(module_key)` factory — used only inside `require_org_module_enabled`/`require_project_module_enabled`/`require_module_role` — decodes either a normal token (unchanged behaviour) or a module-frame token scoped to exactly that `module_key` (401 otherwise), stamping `request.state.module_frame_scope` only in the latter case. A new `rbac._enforce_module_frame_scope(request, organization_id=, project_id=)` helper, called as the *first* check in all three dependencies' bodies — before `check_pat_scope`, before `is_server_admin`/`ORG_ADMIN`/`PROJECT_MANAGER` bypasses — 403s if a present `module_frame_scope`'s own `organization_id`/`project_id` claim doesn't match the specific resource this request names. This ordering is the load-bearing decision: a module-frame token minted for org A must 403 against org B's endpoints *even for a server admin's own token*, since the whole point of handing a remote module a narrower token is that it must not inherit the real user's broader access just because the request happens to be authenticated as that user underneath.

**Frontend.** `frontend/src/modules/registry.ts` (new) exports `installedModules: TierAModuleDefinition[]` (empty — Phase 12 registers Compliance here) and `getInstalledModule(key)`; `frontend/src/modules/types.ts` (new) declares the `TierAModuleDefinition`/`TierAModuleRoute` shapes. `frontend/src/modules/buildModuleRoutes.tsx` (new — split out of `App.tsx` itself to avoid a Fast Refresh lint break from mixing component/non-component exports in one file) builds one `<Route>` per currently-enabled module: a Tier A module's own registered routes, or a generic `<Route element={<ModuleFrame .../>}>` for a Tier B one; `App.tsx`'s `ProtectedRoutes` spreads its output directly into `<Routes>`'s children (React Router's `createRoutesFromChildren` only recognises literal `<Route>`/`<Fragment>` elements in that tree — an early draft wrapped the array in a rendered component instead, which `<Routes>` silently doesn't see into; caught before it shipped). `frontend/src/components/ModuleFrame.tsx` (new) is the Tier B host: mints a token on mount (`POST .../frame-token`), sends `init` once the iframe's `load` fires, and relays `toast`/`confirm` messages from the iframe onto the real `useToast()`/`ConfirmDialog` — every message checked both ways against the iframe's own declared origin, never `"*"`. It reads the current resolved theme directly off `document.documentElement`'s `data-theme` attribute rather than via `useTheme()`/`ThemeContext` — `ThemeProvider` already stamps the *resolved* value there for CSS to cascade from, so this is equivalent without pulling in a context dependency, and kept its own Storybook story from needing a provider wrapper no other story in this codebase has needed yet. `frontend/src/hooks/useProjectEnabledModules.ts` (new) fetches the new `GET /projects/{project_id}/enabled-modules` endpoint (`ModuleNavEntryOut[]`) and is called independently by `Layout.tsx` (nav rendering) and `App.tsx` (route splicing) rather than through a shared context provider — mirrors `BrandingContext`/`TerminologyContext`'s existing "each concern fetches its own project-derived data" convention rather than introducing a new provider-tree layer for a small, cheap GET. `Layout.tsx`'s project-scoped nav group gains one `NavRailLink` per enabled module with a usable manifest, rendered generically (a placeholder `Wrench` icon, since no per-module icon concept exists yet).

`GET /projects/{project_id}/enabled-modules` was a new endpoint, not a reuse of the existing `GET /orgs/{id}/modules` — that one is `OrgRole.ORG_ADMIN`-gated and deliberately includes non-entitled/disabled modules greyed out for the admin bookkeeping view, the wrong shape and the wrong gate for "what should any project member's nav rail show." It's gated `require_project_view_or_manage`, the same "structure, not content" bar Phase 2 already established for `GET /projects/{id}/module-roles`. `OrgModuleOut` (the admin view) also gained a `frontend_manifest` field, computed the same way via `get_frontend_manifest`, so the two views stay consistent.

**Judgment calls the plan's own spec left open:**
- Sandbox flags: `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms"` — `allow-same-origin` scopes to the iframe's own distinct (always cross-origin, by construction) origin, needed for the module's own script/storage/fetch to function normally; not a same-origin-escape risk since the frame is never same-origin with the host to begin with.
- No shared context provider for enabled-modules state (see above) — a deliberate departure from a `ModulesProvider` design considered and rejected in favour of matching this codebase's existing per-concern-fetches-its-own-data convention.
- `docs/soc2/policies/access-control-policy.md`'s Authorization section item 4 gained a new paragraph (after this section's existing module-contributed-roles paragraph) documenting the module-frame-token mechanism as a fifth, narrower *authentication*-layer restriction — not a sixth RBAC scope — composing underneath the existing scopes rather than replacing any of them.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_module_frontend_integration.py` (new, 26 tests): `ModuleFrontendManifest.__post_init__` validation; `get_frontend_manifest`'s allowlist accept/reject (including "declares an origin allowlisted for a *different* module" and "no manifest at all" cases); CSP `frame-src` header defaults to `'none'` and reflects a configured allowlist; both frame-token minting endpoints (success, 404 on disabled/unregistered module, a module-frame token can't mint another); `get_current_user_or_module_frame`'s token resolution (valid token, wrong-module-key rejection, still accepts a normal access token); module-frame scope enforcement on `require_org_module_enabled`/`require_project_module_enabled`/`require_module_role` (mismatched org, mismatched project, an org-scoped token rejected against a project-scoped endpoint, a scope mismatch 403s even when constructed with a server-admin `current_user` — proving the ordering-before-bypass decision above actually holds); the two nav-facing endpoints. Full backend suite re-run exclusively (no concurrent DB-touching process, per this project's own documented wedge-avoidance practice): **839 passed, 0 failed, 3 warnings** (same pre-existing count as Phase 2's own baseline, no new ones) in 879s.

Frontend: `frontend/src/components/ModuleFrame.stories.tsx` (new, 5 stories) exercises the full Host UI Bridge contract — init/token-minting on load, toast relay, untrusted-origin messages ignored, both `ConfirmDialog` tiers' round trip (confirm and cancel) — by dispatching synthetic `MessageEvent`s at the rendered iframe's own `contentWindow` with a controlled `origin`, rather than depending on a real external origin loading inside the test browser. An early version used a genuinely cross-origin fixture `frameUrl`; the *first* story passed, but every subsequent one failed with a real `SecurityError` on `spyOn(...).mockRestore()` — the browser had, by then, actually completed (or attempted) cross-origin navigation, turning `contentWindow` into a inaccessible cross-origin proxy no test can redefine properties on. Fixed by making the story's fixture `frameUrl` same-origin to the Storybook test page itself (`window.location.origin`-based) — every assertion in these stories only depends on the `origin` *string* carried on each synthetic message, which is exercised identically either way, so this is a test-environment fix, not a narrowing of what's actually verified. `frontend/src/App.stories.tsx` (new, 2 stories, `TierARoutingHarness`) proves the Tier A mechanism end-to-end against a fixture module pushed into the real `installedModules` registry (module-scope, not per-test — mirrors this codebase's existing fixture-constant convention, and is harmless since no other story file reads `installedModules`) and rendered through the real, unmodified `buildModuleRoutes` — including that the fixture route's own component genuinely calls `useToast()` and a real toast appears, the concrete proof of "not a lookalike." `tsc -b --noEmit`, `eslint` (all touched files), and `npm run build` all clean; `vitest run --project=storybook` for every touched/new stories file individually clean (`ModuleFrame.stories.tsx` 5/5, `App.stories.tsx` 2/2, `OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx` re-run in full at 64/64 to confirm the `OrgModule.frontend_manifest` field addition didn't regress its existing fixtures).

**Not built, deliberately, consistent with Phase 1/2's own precedent:** no new Playwright spec. No real Tier A or Tier B module exists until Phase 12, so there is nothing in the actually-running app for a spec to click through beyond "the nav rail renders its existing entries with no crash" — already covered more directly, and more informatively, by the Storybook coverage above. Revisit once Phase 12 registers Compliance's own frontend module here.

## Compliance module plan, Phase 4: module-contributed MCP tools (2026-09-05)

Fifth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, and the last of the five module-system infrastructure phases (0–4) before Compliance itself (Phase 5+) becomes the first real module built on top of it: lets a module declare its own `mcp-server/` tools — `ModuleDefinition.mcp_tools`, a tuple of `McpToolDefinition` — proxied declaratively through `mcp-server`'s existing `_call_backend` pattern rather than a second implementation of it. Unlike Phases 0–3, this phase's own design was self-reviewed and hardened *during planning*, before any code existed (see the plan's own "SOC2 / Security Planning" section, addenda 2–3): three real gaps in the original design (self-declared `mutates`/`is_approval_action`, an unconstrained `path_template`, an unauthenticated boot-time manifest fetch) were found and fixed on paper first. Implementing exactly that already-hardened design is what this entry records — no new gap was found this time, which is itself the outcome of doing the identify→verify→remediate pass early rather than a sign the pass wasn't needed.

**Design continuity, not re-derivation.** `docs/modules.md` — a readable, example-driven module-authoring guide — was already written and merged into this repository ahead of this phase's implementation, and turned out to pin down exact, load-bearing details this phase needed: the `params` dict shape (`{"name", "type", "required", "in", "description"}`, with `"in"` rather than a more generic `"location"` key, and `"type": "uuid"` as a display hint rather than a strict JSON-Schema primitive), the literal function names `_register_declarative_tool`/`_call_backend`, and the ~10-minute manifest cache window. This phase's implementation matches that document precisely rather than inventing an equivalent but differently-shaped API, since a future module author (including whoever builds Compliance itself in Phase 5+) will read `docs/modules.md`, not this decisions-log entry, to learn the contract.

**Backend.** `app.modules.registry.McpToolDefinition` (new frozen dataclass: `name, description, method, path_template, params: list[dict]`) is what `ModuleDefinition.mcp_tools` now actually holds — that field's type hint changed from a placeholder `tuple` to `tuple[McpToolDefinition, ...]`. `app.modules.registry.build_mcp_tool_manifest()` is the one function that turns a live registry's declarations into `ResolvedMcpTool` entries (`name, description, method, path_template, mutates, params`), re-deriving or verifying every security-relevant part rather than trusting the module's own declaration: `name` is always `f"{module.key}_{tool.name}"` regardless of what local name a module supplies; `mutates` is `method != "GET"`, nothing for a module to misdeclare; `path_template` must both start with the declaring module's own `get_router().prefix` and resolve to a real route on that same router with a matching method (looked up directly in that router's own `.routes`, keyed by `(path, method)`); and whether the resolved route is an approval action is read from that route's own `openapi_extra.get("x-approval-action")` (a new exported marker, `APPROVAL_ACTION_ROUTE_EXTRA`, for a module's own route decorators to spread in), never from the module's `McpToolDefinition`. Each of these checks fails closed and per-tool (excluded + logged at `WARNING`), never aborting the whole manifest for one bad declaration — extended one level further to a single malformed param dict inside an otherwise-valid tool, which is dropped on its own rather than disqualifying that tool. A key implementation finding, confirmed by direct experimentation before writing the real code rather than assumed: a FastAPI `APIRoute`'s `.path` is already the *full*, prefix-combined path the instant it's added to an `APIRouter(prefix=...)` — prefix combination happens at route-registration time on the router itself, not later at `app.include_router()` — so `build_mcp_tool_manifest()` needs no live `Request`/`app` reference at all; it reads everything it needs straight off `definition.get_router()`, whether or not that router has actually been mounted into the running app yet. `GET /api/v1/system/modules/mcp-tools` (`routers/system.py`, new `ModuleMcpToolOut` schema) returns this manifest, gated by plain `get_current_user` — deliberately no admin-role exemption or requirement, matching this phase's own hardening commitment that the fetch must be authenticated but the manifest itself is not privileged data (per-call access to whatever a listed tool actually proxies to is still fully enforced by that endpoint's own real gating dependency, exactly like an already-listed core tool such as `list_projects` today).

**`mcp-server`.** A new, clearly-bannered "Module-contributed tools" section in `server.py` (matching the existing write-mode section's own inline-not-split-file convention, consistent with this file's deliberate single-file-app design) adds: `_ModuleToolParam`/`_ModuleToolSpec` (parsed manifest entries), `_json_schema_for_params` (builds each tool's MCP `inputSchema` directly from its params — no separate validation layer, since real validation happens at the proxied backend endpoint, the single source of truth every other request already goes through), `_DeclarativeModuleTool` (a `fastmcp.tools.Tool` subclass whose `run()` builds one `_call_backend` call from its spec — path-location values are `urllib.parse.quote(..., safe="")`-encoded before substitution into `path_template`, *unconditionally*, since this server has no way to know ahead of time which declared params are UUIDs versus arbitrary strings, the same "encode by construction" reasoning `_get_org_login_info`'s existing `quote(slug, safe='')` already uses one section up), `_register_declarative_tool` (the literal name `docs/modules.md` already committed to), `_parse_module_tool_manifest`/`_fetch_module_tool_manifest` (network fetch, tolerant of a single malformed entry the same way the backend tolerates a malformed param), `_apply_module_tool_manifest` (diffs desired vs. currently-registered tools, calling `mcp.add_tool`/`mcp.local_provider.remove_tool` only for what actually changed), `_maybe_refresh_module_tools` (rate-limited to once per `MODULE_TOOLS_REFRESH_SECONDS`, default 600s, using whichever connecting session's own already-presented token is on hand — skipping the cycle cleanly, not erroring, if none is present or the backend is momentarily unreachable), and `ModuleToolsRefreshMiddleware` (a `fastmcp.server.middleware.Middleware` triggering that refresh on every `tools/list`/`tools/call`). A mutating tool is only ever included in what gets registered when this server's own `MCP_WRITES_ENABLED` is set, the same gate its hand-written write tools already use, applied generically rather than per-tool. No packaging change to `mcp-server`'s own Docker image was needed — every declarative tool is a plain HTTP proxy call, so a module's own Python code never runs in this process.

**Judgment calls the plan's own spec text left open, recorded here so a future session doesn't re-derive them:**
- `McpToolDefinition.params` is a plain `list[dict]`, not a nested dataclass — a deliberate match to `docs/modules.md`'s own already-published worked example rather than a "more type-safe" alternative this phase might otherwise have preferred; the params are display/JSON-Schema hints for an AI client, not something this codebase itself needs to validate structurally.
- The approval-action marker's literal `openapi_extra` key (`"x-approval-action"`) and its exported constant name (`APPROVAL_ACTION_ROUTE_EXTRA`) were not specified by either the plan or `docs/modules.md`, both of which describe the mechanism without naming the key. No existing route needed retrofitting with it — the path-prefix constraint means only a module's *own* router can ever be legally referenced by that module's own tool declarations, and no such router exists yet.
- `mcp.local_provider.remove_tool(name)` is used throughout, not the top-level `mcp.remove_tool(name)` — the installed, pinned `fastmcp==3.4.5` marks the latter `.. deprecated::` in favour of the former; per this repo's standing "fix the underlying code, don't suppress the warning" rule, the non-deprecated call is used directly rather than silencing the deprecation warning.
- `_apply_module_tool_manifest` diffs before registering, rather than unconditionally re-adding every desired tool on every refresh — confirmed by direct experimentation against the pinned `fastmcp` version that re-registering an existing tool name doesn't raise (despite `LocalProvider.__init__`'s own documented `on_duplicate: DuplicateBehavior = "error"` default; the server's actual runtime default falls through to "warn" and replaces) but does log a `WARNING` every time, which diffing avoids doing every 10-minute cycle for every unchanged module tool.
- No SOC 2 policy-document edits were made this phase (unlike Phases 0–2), and that absence is deliberate, not an oversight: this phase's own design-time hardening pass (recorded in the plan's "SOC2 / Security Planning" section, written before this phase's code) already anticipated and closed the gaps a request-time identify→verify→remediate pass would otherwise surface; there was nothing left to find and therefore nothing new to document as remediated.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_module_mcp_tools.py` (new, 11 tests) — a fixture module with a real `APIRouter` (three routes, one `openapi_extra`-marked as an approval action) proves every exclusion/inclusion path described above, plus that a module trying to pre-prefix its own local tool name still gets double-prefixed (no special-casing), that a module with `mcp_tools` declared but no router yields zero resolved tools, and the manifest endpoint's 401-with-no-token / 200-for-a-plain-non-admin-member gating. `mcp-server/tests/test_module_tools.py` (new, 12 tests, unit-style against a mocked backend response and a mocked `_call_backend` — no live backend needed, consistent with Phases 1–3's own "unit-test declarative infrastructure against a fixture, not a fabricated production module" precedent) — manifest parsing, tool registration/removal round-tripping through the real `mcp.list_tools()`, the `MCP_WRITES_ENABLED` gate, full param-mapping proof (including the URL-encoding of a deliberately hostile `"org/../evil"` path value, confirmed to arrive at the backend call as `org%2F..%2Fevil`, never escaping its intended path segment), a clean `ValueError`/`ToolError` on a missing required argument, no-op re-registration of an identical manifest, and the refresh-window rate-limiting (including the no-token-presented skip path). Both files run clean: the backend tests against a live `reqtrack_pytest_test` database, followed by an exclusive full-suite re-run (no other DB-touching process active, per this project's own documented wedge-avoidance practice) confirming no regression; the mcp-server tests against the exact pinned `fastmcp==3.4.5`/`httpx==0.28.1` in a throwaway venv, with the full `mcp-server/tests/` collection (36 tests) confirmed to still collect cleanly alongside the pre-existing, live-backend-only `test_server.py`. `ruff check` clean on every touched file in both components. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes were needed — this phase persists nothing new (`mcp_tools` is a pure code declaration, resolved fresh per manifest request), and there is still no first-party module with tools to demonstrate until Phase 5.
