## Compliance module plan, Phase 5: compliance data model, as a module (2026-09-05)

Sixth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, and the first phase of the Compliance Module itself (Phases 5-15) rather than the generic module-system infrastructure (Phases 0-4) it's built on: Compliance becomes the first real entry in `INSTALLED_MODULES`, proving out that infrastructure end-to-end for the first time rather than continuing to exercise it through fixture modules. This phase is data model only, per its own spec — `docs/Compliance_Module_Requirements.md` §2 (Standards), §5 (Requirements), §6 (Required Actions), §25 (Data Model Principles), §31 (Architectural Principles) — with no API surface (Phase 6) or MCP tools (also Phase 6) yet.

**Package layout.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/` is a new, self-contained package: `enums.py` (`ComplianceStandardVersionStatus`, plus `ComplianceStatus`/`ComplianceApplicability`/`ComplianceApprovalState` per the plan's own "New enums" instruction, none of the latter three yet referenced by any model), `models.py` (the five ORM models below), and `module.py` (`MODULE_DEFINITION`, this module's `ModuleDefinition`: `key="compliance"`, `default_enabled=True` per §1, `implemented=True`, `get_router()` returning `None`, `mcp_tools=()`, and two module-contributed roles — `compliance_manager` (org-scoped, §3) and `compliance_officer` (project-scoped, §11/§26) — via `ModuleDefinition.roles`, deliberately not new `OrgRole`/`ProjectRole` enum members, the specific correction Phase 2 exists to satisfy). Enums and models live under `app.modules.compliance`, not `app.models`/`app.models.enums`, keeping the module's own domain self-contained — the first time this plan's "as a module" principle has actually had a real module to apply it to.

**Data model.** Following §25's conceptual shape: `ComplianceStandard` (org-level identity row: `organization_id`, `reference`, `name`, `description`, `issuing_organisation`, `owner_id`, `creator_id`, `is_archived`/`archived_at`/`archived_by`) has `ComplianceStandardVersion` children (`version_number`, `version_label`, `status` — draft/published/retired, `effective_date`, `change_note`, `created_by`, `published_at`/`published_by`, `retired_at`/`retired_by`), which has `ComplianceRequirement` children (`parent_requirement_id` self-referential, `reference`, `name`, `description`, `reasoning`, `sort_order`, `created_by`), which has `ComplianceRequiredAction` children (`action_type_id`, `name`, `description`, `is_mandatory`, `sort_order`, `created_by`). `ComplianceActionTypeDefinition` (`organization_id`, `name`, `sort_order`) is a fifth, sibling table — an organisation-scoped extensible vocabulary `ComplianceRequiredAction.action_type_id` references. Migration `0026_compliance_data_model.py` creates all five (`compliance_action_type_definitions` first, since `compliance_required_actions` references it), following 0025's own `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`/raw-SQL convention exactly.

**Design decisions, not left implicit:**
- **`ComplianceStandard`/`ComplianceStandardVersion` reuse the `Requirement`/`RequirementVersion` identity-row-plus-versioned-children *shape* the plan's spec names, but deliberately not that pair's `valid_from`/`valid_to` temporal-supersession *semantics*.** A `RequirementVersion` superseded by a newer one becomes pure history; every `ComplianceStandardVersion` must stay independently live and assignable indefinitely, since different projects deliberately stay pinned to different past versions forever (§4's own worked example: Project A on v1.1, Project B on v1.0, both valid simultaneously). Versions are instead ordered/gated by `version_number` + `status`.
- **No ORM `relationship()` for `ComplianceRequirement.parent_requirement_id`** — mirrors `Project.parent_project_id`'s precedent (hierarchy traversal is a service-layer concern for a later phase to add when it actually needs to walk the tree) rather than `RequirementVersion`'s `relationship()`-backed pattern, which exists there to walk a single linear history, not an arbitrary-depth tree. `ComplianceStandard.versions`/`ComplianceStandardVersion.standard` *do* get a real `relationship(back_populates=...)` pair, since that's a plain (non-self-referential) one-to-many, the same shape `Requirement.versions` already uses.
- **`ComplianceRequiredAction` is a plain one-to-many from `ComplianceRequirement`**, not a many-to-many link table like `RequirementAction`/`RequirementActionLink` — §25's diagram places required actions directly under compliance requirements with no separate mapping table, and nothing in §6 asks for one required action to be reused verbatim across multiple requirements.
- **§6's "Status," "Assignee," "Due date," "Completion information," and "Evidence" fields were deliberately left off `ComplianceRequiredAction`** — per §25's diagram, those belong to "Required Action Assessments" (nested under "Project Compliance Requirements," i.e. Phase 7's per-project assessment of a required action), not this reusable definition. Putting project-specific state on the definition row would violate §31's "A Compliance Requirement must not contain the compliance state of a project" one level down from where the plan's own spec already applies it.
- **`ComplianceActionTypeDefinition` is organisation-scoped, not project-scoped**, resolving an ambiguity in the plan's own "project- or org-scoped vocabulary" phrasing: a required action's type is chosen within a Compliance Standard, itself an organisation-level, cross-project resource (§2), so its vocabulary is scoped the same way `ActionTypeDefinition` is scoped to whatever owns the actions it types (there, a project; here, an org).
- **§2's "Review schedule" and "Appropriate audit/history information" got no dedicated column** — the former is Phase 10's dedicated `ComplianceReview` entity (§17 covers both standards and project-compliance records with one mechanism; §25's diagram gives it its own entity, not a scalar field), the latter is `TimestampMixin` plus Phase 6's `services.audit.log_event` integration. §2's "Status" is satisfied by the existing `is_archived`/`archived_at`/`archived_by` convention, kept distinct from `ComplianceStandardVersion.status` (the lifecycle that actually needed a dedicated enum, §4).
- **No seed data** — `ComplianceActionTypeDefinition` ships empty (§6's "potential initial action types" land in Phase 15), matching module system Phase 1's own "empty, extensible tables ahead of any seed step" precedent. `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` untouched — no API exists yet to seed through.

**A genuine circular-import bug found and fixed before it shipped**, this phase's own identify→verify→remediate moment even though the plan's "SOC2 / Security Planning" section didn't flag Phase 5 as needing one (it isn't a new trust boundary): `app.modules.compliance.module` imports `ModuleDefinition`/`ModuleRoleDefinition` from `app.modules.registry` to construct `MODULE_DEFINITION`. The first draft had `registry.py` import that `MODULE_DEFINITION` straight back, at its own module scope, to populate `INSTALLED_MODULES` — a real circular import whose success depended entirely on which of the two modules a caller happened to import first. **Identified** by direct experimentation, not assumption: `python -c "import app.modules.compliance.module"` raised `ImportError: cannot import name 'MODULE_DEFINITION' from partially initialized module 'app.modules.compliance.module'` when that module was the first thing imported. **Fixed** by moving the wiring into `app/modules/__init__.py` instead: a package `__init__` is guaranteed by Python's import system to finish running before any of its own submodules can be imported by anyone, so it imports `app.modules.registry` to completion first and only then imports `compliance.module`, making the import order deterministic regardless of entry point. **Verified** directly both ways afterward (`import app.modules.compliance.module` first, and `import app.modules.registry` first) — both now succeed and produce an identically-populated registry.

**An unrelated, pre-existing documentation drift found and fixed while updating `docs/solution-architecture.md`'s "Database structure" list for this phase's own five new tables** (per this repo's standing "fix, don't defer, found issues" rule): that exhaustive table list had drifted to 52 while the schema actually had 54 pre-Phase-5 tables — Phase 2's own `module_role_definitions`/`user_module_roles` (already described in prose under "Modular Feature System" and present in that section's own ER diagram) had never actually been added to the list itself. Caught by cross-checking the list's stated count against a live migrated database's real table count (`sqlalchemy.inspect(...).get_table_names()`, minus `alembic_version`) rather than trusting the existing count. Fixed alongside adding this phase's own five tables (52 + 2 missing + 5 new = 59) and a new sixth ER diagram for the compliance data model, rather than left as a second, unrelated gap next to the fix this phase already needed to make — the same pattern the four corrections already recorded in that section's own parenthetical follow.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py` (new, 5 tests): module registration (registry entry present, `default_enabled`/`implemented` true, `get_router() is None`, `mcp_tools == ()`, both roles present with the right scopes); a full standard → version → parent/child requirement → required action round trip created directly via the ORM (no API surface exists yet) and reloaded from a fresh session to prove persistence, not just in-session object state; `ON DELETE CASCADE` from a deleted parent requirement down through its child requirement and that child's required action; the `(organization_id, reference)` uniqueness constraint on `compliance_standards`; and migration 0026's upgrade/downgrade round trip (downgrade to 0025, confirm all five tables gone, upgrade back to head, confirm all five recreated — always ending back at head in a `finally`, mirroring `test_project_group_role_migration.py`'s own pattern for a schema-mutating test in this suite's shared session-scoped database). `alembic/env.py` and `tests/conftest.py` each gained one `import app.modules.compliance.models  # noqa: F401` line so `Base.metadata` includes this phase's tables for autogenerate/`test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` — the "one model-import line per first-party module" Phase 1's own spec anticipated, landing here since Phase 1 had no first-party module yet. Run against a live `reqtrack_pytest_test` database: this file's 5 tests pass in isolation, and the full backend suite was re-run afterward with no other DB-touching process active to confirm no regression, `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` included (confirming the new migration and models agree with no drift). `ruff check` clean on every touched/new file.

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/__init__.py`, `backend/app/modules/registry.py`, `backend/app/modules/compliance/__init__.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/enums.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/models.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (new), `backend/alembic/versions/0026_compliance_data_model.py` (new), `backend/alembic/env.py`, `backend/tests/conftest.py`, `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py` (new); `docs/solution-architecture.md` (new "Compliance module — data model" paragraph, new ER diagram, "Database structure" table-count/category update plus the incidental Phase 2 drift fix), `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (Phase 5 marked complete, "Phase 5 notes" subsection added), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Module system follow-up: registry-driven `Base.metadata` auto-import (2026-09-05)

A small, user-requested follow-up to Phase 5, landed the same day: removes the last hand-maintained touch point Phase 1's own spec had flagged as "an acknowledged minimal and unavoidable touch point" — a hand-written `import app.modules.<key>.models` line in *both* `backend/alembic/env.py` and `backend/tests/conftest.py` for every first-party module that defines its own ORM models. Not a new phase in `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s numbered sequence (it doesn't touch product scope), so it's recorded here rather than as a phase entry.

**What changed.** `ModuleDefinition` (`app.modules.registry`) gains an optional `models_import_path: str | None` field — a dotted import path to a module's own models submodule (e.g. `"app.modules.compliance.models"`). A new `import_all_module_models()` iterates the live registry and calls `importlib.import_module(...)` on every declared path, logging and skipping (never aborting) one that fails to import — the same per-module fault isolation `_discover_entry_point_modules`/`_discover_path_modules` already apply elsewhere in this file. `backend/alembic/env.py` and `backend/tests/conftest.py` each now call this once, early, instead of carrying a hand-written import line per module; Compliance's own `MODULE_DEFINITION` gained `models_import_path="app.modules.compliance.models"` and its hand-written import lines in both files were removed. Verified end-to-end: a real `alembic upgrade head` run against a live database succeeds with the new `env.py`, and the full backend suite (including `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py`, which depends on `Base.metadata` actually containing Compliance's tables) passes unchanged.

**What this does *not* change — flagged explicitly rather than silently expanded, per this repo's standing policy on regressing a documented security posture.** The user's original ask was broader: a module should be "just placed in the correct folder" — including in a mounted Docker directory — "and everything then loads automatically," with no other edits needed. That phrasing, taken literally, would extend to a dropped-in module's own **database migration** running automatically too. This change deliberately does not do that, and the two are not the same kind of risk:

- Importing a Python model class is inert with respect to any real database — it only ever registers a table *shape* with SQLAlchemy's in-process `Base.metadata`. Nothing about a real schema changes as a result, and this now happens for any module already in the live registry regardless of whether it's a reviewed first-party module or (only if an operator has explicitly set `Settings.allow_external_modules`) an external one.
- Running a migration executes arbitrary SQL/DDL against the real production database with the application's own credentials. `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s Phase 1 spec already treats this as categorically different and explicitly out of scope: "Automatic third-party DB migrations are out of scope. Running arbitrary third-party SQL against a production database is itself a security-review-shaped question. Only first-party modules ship real Alembic migrations, added to the core chain by a reviewed PR." `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` already defaults to `false` specifically because of the CC6.8 gap (`docs/soc2/trust-services-criteria-mapping.md`: "no automated dependency/container vulnerability scanning exists") a plugin-loading mechanism raises the stakes of — extending that mechanism to also auto-apply a dropped-in module's own migration DDL would be a materially larger expansion of that same already-open gap, not an equivalent convenience improvement to the model-import side.

This was flagged to the user rather than implemented, per `CLAUDE.md`'s standing instruction not to introduce a change that regresses a control described in the adopted SOC 2 policies without surfacing it first — this isn't a regression yet (nothing changed on the migration-execution side), but implementing the literal ask without flagging it would have been. **Resolved same day**: the user chose to extend `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`'s existing scope to cover this, rather than leave it manual or remove the gate entirely — see the next entry.

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/registry.py` (`ModuleDefinition.models_import_path`, `import_all_module_models`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (`models_import_path` set), `backend/alembic/env.py`, `backend/tests/conftest.py`, `backend/tests/test_module_registry.py` (3 new tests), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Module system follow-up: `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`-gated automatic migrations (2026-09-05, same day)

Resolves the question the previous entry deliberately left open rather than answering unilaterally. Presented the user three options — keep migrations manual/reviewed (status quo); auto-apply an external module's own migration, but only when the deployment operator has already explicitly set `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`; or auto-apply unconditionally, with no gate at all — and explained the risk each one accepts. The user chose the middle option: extend the *existing* opt-in flag's scope, don't remove the gate, and don't leave it fully manual either.

**What changed.** `ModuleDefinition` gains a second optional field, `migrations_import_path: str | None` — a dotted path to a Python module exposing `run_migrations(connection) -> None`. A new `app.modules.registry.apply_external_module_migrations(engine)`, called once at startup from `app.migrations.run_migrations()` right after `alembic upgrade head` completes:

1. Returns immediately, without importing or discovering anything further, unless `Settings.allow_external_modules` is `True` (matches the existing entry-point/path discovery gate's own "not even scanned when off" behaviour, not just "filtered afterward").
2. **Even when external discovery is on, skips any module whose `key` is also present in the static `INSTALLED_MODULES` list** — checked structurally against that real list, not trusted from anything the module claims about itself. A first-party module that declared `migrations_import_path` anyway (it has no reason to) is logged as a warning and ignored; first-party schema changes still go exclusively through a reviewed PR into `backend/alembic/versions/`, exactly as Compliance's own 0026 migration does. This is the load-bearing distinction that keeps this change scoped to what the user actually chose: only a module that arrived via the *already-opted-into* entry-point/path sources gets this, never a module the deployment ships in its own reviewed image.
3. For each qualifying external module, imports its `migrations_import_path`, resolves its `run_migrations` attribute, and calls it inside its **own** `engine.begin()` transaction — one transaction per module, not one shared across all of them, so a mid-migration failure in one module rolls back only its own work and leaves the connection usable for the next module's own fresh transaction rather than poisoning a shared one. A missing/failed import, a missing `run_migrations` attribute, or an exception raised by it is logged (`logger.exception`/`logger.warning`) and that module is skipped — never fatal to startup or to any other module's own migration, the same per-module fault isolation this file already applies to a broken module during discovery itself.

`run_migrations(connection)` must be idempotent — it runs on every process start, matching the same `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`/`CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` convention every migration in the core chain already follows, rather than being tracked against its own per-module revision history the way Alembic tracks `alembic_version` for the core chain.

**Verified end-to-end, not just by unit test**: built a real throwaway fixture module (`module.py` + a sibling `migrations.py` module declaring `run_migrations`) under `Settings.extra_modules_path`, confirmed directly against a live database that (a) with `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` unset, `run_migrations()` leaves the fixture's table absent, and (b) with it set to `true` and the fixture directory as `EXTRA_MODULES_PATH`, the same call creates the table — proving the literal "drop a folder in, including via a Docker-mounted directory, and it just works" scenario the user asked for, for the specific case they explicitly opted into. The fixture and its table were removed afterward; nothing from it is checked in.

**Honesty note, consistent with this file's existing ones for MCP tools and Tier B frames**: this does not and cannot make running an external module's own SQL as safe as a first-party, PR-reviewed migration. It closes the "a core file needs a per-module edit" friction for a module the operator has *already* decided to trust via `allow_external_modules` — the actual trust decision is still that flag, exactly as Phase 1 designed it; this just lets what that flag already permits (arbitrary code loading) extend naturally to that same code's own schema changes, instead of requiring the operator to also hand-run a migration out of band for something they already opted the rest of the way into.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_module_registry.py` (4 new tests, using a real throwaway in-memory SQLite engine so `engine.begin()`/`connection.execute(text(...))` mechanics are genuinely exercised, not mocked): disallowed-by-default is a true no-op (asserts `importlib.import_module` is never even called); an external module's migration runs and its table actually exists afterward; a first-party (`INSTALLED_MODULES`) module's `migrations_import_path` is never imported even when declared and external discovery is allowed; one external module's migration raising doesn't prevent a second, healthy one from running. Full backend suite re-run exclusively afterward (862 passed, no other DB-touching process active — the previous re-run attempt collided with a background full-suite run still executing from this same session, a fresh instance of this repo's own documented pytest/pytest concurrent-run wedge pattern; re-run cleanly once that finished). `ruff check` clean on every touched file.

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/registry.py` (`ModuleDefinition.migrations_import_path`, `apply_external_module_migrations`), `backend/app/migrations.py` (calls it after `alembic upgrade head`), `backend/tests/test_module_registry.py` (4 new tests), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module plan, Phase 6: standards management API (2026-09-05)

Seventh implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, and the first phase to give the Compliance module a real HTTP API: full CRUD for compliance standards, their versions, hierarchical requirements, and required actions, plus an organisation-scoped required-action-type vocabulary, the publish/retire version lifecycle (§4), and this module's first three MCP tools (all read-only). Unlike Phases 0-4, this phase opens no new trust boundary — it reuses Phase 2's already-hardened `require_module_role` and the existing `services.audit.log_event` pattern verbatim, exactly as the plan's own "SOC2 / Security Planning" section anticipated — so it did not need a heavy design-time hardening pass the way Phases 1/4 did; it still gets the lighter identify→verify→remediate review this repo's change-management policy requires for any RBAC/audit-touching change, recorded below.

**Identify→verify→remediate (lighter pass, per the plan's own note that Phase 6 reuses already-hardened mechanisms).** Identify: the two things that could regress an existing control here are (a) a mutating endpoint accidentally gated by the weaker `require_org_module_enabled` instead of `require_module_role`, and (b) a cross-org id substitution attack (one org's compliance manager guessing another org's standard/version/requirement/action UUIDs). Verify: every mutating endpoint in `router.py` was checked against the `_require_manage`/`_require_view` dependency it actually declares (13 mutating endpoints, all `_require_manage`; 9 read endpoints, all `_require_view` — no mismatches found), and every id-addressed endpoint routes through one of `_get_standard_or_404`/`_get_version_or_404`/`_get_requirement_or_404`/`_get_required_action_or_404`, each of which walks the full ownership chain back to `organization_id` (covered directly by `test_cross_org_isolation_returns_404`, including the symmetric org-B-via-org-A-path case). Remediate: nothing found needing a fix — both mechanisms already existed and composed correctly on first implementation, which is itself the recorded outcome of the pass, not a skipped step.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py` (new): Pydantic request/response models for every resource, every `*Out` schema with `model_config = {"from_attributes": True}` per this codebase's convention. `backend/app/modules/compliance/router.py` (new): `router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/v1/orgs/{organization_id}/modules/compliance", tags=["compliance"])`, with `_require_manage = require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_manager")` and `_require_view = require_org_module_enabled("compliance")` constructed once at module scope (this codebase's established "call the factory at router-definition time" convention). Every id-addressed endpoint verifies ownership transitively via a chain of `_get_*_or_404` helpers mirroring `routers.action_types`' own "wrong scope → 404, not 403" precedent exactly. A `DRAFT`-only guard (`_require_draft_version`) is checked by every requirement/required-action create/update/delete/move endpoint, enforcing §4's "a published version's requirements become immutable." `create_standard_version` optionally deep-copies a prior version's full requirement tree and required actions forward (`_clone_requirement_tree`, recursive, old-id→new-id remap) when `clone_from_version_id` is given. Action types (`ComplianceActionTypeDefinition`) get a full CRUD sub-resource reusing `services.ordering.move_ordered` and `services.definitions.delete_definition_with_reassignment` directly, with `allow_empty=True` (no "must retain at least one" floor, unlike project-scoped `ActionTypeDefinition`). Every mutation calls `services.audit.log_event` before its single `db.commit()`. `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (edited): `get_router()` now returns the real router (imported inside the function body to avoid any import-cycle risk, per Phase 5's own established precedent for this exact concern); `MODULE_DEFINITION.mcp_tools` gains three `McpToolDefinition`s (`list_standards`, `get_standard_version`, `list_requirements`), each `path_template` verified against a real route by `test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s new real-registry test, not just eyeballed.

**Judgment calls the plan's own Phase 6 spec text left open** — see `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s "Phase 6 notes" subsection for the full list (exact path segments, reference immutability, version cloning as part of version creation rather than a separate endpoint, flat-DFS-ordered requirement listing, symmetric cross-org 404 isolation, extending the immutability rule to `move`, 400-not-404 for a bad `action_type_id`, exact audit action-name strings, no reparenting endpoint) — not repeated here to avoid the same content drifting out of sync between the two documents.

## Compliance module plan, Phase 7: project compliance assignment & assessment (2026-09-05)

Eighth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`: the project-specific assessment layer on top of Phase 5/6's organisation-level standard definitions — assigning a published standard version to a project, per-requirement applicability (including §9's hierarchical inheritance/override) and compliance-status assessment with §9/§16's mandatory-justification rules, per-required-action assessments (assignee/due date/completion), a requirement's own assessment history, the §20 overall-status calculation this phase is required to fully define, and two more read-only MCP tools.

**A real module-system infrastructure change, not anticipated by earlier phases.** Phase 4's own MCP tool scoping rule requires `compliance_get_project_status(project_id)`/`compliance_list_non_compliant_requirements(project_id)` to take `project_id` as their *only* path parameter (mirroring hand-written tools like `get_project(project_id)`), which is impossible for a route nested under the module's existing org-scoped router (which necessarily carries `{organization_id}`). `app.modules.registry.ModuleDefinition` gained a second, optional router field, `get_project_router: Callable[[], APIRouter | None] | None = None`, mounted by `app.main`'s loop exactly like `get_router`; `build_mcp_tool_manifest` now validates a tool's `path_template` against *either* of a module's router prefixes (whichever one actually has the matching route on its own `.routes`), not just one — a mechanical extension of Phase 4's existing "verify against the module's own router, don't trust the module's declaration" guarantee, not a weakening of it (a tool must still resolve to a route on one of *that same module's* own routers). `docs/modules.md` and `docs/solution-architecture.md` were both updated so a future module author can use this for the same reason Compliance needed it. Compliance's own `router.py` (org-scoped, gains standard-to-project assignment/archive/unarchive endpoints) and new `project_router.py` (project-scoped, `/api/v1/projects/{project_id}/modules/compliance/...`, no `organization_id` anywhere in its paths) are the first module to use both routers.

**Assigning a standard to a project is a Compliance Manager (org-scoped) decision, not a Project Manager one.** §26's own role-capability lists don't actually say who performs the initial assignment (only what each role can do with an assignment once it exists) — `module.py`'s own Phase 5/6-authored `compliance_manager` role description ("assigns standards to projects") already committed to this reading, and it fits the operational model better regardless: the org-wide catalog owner decides which projects adopt which standards; day-to-day assessment is a project-level concern for whoever is assigned there. This is why assignment/archive/unarchive live on the org router (`require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_manager")`) while viewing, applicability, assessment, required actions, history, status, and the non-compliant list all live on the project router (`require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_officer")` for mutations — already composing `is_server_admin`/`ProjectRole.PROJECT_MANAGER`, per Phase 2's existing, unreimplemented design — and the weaker `require_project_module_enabled("compliance")` for reads).

**Identify→verify→remediate.** Identify: the two things that could regress an existing control here are (a) a mutating endpoint on `project_router.py` accidentally gated by the weaker `require_project_module_enabled` instead of `require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_officer")`, and (b) a cross-scope id substitution attack (one project's requirement/required-action-assessment ids guessed against a different project's path). Verify: every mutating endpoint (`update_requirement_applicability`, `update_requirement_assessment`, `update_required_action_assessment`, `complete_required_action_assessment`, `uncomplete_required_action_assessment`) was checked against `_require_officer`; every id-addressed endpoint routes through `_get_project_compliance_or_404`/`_get_pcr_or_404`/`_get_required_action_assessment_or_404`, each walking the full ownership chain back to `project_id` — covered by `test_cross_org_project_assignment_isolation`'s cross-project 404 case. Remediate: nothing found needing a fix on first implementation (both mechanisms composed correctly), which is itself the recorded outcome, not a skipped step — this phase reuses Phase 2's already-hardened `require_module_role` and Phase 6's own `_get_*_or_404`/404-not-403 convention verbatim, exactly as the plan anticipated for a phase that opens no new trust boundary of its own (the `get_project_router` addition is new *infrastructure*, but re-derives its safety property mechanically from the same manifest-builder logic Phase 4 already hardened, not a new, separately-reasoned mechanism).

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/models.py`: three new tables — `ProjectCompliance` (project ↔ always-`PUBLISHED` standard-version assignment, soft-archivable, never hard-deleted so its children's real assessment/audit history survives), `ProjectComplianceRequirement` (one row per requirement per assignment: nullable `explicit_applicability` distinct from "never decided," a single `justification` column serving both §9's and §16's mandatory-justification rules since the two conditions are never true at once, actor+timestamp pairs for applicability/assessment changes, and an `approval_state` column reserved for Phase 9 — present now because §20's own calculation, which this phase must fully define, explicitly folds approval state in), and `ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment` (one row per required action per requirement-assessment, shaped as a completion overlay — `is_completed`/`completed_at`/`completed_by` — mirroring `Requirement.completed_at`'s own pattern rather than reusing `ComplianceStatus`). `backend/alembic/versions/0027_project_compliance.py` (new): all three tables, `IF NOT EXISTS` throughout, matching Phase 5/6's established raw-SQL migration style. `backend/app/modules/compliance/enums.py`: new `ComplianceApplicabilitySource` (`explicit`/`inherited`/`overridden`, §9's own explicit UI-distinction **Tests.** `backend/tests/test_project_compliance_api.py` (new, 11 tests): compliance-manager-can-assign/plain-member-cannot, draft-version-assignment-409, assignment materialisation + duplicate-assignment-400, hierarchical applicability inherit/override (plus mandatory-justification-400), mandatory-justification-for-non-compliant (plus history assertions with previous/new state), the officer-grant/PROJECT_MANAGER-override/plain-member-403/any-member-read RBAC composition, the full §20 calculation (including the has-non-compliant/overall-state flip and the cross-project compliance-manager view), required-action-assessment complete/uncomplete (plus 409-already-completed), cross-project/cross-scope isolation, and archive/unarchive. `backend/tests/test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s real-registry compliance section was extended to the two new tools — concrete proof the two-router manifest-validation mechanism actually works, not just the single-router case Phase 4 originally proved. `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py`'s module-registration assertion was updated for `get_project_router`/five tools. A first full-suite run caught a real, unrelated-to-logic bug: `ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment.project_compliance_requirement_id`'s auto-generated index name is 75 characters, over Postgres's 63-byte identifier limit — Postgres silently truncated it at `CREATE INDEX` time, permanently failing `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` since the truncated reflected name never matched SQLAlchemy's own untruncated computed name regardless of what the migration named it. Fixed by giving that index an explicit, short name via `Index(...)` in `__table_args__` instead of `index=True` (see `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s Phase 7 notes for the lesson recorded for future phases). Re-run clean afterward against a live `reqtrack_pytest_test` database with no other DB-touching process active: 66 passed across the four touched/new test files in isolation, and the full backend suite — 867 passed, the same 14 pre-existing `mailhog`-hostname-resolution failures Phase 6 already documented (`test_invites_and_external_users.py`/`test_oidc_provisioning.py`/`test_org_export_import.py`) plus zero new ones. `ruff check` clean on every touched/new file. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes were made — per Phase 5/6's own established precedent, seeding compliance data (now including a real project assignment) remains Phase 15's own, already-documented responsibility.

## Compliance module plan, Phase 8: evidence (2026-09-05)

Ninth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`: supporting evidence for a project's compliance assessments (§13-§15) — evidence rows with issue/expiry metadata, many-to-many linkage to a project's own `ProjectComplianceRequirement`/`ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment` rows (not the reusable standard-level definitions), file attachments reusing the existing `services.files.upload_file` mechanism, §15's append-only revalidation history, §14's valid/expiring/expired derivation, and this module's sixth read-only MCP tool.

**A small, generic module-system extension, not a compliance-specific hack.** Evidence needs file attachments to be downloadable through the single, existing, generic `GET /api/v1/files/{id}` endpoint (`app.routers.files.download_file`) — but that router is deliberately module-agnostic (it already walks `RequirementFile`/`RequirementActionFile`/`CommentFile` in a fallback chain for core attachment types) and must stay that way, per the module system's own founding "core code shouldn't need much modification per module" goal. Rather than importing `app.modules.compliance.models` into that core router (a real architectural regression — core code depending on one specific module, the opposite of every module-system phase's own direction), `ModuleDefinition` gained an optional `resolve_file_owner_project_id` hook (`app.modules.registry`), and a new `resolve_module_file_project_id(db, file_id)` function tries every registered module's hook, in registry order, as one more fallback after the existing core checks. Compliance's own `resolve_evidence_file_project_id` (`app.modules.compliance.service`) is the first implementation, but the mechanism is generic — any future module with its own file attachments (the plan's own "first of four planned major uplifts" framing means there will be more) gets the same hook for free, mirroring exactly how Phase 7's `get_project_router` generalised a compliance-specific need into reusable module-system infrastructure.

**Evidence is project-scoped, not tied to one specific `ProjectCompliance` assignment.** §13's own "a single piece of evidence should be capable of supporting multiple compliance requirements" reads most naturally as spanning more than one of a project's standard assignments at once (e.g. one certificate satisfying requirements under two different standards a project is assigned). `ComplianceEvidence.project_id` points directly at the project; `ComplianceEvidenceRequirementLink`/`ComplianceEvidenceActionLink` are genuine many-to-many join tables pointing at `ProjectComplianceRequirement`/`ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment` — the project-specific assessment layer Phase 7 established — never at the reusable `ComplianceRequirement`/`ComplianceRequiredAction` definitions, the same §31 "state belongs to the project-specific assessment layer" principle extended one concept further.

**§15's revalidation history is genuinely append-only, not reconstructed from `updated_at`.** `ComplianceEvidenceRevalidation` mirrors `RequirementFile`'s own "no `updated_at`, insert-only" shape (a plain `created_at` column) rather than `TimestampMixin` — each row records `previous_expiry_date`/`new_expiry_date`/`revalidated_by`/`revalidated_at`/`justification` at the moment of that one revalidation, so a second revalidation can never overwrite the first's own "previous expiry" value the way a single mutable history field would. `ComplianceEvidence.expiry_date` itself is updated in place to the new, current effective expiry — the "live" value every other read (including §14's validity derivation) uses; the append-only table is purely history, never itself queried for "what is the expiry right now."

**§14's valid/expiring/expired state is computed, never stored — extending Phase 7's own precedent for `ComplianceApplicabilitySource`.** `service.compute_evidence_validity_state` derives `ComplianceEvidenceValidityState` (`no_expiry`/`valid`/`expiring_soon`/`expired`) from `expiry_date` at read time, using a plain module-level constant (`EVIDENCE_EXPIRY_WARNING_DAYS = 30`) rather than a configurable setting — §14 names no specific lead time, and this repo's own precedent for an analogous "how many days before X is this worth flagging" setting (`Project.review_reminder_lead_days_default`) only exists because a real notification consumer (the review-reminder scheduler job) needed it configurable; Phase 8 has no notification delivery of its own yet (that's Phase 10), so promoting this constant to a setting now would be speculative. `list_expiring_or_expired_evidence` (the `GET .../expiring-evidence` endpoint and `compliance_list_expiring_evidence` MCP tool) excludes archived evidence — a deliberate, documented distinction between "no longer applicable" (§13, `is_archived`) and "no longer valid" (§14, `expiry_date`-derived): an archived row is still assigned a real validity state (so nothing drifts silently), but isn't surfaced by a listing meant to flag things needing attention.

**Identify→verify→remediate.** Identify: the two things that could regress an existing control here are (a) a mutating evidence endpoint on `project_router.py` accidentally gated by the weaker `require_project_module_enabled` instead of `require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_officer")`, and (b) a cross-project id substitution attack (one project's evidence/requirement/assessment ids guessed against a different project's path or a different project's evidence-link payload). Verify: every mutating evidence endpoint (`create_evidence`, `update_evidence`, `archive_evidence`, `unarchive_evidence`, `revalidate_evidence`, both link/unlink pairs, both file endpoints) was checked against `_require_officer`; every id-addressed or payload-referenced evidence/pcr/assessment lookup routes through `_get_evidence_or_404`/`_get_pcr_for_project_or_404`/`_get_assessment_for_project_or_404`, each verifying the row's ownership chain back to `project_id` — covered by `test_create_evidence_rejects_pcr_id_from_a_different_project` and `test_cross_project_evidence_isolation`. A third thing specific to this phase's own new file-download hook was also verified: that `resolve_module_file_project_id` correctly authorizes a Compliance evidence file for a real project member and correctly 403s an org member with no access to that specific project (`test_evidence_file_upload_download_and_isolation`) — the mechanism composes with the download endpoint's existing checks rather than replacing them. Remediate: one real bug found and fixed during this phase's own test run (not a pre-existing gap) — see "Tests" below.

**Judgment calls the plan's own Phase 8 spec text left open**, recorded in full in `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s "Phase 8 notes" subsection (not repeated here to avoid drift): evidence's project-vs-assignment scoping; `is_archived` as the answer to §13's "whether it remains applicable"; why `ComplianceEvidenceUpdate` excludes `expiry_date` entirely; the two convenience read-only endpoints viewing evidence from the requirement/required-action side; and the `EVIDENCE_EXPIRY_WARNING_DAYS` constant.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/models.py`: five new tables — `ComplianceEvidence`, `ComplianceEvidenceRevalidation`, `ComplianceEvidenceFile`, `ComplianceEvidenceRequirementLink`, `ComplianceEvidenceActionLink` — none of the three join/link tables indexed beyond their primary key, mirroring `RequirementFile`'s own convention (and sidestepping the 63-byte identifier-length problem Phase 7's own notes already documented for a different table). `backend/alembic/versions/0028_compliance_evidence.py` (new): all five tables, `IF NOT EXISTS` throughout. `backend/app/modules/compliance/enums.py`: new `ComplianceEvidenceValidityState`. `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py`: `ComplianceEvidenceCreate`/`Update`/`Out`, `ComplianceEvidenceRevalidateRequest`/`RevalidationOut`, and the two link-create schemas. `backend/app/modules/compliance/service.py`: `compute_evidence_validity_state`, `build_evidence_out`, `list_expiring_or_expired_evidence`, `resolve_evidence_file_project_id`. `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py`: the full evidence CRUD/linkage/file/revalidation surface, plus two convenience read endpoints (`.../requirements/{pcr_id}/evidence`, `.../required-action-assessments/{id}/evidence`) viewing evidence from the assessment side. `backend/app/modules/registry.py`: `ModuleDefinition.resolve_file_owner_project_id`, `resolve_module_file_project_id`. `backend/app/routers/files.py`: one new fallback branch in `download_file`, after every existing core attachment-type check. `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py`: `resolve_file_owner_project_id` wired in, plus the `list_expiring_evidence` MCP tool declaration.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_compliance_evidence_api.py` (new, 10 tests): creation with initial multi-linkage (plus the two convenience read-side views), cross-project pcr-id rejection at creation (404), idempotent link/not-found unlink, `expiry_date` immunity to a plain `PATCH`, archive/unarchive (plus 409-double-transition), two-revalidation history proving the first's own "previous expiry" survives the second, the full §14 validity-state matrix (`no_expiry`/`valid`/`expiring_soon`/`expired`) plus the expiring-evidence listing's archived-row exclusion, the officer-grant/PROJECT_MANAGER-override/plain-member-403/any-member-read RBAC composition (mirroring Phase 7's own established shape exactly), and file upload/download/cross-project-outsider-403/unlink-then-404. `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py`'s module-registration assertion was updated for six tools and the new `resolve_file_owner_project_id` hook. `backend/tests/test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s real-registry compliance section was extended to the sixth tool. A first test run caught a real bug (not a pre-existing gap, introduced by this phase's own `unlink_evidence_file`): deleting the link row and the underlying `FileAsset` in the same flush let the `file_assets.compliance_evidence_files` `ON DELETE CASCADE` race the ORM's own pending `DELETE` for the link row, producing a benign-looking but real `SAWarning` ("0 were matched") — fixed by adding the same `db.flush()` between the two deletes that `routers.requirements.unlink_requirement_file` already has, for exactly the same reason. Re-run clean afterward (verified with `-W error::sqlalchemy.exc.SAWarning` to make sure the warning was actually gone, not just unobserved) against a live `reqtrack_pytest_test` database with no other DB-touching process active: the new/touched test files pass in isolation, and the full backend suite was re-run afterward to confirm no regression. `ruff check` clean on every touched/new file. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes were made — per this plan's own established precedent, seeding compliance data remains Phase 15's own, already-documented responsibility.

## Compliance module plan, Phase 9: approval / sign-off workflow (2026-09-06)

Tenth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`: activates the `approval_state` state machine `ProjectComplianceRequirement` has carried, unused, since Phase 7 (§12, §16, §27) — `submit-for-approval`/`approve`/`reject` actions enforcing `NOT_ASSESSED → ASSESSED → PENDING_APPROVAL → APPROVED/REJECTED` ordering, the two automatic transitions that keep an approval from silently surviving a material change, a `pending-approvals` cross-assignment listing, and one more read-only MCP tool.

**One state-machine rule, not two, covering both mutation triggers.** The plan's own Phase 9 spec text names two distinct triggers for "must not silently remain Approved" (a fresh reassessment; a material change to evidence/the underlying requirement) but doesn't specify whether they should land on the same resulting state. They don't, deliberately: `service.advance_approval_state_on_assessment` always sets `ASSESSED` when `update_requirement_assessment` runs — unconditionally, including from `APPROVED` — because performing the assessment endpoint's own action *is* the reassessment; landing on `REQUIRES_REASSESSMENT` (a state whose own docstring, written ahead of this phase in Phase 7, means "a reassessment is still needed") would be self-contradictory the instant one was just done. `service.invalidate_approval_if_in_flight` instead downgrades `PENDING_APPROVAL`/`APPROVED` to `REQUIRES_REASSESSMENT` for the *other* kind of change — one that happens without any accompanying reassessment: an applicability change (`update_requirement_applicability`, only when the value actually changes) or a material change to supporting evidence (`archive_evidence`/`revalidate_evidence`, via a new `service.find_pcrs_linked_to_evidence` lookup spanning both direct requirement links and required-action-assessment links). Every other `approval_state` value is left untouched by both an applicability change and an evidence change — nothing to invalidate on a row that was never in flight or decided.

**§27's "standard version change" trigger is a documented, deliberate no-op in this phase, not a silent gap.** The plan's own bullet lists a version change alongside evidence expiry as a material-change trigger, but `ProjectCompliance.standard_version_id` never changes after assignment (Phase 7's own design — pinned to one version forever) and there is no version-migration action yet (that's Phase 11). `invalidate_approval_if_in_flight` is written generically enough that Phase 11's eventual migration action can call it per affected `ProjectComplianceRequirement`, but nothing in this phase triggers it for that case, since nothing in this phase *can* — called out here and in `models.py`'s own Phase 9 notes so a future session doesn't read the absence as an oversight.

**No bespoke approval-history table.** §12's "approval/sign-off history" requirement is satisfied entirely by the existing `AuditEvent`/`get_requirement_history` trail Phase 7 already exposed over HTTP — `submit_for_approval`/`approve_requirement`/`reject_requirement`/`_invalidate_approvals_supported_by_evidence` all log through `services.audit.log_event` exactly like every other mutation on this router, rather than introducing a second, parallel history mechanism for one workflow. `approval_decided_at`/`approval_decided_by`/`decision_note` are the only new columns — one pair serving both an approval and a rejection decision, mirroring `justification`'s own Phase-7-established "one field, meaning depends on which transition is happening" shape, since a row is never both approved and rejected at once and `approval_state` itself already disambiguates which decision `decision_note` belongs to.

**Rejection requires a `decision_note`; approval doesn't — a deliberate extension of §16's existing pattern, not an invented requirement out of nothing.** §12 itself doesn't explicitly mandate a rejection rationale, but §16 already establishes, twice (Not Applicable, Non-Compliant), that this codebase requires a rationale for exactly this class of negative/blocking decision — enforced at the API layer (400), not the schema layer, the same conditionally-mandatory pattern as `ProjectComplianceApplicabilityUpdate.justification`/`ProjectComplianceAssessmentUpdate.justification`.

**`approve`/`reject`/`submit-for-approval` are defended against ever becoming MCP tools two ways, not one.** The primary defence is simply that `module.py` declares no `McpToolDefinition` for any of the three at all. `approve`/`reject` (the two actual decisions) are additionally marked with `app.modules.registry.APPROVAL_ACTION_ROUTE_EXTRA` (`openapi_extra`) — the plan's own Phase 9 spec text asked for this defence-in-depth explicitly ("mark it `is_approval_action: true` if it's ever tempting to add one... so Phase 4's manifest-builder exclusion catches it even if a future session forgets why"), and this is the first phase to actually consume that Phase-4-built, previously-unused mechanism. `submit-for-approval` is marked the same way too, even though it only queues a decision rather than making one — §11 describes the whole flow ("Request/perform assessment... Approve/sign off compliance") as one accountable-human action set, so it gets the same belt-and-braces treatment as the two real decisions.

**Identify→verify→remediate.** Identify: the two things that could regress an existing control here are (a) `approve`/`reject` resolving as an MCP tool despite the plan's explicit prohibition, and (b) the state-machine ordering endpoints (`submit-for-approval`/`approve`/`reject`) being reachable from the wrong `approval_state`, letting a caller skip a step (e.g. approving something never submitted). Verify: `test_compliance_data_model.py`'s registration test now asserts no tool named `compliance_submit_for_approval`/`compliance_approve`/`compliance_reject` exists in the live registry, and `test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s real-registry test asserts the same, plus that `compliance_list_pending_approvals` (the one real new tool) is read-only; `test_compliance_approval_workflow.py::test_state_machine_ordering_is_enforced` covers approve-before-submit, reject-before-submit, submit-with-nothing-assessed, and double-submit, all 409. Remediate: nothing found needing a fix — both mechanisms composed correctly on first implementation, consistent with this being an activation of an already-hardened Phase 7 column/RBAC composition rather than a new trust boundary.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/models.py`: `ProjectComplianceRequirement` gains `approval_decided_at`/`approval_decided_by`/`decision_note`. `backend/alembic/versions/0029_compliance_approval_workflow.py` (new): the three columns, `IF NOT EXISTS`, matching the established raw-SQL migration style. `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py`: `ComplianceApprovalDecisionRequest` (shared by `approve`/`reject`), `PendingApprovalOut` (mirrors `NonCompliantRequirementOut`'s shape); `ProjectComplianceRequirementOut` gains the three new fields. `backend/app/modules/compliance/service.py`: `advance_approval_state_on_assessment`, `invalidate_approval_if_in_flight`, `find_pcrs_linked_to_evidence` — see the design-decision paragraphs above. `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py`: `submit_requirement_for_approval`/`approve_requirement`/`reject_requirement` (state-machine actions), `list_pending_approvals` (cross-assignment listing, placed next to `list_non_compliant_requirements`), `_invalidate_approvals_supported_by_evidence` (shared helper called from `archive_evidence`/`revalidate_evidence`); `update_requirement_assessment`/`update_requirement_applicability` extended to call the two new `service.py` transitions. `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py`: `compliance_list_pending_approvals` MCP tool declaration, plus a module-docstring note on why the three real workflow actions are deliberately never declared as tools.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_compliance_approval_workflow.py` (new, 9 tests): the submit→approve happy path (including the full history-action sequence), reject requiring/recording a `decision_note`, state-machine ordering (approve/reject-before-submit, never-assessed-submit, double-submit, all 409), reassessing an `APPROVED` row resetting to `assessed` (not `requires_reassessment`), an applicability change on an `APPROVED` row requiring reassessment, archiving and revalidating linked evidence each invalidating an in-flight/decided approval, the `pending-approvals` listing appearing/disappearing across the workflow, and the officer-grant/PROJECT_MANAGER-override/plain-member-403/any-member-read RBAC composition mirroring Phase 7/8's own established shape. `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py`'s module-registration assertion was updated for seven tools plus the no-approval-tool-declared assertion. `backend/tests/test_project_compliance_api.py::test_project_status_calculation`'s `overall_approval_state` assertion was updated from `"not_assessed"` to `"assessed"` — a Phase 7-era assumption this phase's own, correct new behaviour (assessing a row always advances its `approval_state`) makes stale, not a regression. `backend/tests/test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s real-registry compliance section was extended to the seventh tool and to assert the three workflow actions resolve to no tool at all. Full backend suite run against a live `reqtrack_pytest_test` database (the already-running `tests/container` stack's `db` service, no other DB-touching process active): 99 passed across every compliance-related test file plus the module-system RBAC/registry/MCP-tools files in isolation, and `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` confirmed the new migration matches the model with zero drift. The full suite was then re-run end to end: 886 passed, 14 failed — the same 14 pre-existing `mailhog`-hostname-resolution failures Phase 6/7 already documented (`test_invites_and_external_users.py`/`test_oidc_provisioning.py`/`test_org_export_import.py`, a host-run-pytest-only DNS gap, not reproducible inside the `tests/container` stack itself), zero new failures. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes were made — per this plan's own established precedent, seeding compliance data remains Phase 15's own, already-documented responsibility.

## Compliance module plan, Phase 10: scheduled reviews + notifications (2026-09-06)

Eleventh implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (§17, §18, §28): a `ComplianceReview` entity covering both standard-level and project-level scheduled reviews, four date-driven APScheduler sweeps, and six event-driven notifications wired into endpoints Phases 6/7/9 already shipped — the first phase in this plan to touch the notification system at all.

**A new generic module-system mechanism (`ModuleDefinition.scheduled_jobs`/`ModuleScheduledJob`), not core scheduler code importing Compliance directly.** The plan's own spec text ("New APScheduler jobs, `services/scheduler.py` pattern") could have been read as "hand-add four calls to that core file," but doing so would have broken this module system's own established principle — first established by Phase 7's `get_project_router` and Phase 8's `resolve_file_owner_project_id`, each added the moment a real module first needed a capability core code didn't yet expose generically — that core files shouldn't need per-module edits. `app.services.scheduler.start_scheduler` now iterates `app.modules.registry.get_all_module_scheduled_jobs()` generically (job-id-prefixed with the declaring module's own key, to avoid any cross-module collision) alongside its own two pre-existing core jobs. Compliance's four sweeps are the first, and so far only, consumer.

**`ComplianceReview` is one entity with a `CHECK` constraint, not two tables or a polymorphic "reviewable" abstraction.** §17 names two distinct owners — a compliance standard itself, and a project's own compliance assignment — but every other field (frequency, next due date, owner, status, notes, outcome) is identical between the two, so a `(standard_id IS NOT NULL) != (project_compliance_id IS NOT NULL)` constraint enforces exactly one owner per row rather than duplicating the whole shape. `frequency_label` (free text) plus an optional `recurrence_days` (nullable — `None` means one-off, doesn't auto-recur) was chosen over a fixed calendar-frequency enum specifically because §17's own worked examples include non-calendar, event-triggered reviews ("Review before product release," "Review after a significant standard change") a rigid enum can't represent without an awkward escape hatch.

**§17's "Review history" is the retained chain of rows itself, not a second history table.** Completing a `SCHEDULED` review (`service.complete_review`) always marks it `COMPLETED` — retained forever, never deleted or reopened — and, only when `recurrence_days` is set, creates a **new** `SCHEDULED` row for the next cycle (`next_due_date = today + recurrence_days`). Listing every review for one owner in creation order *is* that owner's complete review history. This mirrors the same call this module already made twice before for a different underlying mechanism: Phase 7 reused the existing `AuditEvent` trail instead of a bespoke assessment-history table, and Phase 9 did the same for approval/sign-off history; Phase 10 doesn't need a third mechanism, since chained review rows already are the history.

**`schedule_state` (upcoming/due/overdue) is computed at read time, never stored** — the third time this module has applied this exact "can't drift" reasoning (`ComplianceApplicabilitySource` in Phase 7, `ComplianceEvidenceValidityState` in Phase 8), now to a review's own due-date state. `COMPLIANCE_REVIEW_DUE_WARNING_DAYS = 14`, shorter than evidence's 30-day window, on the reasoning that a review is an activity someone must still schedule time to perform, unlike a certificate typically renewed well ahead of its own expiry.

**A full CRUD + complete + evidence-linkage surface, on both routers, not just the read-only "identify due/overdue" capability the spec bullet list technically asked for.** Without create/update/complete endpoints there would be nothing to actually schedule §17's reviews *with*. Mutability follows this module's existing "immutable once it matters" convention: a review can only be edited or deleted while still `SCHEDULED` (409 once `COMPLETED`), the same shape as a published standard version's requirements or a decided approval. A new unified `GET /reviews-due` endpoint on the project router (also the `compliance_list_reviews_due(project_id)` MCP tool, the 8th, all still read-only) gathers a project's own project-level reviews *and* every review of a standard it's currently assigned to — a standard-level review affects every project on that standard, so a project dashboard shouldn't need to separately query the org router to see both.

**Ten of §18's fourteen listed notification events are new triggers wired into *existing* Phase 6/7/9 endpoints, confirmed to have had zero notification wiring before this phase** (verified by grepping the whole module for `notify`/`notifications.` before starting — Phase 9's own notes never mention notifications at all, and the grep confirmed it): a Non-Compliant assessment (`update_requirement_assessment`), submitting for approval (`submit_requirement_for_approval`), a rejection (`reject_requirement`, notifying the original assessor specifically — not a broadcast), an applicability or evidence change invalidating an in-flight/decided approval (`update_requirement_applicability`/`_invalidate_approvals_supported_by_evidence`, via a new shared `_notify_approval_invalidated` helper so the same notification isn't implemented twice), a new standard version being published (`publish_standard_version`, notifying compliance officers of every project still pinned to an *older* version of that standard — informational only, since Phase 7's own design keeps an existing assignment pinned to its version regardless), and a new project assignment (`create_project_compliance`). The remaining four events (required-action due/overdue, evidence expiring/expired, review due/overdue, target-date approaching/exceeded) are the four date-driven sweeps.

**Two new recipient-resolution helpers, deliberately *not* a second authorization mechanism.** `service.get_effective_compliance_officers`/`get_effective_compliance_managers` answer "who should be told about this," reusing `rbac.get_effective_project_managers` for the project case (so group-inherited/forward-inherited managers are covered, the same set `require_module_role` itself would accept) but a direct-only `UserOrgRole` query for the org-admin case, since this codebase's org groups have no `OrgGroupRole` table the way project groups do — there is no inheritance path to cover there. Documented explicitly as a lower-stakes class of correctness than an RBAC gate: a missed edge case here is a missed notification, never an access-control gap, since every mutating endpoint's actual authorization stays exactly `require_module_role`, entirely untouched by this phase.

**Every sweep is idempotent per notification via a `*_reminder_sent_at`/`*_notified_at` timestamp pair on the owning row**, mirroring `RequirementVersion.review_reminder_sent_at`'s own Massif-era convention exactly rather than inventing a new one — added to `ComplianceEvidence`, `ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment`, `ProjectCompliance`, and `ComplianceReview`. Each pair resets to `None` whenever the underlying due/expiry date is actually rescheduled (`update_required_action_assessment`, `revalidate_evidence`, the review update endpoints), so a rescheduled date gets its own fresh reminder cycle rather than silently inheriting the old date's "already reminded" state. `ProjectCompliance.target_compliance_date` needed no such reset — confirmed there is no update endpoint for it at all (set once, at assignment time, per Phase 7's own design), so it can never need rescheduling.

**Identify→verify→remediate.** Identify: the two things that could regress an existing control here are (a) the new `scheduled_jobs` mechanism somehow letting a module run code the registry hasn't already vetted (the same class of concern Phase 1's `INSTALLED_MODULES`/`ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` boundary already governs), and (b) a notification recipient-resolution bug leaking assessment detail (a justification/decision note) to a user who shouldn't see it. Verify: `get_all_module_scheduled_jobs()` only ever iterates `get_module_registry()`'s already-resolved entries — a job can only run if its declaring module already cleared Phase 1's existing trust boundary, so this mechanism grants no new capability, only a generic place to register one already-trusted module's own callable; confirmed by reading `start_scheduler`'s own loop, which takes no module-supplied path/import string, only a plain Python callable the registry already holds a reference to. For (b): every notification recipient set in this phase is built from `get_effective_compliance_officers`/`get_effective_compliance_managers`/an explicit `assignee_id`/`assessed_by`/`owner_id` column already scoped to the same project/org the notification's own `project_id` field carries — no cross-project/cross-org recipient set is ever constructed. Remediate: nothing found needing a fix — both mechanisms composed correctly on first implementation, consistent with this phase reusing already-hardened Phase 1 (registry trust boundary) and Phase 7-9 (RBAC composition) mechanisms rather than opening a new one of its own.

**A pre-existing, larger documentation drift found and fixed in passing, not introduced by this phase.** `docs/solution-architecture.md`'s exhaustive table-count list had a "Compliance module" group frozen at only Phase 5's original five tables ever since Phase 7 shipped — the eight tables Phases 7 and 8 actually added were each individually described in that document's own prose sections and present in its ER diagram, but never carried over into the exhaustive list itself. Found by cross-checking the list's implied total against a live migrated database's real table count (`information_schema.tables`, 69 tables) rather than assuming the stale "59" was still correct — the same method that document's own fifth/sixth recorded drift-corrections already used. Fixed in the same pass as adding Phase 10's own two new tables, per this repo's "fix, don't defer, found issues" rule, rather than left as a second, unrelated gap. `docs/mcp-server.md`'s "Compliance itself doesn't land until a later phase" sentence (stale since Phase 6) was also corrected while already editing that section for the 8th tool.

**No new SOC 2 policy-document edits were needed this phase** — this phase reuses Phase 1's already-hardened module-registry trust boundary (for `scheduled_jobs`) and Phase 6/7/9's already-hardened `require_module_role`/audit-logging conventions (for the review CRUD/complete endpoints) verbatim; it opens no new trust boundary of its own. A short identify→verify→remediate pass was still recorded above per this repo's change-management policy for any change touching background processing/notifications — it found nothing new to fix, which is itself the recorded outcome, not a skipped step.

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_compliance_reviews_and_notifications.py` (new, 20 tests): project-level and standard-level review create/list/get/update/delete/complete, RBAC composition (officer/PROJECT_MANAGER-can, plain-member-403, any-member-read), `schedule_state` across upcoming/due/overdue, reminder-stamp reset on reschedule, complete-with-recurrence creating the next cycle (asserted via the two-row history listing) and complete-without-recurrence not recurring, delete-only-while-`SCHEDULED` (409 once completed), evidence linkage (link/unlink, `linked_evidence_ids`), the unified `reviews-due` listing spanning both project-level and standard-level reviews while excluding a not-yet-due one, all six event-driven notifications (non-compliant, approval-requested, rejected-notifies-the-assessor, applicability-change-invalidates-approval, standard-update-notifies-officers-of-projects-on-older-versions, new-assignment), and all four sweeps (evidence expiry, required-action due, target date, review due) each run twice in the same test to prove idempotency via the reminder-stamp columns. `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py`'s module-registration assertion was updated for eight tools and a new four-scheduled-jobs assertion. `backend/tests/test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s real-registry compliance section was extended to the eighth tool (`compliance_list_reviews_due`). Run against a live `reqtrack_pytest_test` database (the already-running `tests/container` stack's `db` service, exposed on `localhost:5432`, reached from a host Python venv rather than `docker compose exec` since the backend image isn't rebuilt for every code change): the new file's own 20 tests pass in isolation, and the full backend suite was re-run afterward with no other DB-touching process active to confirm no regression, `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` included (confirming migration 0030 matches the models with zero drift). `ruff check` clean on every touched/new file. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes were made — per this plan's own established precedent, seeding compliance data (reviews included) remains Phase 15's own, already-documented responsibility.
