## Compliance module plan, Phase 11: cross-standard mapping + version impact (2026-09-06)

Twelfth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (§19, §27): a general-purpose cross-standard requirement mapping model with an extensible relationship-type vocabulary, a computed added/removed/modified/replaced/re-mapped diff between any two versions of a standard, and an explicit, user-triggered project action to migrate an existing assignment onto a newer standard version — the version-migration action Phase 7's own docstring and Phase 9's own notes both already flagged as deliberately left undone until this phase.

**A durable clone-lineage column, not a best-effort name/reference heuristic, backs the version diff.** `ComplianceRequirement.cloned_from_requirement_id` (nullable, self-referential, `ON DELETE SET NULL`) is new, stamped by `router.py::_clone_requirement_tree` at clone time. Before this phase, cloning a standard version remapped old-id → new-id only in memory, for the duration of one clone call, and persisted nothing — so a version diff could only ever guess "same name/reference → probably the same requirement," which breaks the moment a requirement is renamed *and* edited in the same version (indistinguishable from one being removed and an unrelated one added). `ON DELETE SET NULL`, not `CASCADE`: this deliberately differs from `parent_requirement_id`'s own `CASCADE` one column up on the same model — `parent_requirement_id`'s cascade exists because a compliance requirement has no "stand alone once detached" concept *within its own tree*, but the *source* requirement a later version's requirement was cloned from is a fully independent row in an already-published version that must keep existing regardless of what later happens to the draft version it was cloned from; `service.diff_standard_versions` already treats "lineage record detached" identically to "never had one" (i.e. `added`), the correct fallback either way. `diff_standard_versions` walks this chain multiple hops when the two versions being compared aren't directly adjacent (e.g. diffing v1 against v3 when v3 was itself cloned from v2, not v1) — every requirement ever created under the standard, across every version, is loaded once so the walk always has what it needs regardless of how many versions apart the two given versions are.

**One mapping table serves both §19's cross-standard mapping and §27's "replaced" version-diff category, not two.** `ComplianceRequirementMapping` records a directed relationship (`from_requirement_id` → `to_requirement_id`, typed by an extensible `relationship_type_id`) between any two `ComplianceRequirement` rows — deliberately *not* restricted to requirements in different standards. A Compliance Manager marking "the new v2.0 clause 5.3 replaces the old v1.0 clause 4.9, which was deleted outright rather than cloned forward" is structurally the same fact ("these two requirement rows are related, and here's how") as marking an ISO 27001 clause equivalent to a corporate standard's clause, so `diff_standard_versions`'s `replaced` category is computed by looking for exactly this shape of mapping: a new-version requirement with no clone lineage into the old version, explicitly linked to a not-yet-matched old-version requirement of the *same* standard. A mapping to a requirement in a genuinely different standard can never satisfy this (its target's `standard_version_id` can never equal the old version being diffed), so the two use cases never collide. Directed, not symmetric, because several of §19's own named relationship types are inherently directional (`Derived From`, `Satisfies`); a `UNIQUE (from_requirement_id, to_requirement_id, relationship_type_id)` constraint blocks recording the exact same relationship twice while still allowing more than one relationship type between the same pair.

**The relationship-type vocabulary is a new, organisation-scoped, extensible table — `ComplianceMappingRelationshipTypeDefinition` — mirroring `ComplianceActionTypeDefinition`'s existing pattern exactly**, per §19's own "exact relationship types should be configurable or extensible where practical," rather than a hardcoded Python enum. Its table name (`compliance_mapping_relationship_types`) is deliberately shorter than its own column-derived naming would suggest (`..._type_definitions`, matching `compliance_action_type_definitions`'s own shape) — the longer name's auto-generated `organization_id` index name is 67 characters, over Postgres's 63-byte identifier limit, the exact class of problem `ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment`'s own comment already documents for a different table; solved there with an explicit shortened index name, solved here by shortening the table name itself instead, which reads more naturally alongside a normal-length index name. No rows are seeded by this phase, consistent with every other vocabulary table in this module — seed data remains Phase 15's job.

**`re_mapped` is deliberately built on "mapping links are never auto-cloned," not treated as a bug to fix.** For every lineage-matched requirement pair (modified or unchanged alike), `diff_standard_versions` compares the old requirement's own non-archived mapping-target ids against the new requirement's — and since `_clone_requirement_tree` never touches `ComplianceRequirementMapping` at all, a freshly cloned requirement always starts with zero mappings of its own. That is exactly the useful signal: a cross-standard relationship asserted against one specific version's wording may no longer hold once that wording changes (or even if it doesn't — nobody has re-confirmed it against the new row), so silently re-pointing it forward would assert something nobody actually checked. `re_mapped` is how a Compliance Manager discovers which requirements need their mappings re-established after publishing a new version, reported only when the *old* side had at least one mapping to begin with (nothing to lose otherwise).

**The version-migration action creates a new `ProjectCompliance` row and archives the old one — it never mutates `standard_version_id` in place.** This was the strongly-recommended design handed down from Phase 7/9's own notes, and nothing surfaced during implementation to deviate from it: §27's "Existing Project Compliance assignments must remain associated with their original version" and "migration must not silently change historical compliance assessments" are both satisfied structurally rather than by convention, since the old row (and every `ProjectComplianceRequirement` under it) is never touched at all — confirmed by a dedicated test (`test_migrate_does_not_change_old_assignment_or_its_assessments`) that diffs the old assignment's full requirement listing before and after migration and asserts byte-for-byte equality. `service.migrate_project_compliance` materialises the new assignment exactly like a fresh one (`materialize_assessment_rows`, reused verbatim, per this repo's own "reuse, don't reimplement" rule), then uses `diff_standard_versions`'s `unmodified_lineage_map` (lineage-matched *and* content-identical pairs only) to decide, per new requirement, whether to carry forward the old assignment's own assessment (`compliance_status`/`explicit_applicability`/`justification`/`notes`/who/when) — a `modified` or `added` requirement is always left at materialised defaults, never guessed at. (A `replaced` requirement was originally always treated the same way; see this same day's follow-up entry below for why and how that changed.)

**A carried-forward `APPROVED`/`PENDING_APPROVAL` row is downgraded by reusing `invalidate_approval_if_in_flight` verbatim — exactly the "future caller" that function's own Phase 9 docstring already anticipated for "a standard version change."** The copied `approval_state` value is set first (so the row genuinely represents what the old assignment last had), then that existing function is called on it, which downgrades `PENDING_APPROVAL`/`APPROVED` to `REQUIRES_REASSESSMENT` and leaves every other state (`NOT_ASSESSED`/`ASSESSED`/`REJECTED`) untouched. `approval_decided_at`/`approval_decided_by`/`decision_note` are deliberately **not** copied onto the new row — those describe one specific human sign-off decision against the *old* row's own id, which stays intact in that row's own audit trail; the new row needs a fresh decision if/when it reaches `PENDING_APPROVAL` again, and copying stale decision metadata onto a row now marked `REQUIRES_REASSESSMENT` would misrepresent that a decision had already been made about content nobody has re-confirmed. `assessed_at`/`assessed_by`/`applicability_set_at`/`applicability_set_by` *are* copied, preserving the true provenance of when/who actually performed the underlying assessment — attributing it to the user running the migration instead would misrepresent history in the other direction.

**A `replaced` requirement was originally treated the same as `added` for carry-forward purposes, with no middle-ground treatment — revisited the same day, see the follow-up entry below.** Clone lineage is a mechanical, always-reliable fact about how a row was created; a "replaces" mapping's relationship type is a human's open-vocabulary judgement call (`Equivalent`, `Related To`, ...) whose real-world strength this code has no way to evaluate on its own — carrying an assessment forward on the strength of a possibly-approximate mapping would risk exactly the "migration must not silently change historical compliance assessments" failure §27 warns against, one step removed. This reasoning still holds and is exactly why the follow-up mechanism requires an explicit, separate signal that a *specific* relationship type's strength has been vetted (`implies_equivalence`), rather than trusting the mapping's mere existence — the conclusion "don't trust an unqualified mapping" wasn't wrong, it just turned out to have a real, previously-unbuilt qualification path rather than being permanent.

**The migration endpoint is gated `compliance_officer`/`PROJECT_MANAGER` on the project router, not `compliance_manager` on the org router — a deliberate split from the org router's own initial-assignment endpoint.** Choosing *which* standard a project tracks at all is a Compliance Manager decision (§26); rolling an *already-tracked* standard forward to a newer version is project-level maintenance of an existing assignment, the same class of action as every other mutating endpoint already on `project_router.py` (applicability/assessment/evidence/reviews). This was flagged as an open judgment call in this phase's own brief and resolved in favour of matching `project_router.py`'s existing convention rather than inventing a third gating shape.

**No MCP tool for the migration action itself — only for its "preview before you commit" companion.** Two new read-only tools are declared (`compliance_list_requirement_mappings`, `compliance_get_standard_version_diff`), both plain GETs with no side effects. The migration action is a significant mutation with wide blast radius (every requirement row on an assignment, potential approval downgrades across many rows) and nothing in this phase's own spec asks for a tool — mirroring this module's now-repeated, explicitly-stated principle (Phase 9's approve/reject/submit-for-approval) of adding mutating MCP tools narrowly and only when asked for, not by default. `module.py`'s own docstring states this reasoning explicitly so a future session doesn't need to re-derive it.

**Identify → verify → remediate.** Identify: the two things most likely to regress an existing control in this phase are (a) the migration action bypassing or weakening the existing RBAC composition on a *new* kind of mutating action, and (b) the mapping/diff endpoints leaking cross-org visibility — either a mapping created between two requirements a caller shouldn't be able to see the org boundary of, or a diff/listing endpoint returning data from an organisation other than the one named in the path. Verify: the migration endpoint uses the exact same `_require_officer = require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_officer")` dependency every other mutating endpoint on `project_router.py` already uses — no new dependency was written — and `test_migrate_rbac_officer_and_pm_allowed_plain_member_forbidden` proves the officer-grant/PROJECT_MANAGER-override/plain-member-403 composition applies to it identically; `test_migrate_cross_project_isolation` proves a `project_compliance_id` from one project 404s (not 403, not 200) via another project's path, the same convention `router.py`/`project_router.py` already use everywhere else. For the mapping/diff surfaces: every mapping-creation/lookup path resolves a bare `requirement_id` back to its owning standard/organisation via `_get_org_requirement_or_404` before touching it, and `test_mapping_cross_org_requirement_is_404_not_403` proves a requirement from a genuinely different organisation 404s when named in a mapping payload; `test_diff_rejects_same_version_and_cross_standard_version` proves a version belonging to a different standard 404s when named as the second half of a diff. Remediate: nothing found needing a fix — both the migration action and the mapping/diff surfaces compose correctly against already-hardened Phase 2 (`require_module_role`)/Phase 6-10 (this module's own 404-not-403 convention) mechanisms on first implementation, reusing rather than reimplementing every piece.

**No new SOC 2 policy-document edits were needed this phase.** Checked deliberately, not skipped: the migration action's RBAC gate, audit logging, and soft-archive-not-delete behaviour are all the same already-hardened `require_module_role`/`services.audit.log_event`/`is_archived` conventions every other mutating endpoint in this module already uses; the mapping/diff endpoints introduce no new secret, credential, PII, or retention-relevant data path — a mapping is metadata about two requirement rows, and archiving one (or an old `ProjectCompliance` row post-migration) uses the identical soft-delete convention `docs/soc2/policies/data-retention-and-disposal-policy.md` already covers generically for this codebase's soft-deletable entities. This phase opens no new trust boundary of its own, consistent with Phase 6/9/10's own identical conclusion for the same reason.

**`backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` were not touched.** Both were checked: neither references any Compliance Module model today (their own uses of the word "compliance" are unrelated generic project/requirement content, not `ComplianceStandard`/etc.), so there is nothing yet for Phase 11's new tables to be reconciled against — consistent with this plan's own repeatedly-stated precedent (every phase from 5 through 10) that seeding Compliance Module data, mapping/relationship-type vocabulary included, remains Phase 15's own, already-documented responsibility.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/models.py` (`ComplianceRequirement.cloned_from_requirement_id`; new `ComplianceMappingRelationshipTypeDefinition`/`ComplianceRequirementMapping` models; a new "Phase 11 design decisions" section in the module docstring), `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py` (`ComplianceMappingRelationshipType*`, `ComplianceRequirementMapping*`, `ComplianceRequirementSummaryOut`, the five `*RequirementOut` diff-category schemas, `StandardVersionDiffOut`, `ProjectComplianceMigration*`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/service.py` (`diff_standard_versions`/`build_diff_out` and their private helpers `_changed_content_fields`/`_find_replacement_mapping`/`StandardVersionDiff`; `migrate_project_compliance`/`build_migration_result_out` and `ProjectComplianceMigrationImpact`/`ProjectComplianceMigrationOutcome`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/router.py` (`_clone_requirement_tree` now stamps `cloned_from_requirement_id`; new mapping-relationship-type vocabulary CRUD; new requirement-mapping CRUD + requirement-scoped mapping listing; new `get_standard_version_diff` endpoint), `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py` (new `migrate_project_compliance_version` endpoint), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (two new read-only MCP tools; Phase 11 docstring section explaining the migration-action tool exclusion), `backend/alembic/versions/0031_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` (new).

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` (new, 21 tests): the relationship-type vocabulary's create/list/rename/delete-with-reassignment/RBAC; requirement-mapping create/visible-from-both-sides/navigable/self-link-rejected/duplicate-rejected-but-a-different-relationship-type-allowed/cross-org-404/archive-unarchive/audit-logged/RBAC; the version diff's `added`/`removed`/`modified` built from a real cloned-then-independently-edited-and-deleted tree (plus order-independence and same-version/cross-standard-version rejection), `replaced` built from a real explicit same-standard mapping, and `re_mapped` built from a real cross-standard mapping that a clone doesn't carry forward; the full migration action's happy path (carrying forward an unmodified-and-previously-approved requirement while downgrading it to `requires_reassessment`, a modified requirement landing at defaults, an added requirement landing at defaults, and the exact per-requirement `requirement_impacts` breakdown), the old assignment staying archived-not-deleted with its own assessments completely untouched (asserted via a before/after equality check — the load-bearing guarantee), version/publish/standard/already-assigned/already-archived validation, RBAC composition, cross-project isolation, and audit-event logging. `backend/tests/test_compliance_data_model.py`'s module-registration assertion was updated for ten tools plus a new assertion that no tool name contains "migrate". `backend/tests/test_module_mcp_tools.py`'s real-registry compliance section was extended to both new tools. ## Compliance module plan, Phase 11 follow-up: confirmed carry-forward across a `replaced` mapping (2026-09-06, same day)

Direct user feedback on the Phase 11 entry above, received the same day: always treating a `replaced` requirement's project assessment the same as a genuinely new (`added`) one — forcing it back to blank defaults on every migration — was too blunt in the case the feedback named explicitly: a Compliance Manager has already, deliberately linked an old requirement to its new successor (the feedback's own example: an old "IPX6 water ingress" requirement explicitly mapped to a new "IP67 water ingress" requirement) and judges them equivalent enough that starting the new project assessment from a blank slate is needless rework. Presented back to the user as a concrete choice among three shapes (an org-level type flag with automatic carry-forward; a purely manual per-migration tick-list with no system suggestion; or both together — a type-level flag that only ever makes carry-forward *possible*, with a separate, mandatory per-migration human confirmation) before building anything — the user chose the third, and this entry records that design as built.

**Two independent gates, not one, and neither alone is sufficient — the exact shape the user asked for.** (1) `ComplianceMappingRelationshipTypeDefinition.implies_equivalence` (new boolean column, default `false`) is an org-level, Compliance-Manager-only decision about which relationship types in that org's own extensible vocabulary (§19) are ever strong enough to justify this — nothing in this module hardcodes a fixed allow-list of type *names* (e.g. always trusting "Equivalent" specifically), since §19's vocabulary is explicitly org-defined and open. (2) `ProjectComplianceMigrationRequest.confirmed_replacement_requirement_ids` is a separate, per-migration, per-requirement human decision the compliance officer performing *that specific* migration must make — a mapping existing and being of a strong-enough type only ever makes carry-forward *possible*, never automatic. This two-gate shape is what keeps the mechanism from becoming the kind of automatic cross-requirement inference §19 explicitly rules out ("must not imply that satisfying one requirement automatically satisfies another unless the relationship explicitly supports that behaviour") — the relationship type's own flag is exactly that explicit support, and the per-migration confirmation is exactly what keeps it from being automatic.

**The confirmation list is validated against a freshly computed diff before the migration ever runs, not trusted blindly.** `project_router.py::migrate_project_compliance_version` calls `diff_standard_versions` itself before calling `service.migrate_project_compliance`, builds the set of new-requirement ids that are both part of this migration's `replaced` category *and* linked by a type with `implies_equivalence=True`, and 400s naming every submitted id that fails either check — a stale confirmation (built from an earlier diff, or against a relationship type since toggled back off) is rejected outright, never silently ignored, matching this module's established "never silent" convention applied here to a client-supplied id list rather than a single path parameter. `service.migrate_project_compliance` itself independently re-derives eligibility from its own freshly computed diff regardless of what the caller already validated — belt and suspenders, not a redundant check removed for tidiness, since a service function in this module is never written to trust a caller's id list blindly when it can cheaply re-verify.

**A confirmed `replaced` carry-forward copies the same field set as an `unchanged` one, but `requires_reassessment` is reported unconditionally `True`, unlike `unchanged`'s conditional reporting.** For an `unchanged` (content-identical, lineage-matched) pair, `requires_reassessment` reflects only whether `invalidate_approval_if_in_flight` actually downgraded something — nothing changed about the requirement's own wording, so a row that was merely `ASSESSED` (never submitted for approval) needs no flag. A `replaced` pair is different in kind: by definition its content did *not* lineage-match, so even a human-judged-equivalent replacement changed the requirement's actual wording — a reviewer should always be pointed at it, regardless of whether the copied `approval_state` needed downgrading.

**Denormalising `implies_equivalence` onto the diff's own `replaced` entries (`ReplacedRequirementOut.implies_equivalence`), not requiring a second lookup.** A caller deciding what to submit as `confirmed_replacement_requirement_ids` needs to know, per `replaced` pair, whether it's even eligible — reading this straight off the `GET .../diff/...` response (the action's own documented "preview, then confirm" companion) avoids a second round-trip against the relationship-types list and a client-side join.

**Identify → verify → remediate.** Identify: the one thing that could regress an existing control here is the new validation branch letting a caller carry an assessment forward when it shouldn't be allowed to — either by supplying an id for a pair whose relationship type never had `implies_equivalence` set, or by supplying an id that isn't genuinely part of *this* migration's `replaced` set at all (e.g. copied from a different, unrelated diff response). Verify: `test_migrate_confirmed_replacement_rejected_when_type_not_equivalence` proves the first case 400s even though the mapping genuinely exists and links the right two requirements; `test_migrate_confirmed_replacement_rejected_when_id_not_in_replaced_set` proves the second using a real "added" requirement id from an unrelated migration scenario, not a fabricated one; `test_migrate_replaced_defaults_when_not_confirmed` proves the pre-existing safe default (nothing confirmed → nothing carried forward) is unchanged; `test_migrate_confirmed_replacement_carries_forward_when_type_allows` proves the one genuinely-permitted path still downgrades a carried-forward `APPROVED` state exactly like an `unchanged` carry-forward already does, rather than accidentally leaving it `APPROVED`. Remediate: nothing found needing a fix — the two-gate design was correct on first implementation; both gates were exercised by a failing test before being confirmed to reject correctly, not merely asserted to exist.

**No new SOC 2 policy-document edit needed** — this follow-up reuses the same already-hardened `require_module_role`/`services.audit.log_event` conventions the original Phase 11 entry already concluded needed no edit; the new gate is an additional validation rule on an existing mutating endpoint, not a new trust boundary, new data classification, or new retention concern. `implies_equivalence`'s own mutations (create/update the relationship type) are logged through the same `log_event` calls the original endpoints already made, now carrying the flag's value in `detail`.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/models.py` (`ComplianceMappingRelationshipTypeDefinition.implies_equivalence`; a new "Phase 11 design decisions" paragraph in the module docstring explaining the two-gate mechanism and why it doesn't reopen §19's "must not imply... satisfying" guarantee), `backend/alembic/versions/0031_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` (column added to the same not-yet-shipped migration, not a new one, since Phase 11 itself was still uncommitted when this feedback arrived), `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py` (`ComplianceMappingRelationshipTypeCreate`/`Update`/`Out.implies_equivalence`; `ReplacedRequirementOut.implies_equivalence`; `ProjectComplianceMigrationRequest.confirmed_replacement_requirement_ids`; `ProjectComplianceMigrationRequirementImpact.change` gains `"replaced"`; `ProjectComplianceMigrationResultOut.replaced_count`; corrected a pre-existing docstring inaccuracy on that same schema, which had wrongly grouped `replaced` with `removed` as "no row on the new assignment" — a `replaced` pair's new requirement always gets a materialised row, the same as `added`/`modified`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/service.py` (`_find_replacement_mapping`/`diff_standard_versions`/`StandardVersionDiff`/`build_diff_out` now thread the mapping's own relationship type through to the `replaced` category; `migrate_project_compliance` gains the `confirmed_replacement_requirement_ids` parameter and the confirmed-and-eligible carry-forward branch; `build_migration_result_out` computes `replaced_count`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/router.py` (`create_mapping_relationship_type`/renamed `rename_mapping_relationship_type` → `update_mapping_relationship_type` both read/write `implies_equivalence`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py` (`migrate_project_compliance_version` validates `confirmed_replacement_requirement_ids` against a freshly computed diff before calling the service function, and logs a `confirmed_replaced_carry_forward_count` alongside the existing audit detail), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (a note that the migration action's tool-exclusion holds unchanged despite this addition making the action more consequential, not less).

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` gained: `implies_equivalence` create/toggle coverage on the relationship-type vocabulary; the existing `replaced`-diff test asserts `implies_equivalence: false` for its (deliberately non-equivalence) "Derived From" mapping, plus a new test asserting `true` surfaces correctly for an "Equivalent" type marked accordingly; a new `_setup_migration_scenario_with_replacement` helper (parent requirement approved, then deleted-and-replaced in v2 via an explicit mapping) backing four new migration tests — confirmed-and-eligible carry-forward (copies the approved assessment, downgrades it to `requires_reassessment`, `change="replaced"`/`carried_forward=True`), the not-confirmed default (`carried_forward=False`, still `change="replaced"` rather than the pre-follow-up `"added"`), a 400 when the relationship type lacks `implies_equivalence`, and a 400 when a confirmed id isn't part of the migration's own `replaced` set at all. Full file re-run: 27 passed (21 original + 6 new). `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py`/`test_compliance_data_model.py`/`test_module_mcp_tools.py` re-run together: 18 passed, confirming the amended migration 0031 still matches the models with zero drift. Full backend suite re-run afterward with no other DB-touching process active: 927 passed, 14 failed — the same pre-existing, unrelated mailhog-hostname-resolution failures already documented throughout this file for a host-run pytest session, zero new failures. `ruff check` clean on every touched file. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes needed, per this plan's own repeatedly-stated precedent (checked again, not assumed).

## Module system follow-up: first-party migrations/tests colocated in each module's own directory (2026-09-06, same day)

Direct feedback, received the same day as the Phase 11 entries above (before either had been committed): now that a second and third first-party module are planned (the Decisions Record, Pain Points, and Traceability uplifts docs/compliance-module-plan.md's own "Context" section names as the three uplifts following Compliance), would it make more sense for a module's own Alembic migrations and backend tests to live alongside the rest of that module's code, rather than in the flat, shared `backend/alembic/versions/`/`backend/tests/` directories every module has used until now? Presented back to the user as a scope question — apply this only to Compliance's own already-written files, or make it the standing convention for every module going forward — before restructuring anything; the user chose the systemic convention.

**This reverses a decision this plan's own Phase 1 entry stated "full stop," and that reversal is recorded here explicitly, not silently.** Phase 1's original design (see this file's own "Compliance module plan, Phase 1" entry, 2026-09-04) deliberately kept every first-party module's migration in the single `backend/alembic/versions/` directory, reasoning that a module's own schema changes should go through "a reviewed PR into `backend/alembic/versions/`, exactly as before" — full stop, no per-module exception. That reasoning was about *trust* (a first-party migration is reviewed in-repo code, unlike an externally-discovered module's own `run_migrations`), not about *file location* — and it still holds completely: this follow-up changes where a first-party migration's `.py` file physically sits, not whether it's reviewed, not how many Alembic-tracked revision chains exist (still exactly one), and not which `alembic_version` row tracks it (still exactly one). The "full stop" language was correct for the *question it was actually answering* (should a first-party module get a second, less-reviewed schema-change mechanism — no) and is explicitly *not* being walked back here; a different, narrower question (which directory should the reviewed file live in) simply wasn't the one Phase 1 was settling.

**`ModuleDefinition.migrations_dir` + `app.modules.registry.configure_alembic_version_locations`, not a static `alembic.ini` edit per module.** Alembic reads `version_locations` from its `Config` object to build a `ScriptDirectory` *before* `alembic/env.py` ever executes — by the time this project's own Python code could react to which modules are registered, Alembic has already decided which directories to scan. A static, hand-edited `alembic.ini` listing every module's directory by name would work, but would reopen exactly the "core file needs an edit per new module" problem this plan's own module system has spent four phases eliminating one mechanism at a time (`get_router`/`get_project_router` for endpoints, `models_import_path` for `Base.metadata`, `scheduled_jobs` for APScheduler). Instead, `configure_alembic_version_locations(cfg)` — called on a freshly built `Config`, before any Alembic command runs against it — enumerates `get_module_registry().values()` itself and adds every module's declared `migrations_dir` (an absolute path, resolved against a shared `_BACKEND_DIR` constant) alongside the core `alembic/versions` directory, plus sets `version_path_separator = "os"` (required by Alembic whenever more than one location is configured). A new module gaining its own migration directory therefore needs zero edits to `alembic.ini`, `alembic/env.py`, `app/migrations.py`, or `scripts/db.py` — only its own `ModuleDefinition.migrations_dir` field.

**Deliberately not a recursive scan of `app/modules/`, even though Alembic supports `recursive_version_locations`.** Verified directly before choosing this design: Alembic's revision loader does not merely pattern-match filenames in a configured location, it *executes* every `.py` file it finds there (via `importlib`-based module loading) to read that file's own module-level `revision`/`down_revision` assignments. Pointing a recursive scan at the whole `app/modules/` tree would therefore attempt to execute every module's `models.py`/`service.py`/`router.py`/etc. as if each were a candidate revision script — a real correctness and safety risk, not a theoretical one. `configure_alembic_version_locations` instead adds only the exact, finite list of directories the registry's own `migrations_dir` fields name — the same "explicit, not implicit" principle `models_import_path`'s dotted-path (not directory-scan) design already applies one mechanism up, now applied here too.

**A new `scripts/db.py` wrapper is now this project's documented way to run Alembic commands — bare `alembic <command>` from `backend/` no longer sees every module's migrations.** Since Alembic decides `version_locations` before `env.py` runs, and this repo's own `alembic.ini` is a static file with no per-module entries, a developer typing `alembic upgrade head` directly against `backend/alembic.ini` would silently only see the core directory — not erroring, just quietly missing every module's own revisions, the same "not erroring, just wrong" failure mode this plan's own culture treats as worse than a loud one. `scripts/db.py` builds the same registry-aware `Config` `app.migrations.run_migrations()` already does for the boot-time path, then dispatches to the small subset of `alembic.command.*` functions this project actually uses (`revision`, `upgrade`, `downgrade`, `current`, `history`, `heads`) — deliberately not `alembic.config.CommandLine` itself, which constructs its own `Config` internally before any of this project's own code could call `configure_alembic_version_locations` on it. Verified end to end against the real, already-relocated Compliance migrations before considering this done: `python scripts/db.py heads` resolves to `0031 (head)` and `python scripts/db.py history` walks the complete chain (`<base> -> 0001 -> ... -> 0025 -> 0026 -> ... -> 0031`) correctly across both directories, not just one.

**Tests: a top-level `backend/conftest.py` registering `tests/conftest.py` as a `pytest_plugins` entry, not moving `tests/conftest.py` itself.** pytest applies a conftest.py's fixtures to its own directory and everything below it — `app/modules/compliance/tests/` (a sibling subtree of `tests/`, not a descendant) would never inherit `tests/conftest.py`'s fixtures (`client`, `admin_token`, `org_id`, the session-scoped migration setup) through that mechanism alone. `pytest_plugins` is pytest's own supported way to pull in another conftest's fixtures regardless of directory relationship, but it may only be declared in a *rootdir*-level conftest — which is exactly why this is a new, tiny `backend/conftest.py` (confirmed as this project's pytest rootdir via `backend/pyproject.toml`'s presence) rather than being folded into `tests/conftest.py` in place: moving that file's actual content would break the `from tests.conftest import auth_headers, ...`-style plain-Python-import that dozens of existing test files across the whole suite already rely on, for zero benefit. Verified directly: `pytest app/modules/compliance/tests/ -q` (89 tests, all seven of Compliance's moved test files) passes with the real fixtures applied, with no per-file change needed beyond the intra-module cross-imports below.

**Cross-imports between the moved test files needed updating; imports of `tests.conftest` itself did not.** `tests` has no `__init__.py` (confirmed by inspection) and is therefore an implicit PEP 420 namespace package — `from tests.conftest import auth_headers` continues to resolve correctly from any location, including the newly-moved `app/modules/compliance/tests/`, as long as `backend/` stays on `sys.path` (true for both `pytest` and `python scripts/db.py`, which explicitly `sys.path.insert`s it for exactly this reason). Only the *sibling* imports between compliance test files themselves (e.g. `test_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` reusing helpers from `test_compliance_standards_api.py`/`test_project_compliance_api.py`) needed rewriting from `from tests.test_compliance_standards_api import ...` to `from app.modules.compliance.tests.test_compliance_standards_api import ...`, since those specific modules physically moved.

**Three existing tests that build their own bare `alembic.config.Config` (bypassing `configure_alembic_version_locations`) would have silently broken the moment any migration lived outside the core directory — found and fixed as part of this change, not left as a latent trap.** `test_compliance_data_model.py::test_migration_0026_upgrade_and_downgrade_round_trip`, `test_project_group_role_migration.py`, and `test_default_group_migration.py` (the latter two testing *core* migrations, not Compliance's) each had their own `_alembic_config()` helper, duplicated three times, none aware of the new mechanism — confirmed by direct reproduction: running any of them against the post-move repository state failed with `alembic.util.exc.CommandError: Can't locate revision identified by 'head'`/`'0031'`, since resolving `"head"` requires walking the *entire* chain including Compliance's now-relocated revisions, not just the one directory a bare `Config` still pointed at. Fixed by extracting one shared `tests.conftest.build_alembic_config()` (which does call `configure_alembic_version_locations`) and pointing all three at it instead of each keeping (or reinventing) its own copy — a single point of correctness for every future migration-driving test, rather than a fourth call site quietly missing the requirement the next time this happens.

**Identify → verify → remediate.** Identify: the two things that could regress an existing control here are (a) `configure_alembic_version_locations` somehow granting a module's migration a different, less-reviewed trust level than before merely by relocating its file, and (b) the relocation silently breaking an existing migration-driving test or the schema-drift check without anyone noticing until CI or production. Verify, for (a): the function only ever adds directories named by `ModuleDefinition.migrations_dir` on modules already present in the live registry (first-party `INSTALLED_MODULES`, the exact same review gate as before) — confirmed by reading its own implementation, which takes no external input beyond the registry itself, and by the recursive-scan risk being identified and deliberately avoided (see above) rather than only fixed after the fact. Verify, for (b): `test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` (the exact test the original 2026 email-footer incident this file already documents was written to catch) was run immediately after the move and passes with zero drift; the three latent-trap tests above were actually run against the post-move state *before* being fixed, reproducing the real failure first, not merely reasoned about; the full compliance test suite (89 tests, all seven moved files) was run from its new location and passes with real fixtures applied, not skipped or mocked. Remediate: the three bare-`Config` tests were the one real gap found, fixed as described above; nothing else found needing a fix.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/registry.py` (`ModuleDefinition.migrations_dir`; `configure_alembic_version_locations`; `_BACKEND_DIR` constant; docstring corrections on `models_import_path`/`migrations_import_path` reflecting the new mechanism and why it doesn't weaken either), `backend/app/migrations.py` (`run_migrations` calls `configure_alembic_version_locations`), `backend/scripts/db.py` (new — the `revision`/`upgrade`/`downgrade`/`current`/`history`/`heads` wrapper), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (`migrations_dir` set; docstring note), `backend/alembic/versions/0026_compliance_data_model.py` through `0031_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` moved to `backend/app/modules/compliance/migrations/` (six files, `git mv`, contents unchanged), `backend/tests/conftest.py` (`build_alembic_config()`, exported), `backend/conftest.py` (new — the rootdir `pytest_plugins` shim), `backend/tests/test_schema_migrations_match_models.py` (docstring/assertion-message wording updated for the two-location reality), `backend/tests/test_compliance_approval_workflow.py` through `test_project_compliance_api.py` moved to `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/` (seven files, `git mv`/`mv`, cross-imports between them updated, `tests.conftest` imports unchanged), `backend/tests/test_project_group_role_migration.py`/`test_default_group_migration.py` (switched to the shared `build_alembic_config()`, their own duplicated `_alembic_config()` helpers removed).

**Docs.** `docs/modules.md` (the module-authoring "Backend" checklist's migration step rewritten for `migrations_dir`/`scripts/db.py`; a new testing paragraph on `app/modules/<key>/tests/` and the `backend/conftest.py` plugin mechanism), `docs/development.md` (the manual-migration instruction now points at `scripts/db.py`; the backend-tests paragraph now names both test locations), `docs/solution-architecture.md` (a new "Module system follow-up (2026-09-06)" paragraph in the Modular Feature System section), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/registry.py`, `backend/app/migrations.py`, `backend/scripts/db.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py`, `backend/app/modules/compliance/migrations/0026_compliance_data_model.py` through `0031_compliance_mapping_and_version_impact.py` (moved from `backend/alembic/versions/`), `backend/tests/conftest.py`, `backend/conftest.py` (new), `backend/tests/test_schema_migrations_match_models.py`, `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/*.py` (seven files, moved from `backend/tests/`), `backend/tests/test_project_group_role_migration.py`, `backend/tests/test_default_group_migration.py`; `docs/modules.md`, `docs/development.md`, `docs/solution-architecture.md`, `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module plan, Phase 12: frontend — Compliance Manager surfaces (2026-09-06)

Twelfth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`, and the first frontend work the Compliance Module itself has had (Phases 5–11 were backend-only) — the org-level, Compliance-Manager-facing management UI for §2–§6 (standards, versions, the requirement tree, required actions, the two extensible vocabularies) and §19 (cross-standard requirement mapping, including viewing the Phase 11 version diff). Explicitly not the project-level assignment/assessment UI (Phase 13) or the org-wide dashboard (Phase 14) — confirmed against the plan's own Phase 12 spec text before designing any screen, not assumed.

**A real, load-bearing gap found before writing any component: Phase 3's Tier A registry mechanism is project-scoped end to end, with no org-level equivalent.** `frontend/src/hooks/useProjectEnabledModules.ts` fetches `GET /projects/{id}/enabled-modules` and returns `[]` whenever `projectId` is `null`; `Layout.tsx`'s nav rail only renders a module's `NavRailLink` inside its project-scoped block; `App.tsx` only splices `buildModuleRoutes(enabledModules, projectId)`'s output when a `projectId` is present in the URL. All three return "nothing" for any org-level (non-`/projects/:id/...`) page, by construction — none of Phase 3's own tests or notes claimed otherwise (its own notes say the mechanism was "proven only against a fixture module," project-scoped). Compliance's org-level catalogue has no owning project at all, so this isn't a corner case to work around, it's a structural mismatch between what Phase 3 built and what Phase 12 needs. Building a genuine org-level nav/routing equivalent (a new `GET /orgs/{id}/enabled-modules`, an org-scoped nav rendering branch, an org-scoped `buildModuleRoutes` variant) would be new, generic module-system infrastructure — a legitimate thing for a future module-system phase to do once a second org-level-only module actually needs it, but disproportionate to add as a side effect of one module's own frontend phase, and not what "Frontend: Compliance Manager Surfaces" asks for.

**Resolution: mount `ComplianceAdminPanel` as a new group inside the existing `OrgAdminPage`, reusing that page's own established pattern for a section not every viewer can use.** `OrgAdminPage` is already reachable by any org member regardless of role (`/orgs` lists every org a user belongs to and links each to `/orgs/{id}/admin`, confirmed by reading `OrgListPage.tsx` directly) — its own `loadOrgData` already wraps several admin-only fetches (`advanced-settings`, `sso-config`, `scim-token`, the Phase 1 `/modules` list) in `try { ... } catch (err) { if (!(err instanceof ApiError && err.status === 403)) throw err; }`, degrading that one section gracefully rather than gating the whole page. A new `"compliance"` `OrgAdminGroupKey`/`ResourceMenuGroupDef` entry (`/orgs/:orgId/admin/compliance`) follows the same shape: `ComplianceAdminPanel` does its own fetch (`GET .../action-types`, view-gated by `require_org_module_enabled` only — any org member with the module enabled, not just a Compliance Manager) and renders a plain "module isn't enabled, or you don't have access" message on failure rather than crashing or leaving the tab blank. This still satisfies Tier A's actual definition — "installed at build time, direct component imports, full [shared-component] consistency" — every component lives under `frontend/src/modules/compliance/` and is a real, build-time-compiled import (`DirectoryTable`, `FilterPanel`, `Modal`, `SidePanel`, `DefinitionList`, `Tabs`, `ConfirmDialog`, `useToast()`); only the *routing/nav-discovery* half of Phase 3's mechanism, which has no org-scoped analogue, doesn't apply. `installedModules`/`buildModuleRoutes` are left untouched — no fake registry entry was added purely to look "more Tier A," since it would never actually be exercised (`buildModuleRoutes([], null)` on any org-admin URL).

**IA: three `Tabs` (Standards / Action types / Mapping types), not a fourth "requirement mappings" tab or a `ResourceMenu`.** Three groups is inside the style guide's own "≤5 co-relevant views" `Tabs` threshold — `ResourceMenu` is for the opposite case ("more than five, opened rarely as a whole"), and OrgAdminPage's own existing groups are the entity this page's `ResourceMenu` already scopes to; nesting a second `ResourceMenu` a level down for three items would misapply the pattern, not extend it. Cross-standard requirement mappings (§19) got no standalone tab: §19 itself frames a mapping as something "visible from both requirements" and navigated *from* a requirement, not browsed as an independent flat list — so mapping CRUD lives inside a requirement's own `RequirementMappingsModal` (opened from its row in the tree), reached via a target-requirement picker (three cascading selects: standard → version → requirement, since there is no cross-org requirement search endpoint to type-ahead against) rather than a fourth top-level surface with no natural entry point of its own.

**Standard → version → requirement-tree drill-down replaces the content column in place, not a nested `SidePanel`.** `SidePanel`'s own `maxWidth: 420` (confirmed by reading `SidePanel.tsx` directly) is deliberately narrow for a viewer-alongside-a-list pattern — a requirement-tree editor with per-node add/edit/delete/move/mappings controls and nested required actions needs the full content-column width. `StandardsPanel` therefore holds `selectedStandard`(`SidePanel`, narrow: standard fields + a flat versions list + "new version") and `activeVersion` (drill-down: swaps the whole tab body for `VersionWorkspace`, with an explicit "← Back to {standard}" control) as two different depths of the same navigation, matching how a `SidePanel` is reserved for "view an existing entity with the list still visible" while a genuinely heavier child view gets the full column — the same distinction `RequirementsPage`'s own detail view already draws elsewhere in this app.

**Requirement tree is assembled client-side from the backend's flat, DFS-ordered list — there is no nested-tree endpoint.** Confirmed by reading `router.py::list_requirements`/`_flatten_requirements_dfs` directly rather than assumed: `GET .../requirements` returns a flat `list[ComplianceRequirementOut]` with `parent_requirement_id` populated, already depth-first-ordered with each sibling group internally `sort_order`-sorted. `frontend/src/modules/compliance/api.ts::buildRequirementTree` re-nests it (group by `parent_requirement_id`, recurse) without re-sorting — the backend's own ordering is already correct, re-sorting client-side would be redundant work with a chance of disagreeing with it. Required actions are a separate per-requirement fetch (no bulk "every required action for a version" endpoint exists), lazily fetched on a requirement node's first expand and cached in component state, rather than N eager fetches for a tree that may have many collapsed nodes.

**Reused `DefinitionList` for both org-scoped vocabularies (`ActionTypesPanel`, `MappingTypesPanel`) rather than a bespoke list for either — but `DefinitionList` needed a small, generic extension first.** Its existing contract (`fields: DefinitionListField<T>[]`) is text-only (`isValid` requires every field's value non-empty), with no way to express `ComplianceMappingRelationshipTypeDefinition.implies_equivalence`'s boolean toggle. Rather than bolt a boolean variant onto `DefinitionListField` (which would still be text-shaped for every *other* existing call site) or fork a second list component for one different field, `DefinitionList` gained an optional `renderExtra?: (item: T) => ReactNode` slot, rendered between the text field(s) and the reorder/delete buttons, defaulting to nothing so every pre-existing call site (project statuses, link types) is unaffected — confirmed by re-running `DefinitionList.stories.tsx`'s full existing suite unchanged after the addition. `MappingTypesPanel` renders a `ToggleSwitch` in that slot, calling its own `updateMappingRelationshipType` (which always resends both `name` and `implies_equivalence`, since the backend's `PATCH` schema replaces both fields together) independently of `DefinitionList`'s own `onRename` flow — a toggle is a materially different, single-field mutation from a rename, not a variant of it.

**No client-side "can this user manage compliance" precomputation — mutating controls are always rendered; a 403 surfaces as an error toast.** There is no existing "my own effective roles for this org, including module roles" endpoint to check against without adding one, and `require_org_module_enabled("compliance")`'s own view gate already lets any org member with the module enabled reach this page's read data — the same posture `OrgAdminPage`'s own many admin-only sections already take (attempt the mutation, `catch` and show the resulting error) rather than an approach unique to this module.

**Owner reassignment has no dedicated UI** — `StandardFormModal`'s edit path always resubmits the standard's own `owner_id` unchanged (the backend's `ComplianceStandardUpdate` schema requires it on every `PATCH`, with no partial-update semantics). §2 only requires "Owner" exist as an attribute, not that it be reassignable from this phase's UI, and a proper reassignment control needs `UserAutocomplete` wired up for a single field with no other consumer yet in this phase — flagged explicitly here rather than left a silent, undiscoverable gap; a future phase (or a small follow-up) can wire it in the same way `OrgAdminPage.tsx` already does elsewhere.

**Two real, pre-existing issues found incidentally while verifying this phase against a live `tests/container` stack, both fixed as part of this same change, per this repo's standing "fix, don't defer" rule:**

1. **`OrgAdminPage.tsx::grantOrgRole` sent `{ role }` with no `user_id`, but the backend's `OrgRoleAssign` schema (`schemas/org.py`, present since the Aug-1 UI redesign, well before this plan started) requires `user_id: UUID`** — every attempt to grant a core org role (Member/Project creator/Org admin) through the Users table's Roles dropdown has 422'd since that schema was introduced, silently: `grantOrgRole`'s own `catch` block only shows a toast, and no Storybook story or Playwright spec had ever exercised this specific click against a real backend (the Storybook story asserting the call shape, `UsersSectionAndCreateUser`, mocks `api.post` unconditionally — a mock accepts any payload shape, so it had been asserting the *bug's own* shape, `{ role: "project_creator" }` with no `user_id`, as correct). Found only because this session rebuilt `tests/container`'s backend image for the first time since Phase 5 (see next paragraph) and then ran `module-contributed-roles.spec.ts` end-to-end against it while updating that spec (below) — the first time this exact click had ever executed against a live, schema-enforcing backend. Fixed with the one missing field (`{ user_id: u.user_id, role }`); the Storybook assertion pinning the old shape was corrected to match, and the Playwright suite (below) now proves the real round trip. Project-role grants elsewhere in the same file (`assignProjectRole`-style calls, lines ~809/842) already included `user_id` correctly — this was an isolated omission on the org-role path only, not a systemic pattern.
2. **`tests/container`'s backend image had gone stale, pre-dating Phase 5** — `GET /orgs/{id}/modules` returned `[]` against the running container even though Compliance's `MODULE_DEFINITION` (`default_enabled=True`) has existed in the working tree since Phase 5 (2026-09-05); nothing in Phases 5–11 had rebuilt this specific Docker image, since their own verification was pytest-only, per each phase's own notes. Rebuilding it (`docker compose build backend && ... up -d --no-deps backend`) applied migrations 0025→0031 cleanly on startup and made Compliance a real, registered module for the first time in this environment — which is what actually surfaced finding (1) above, and is also why `module-contributed-roles.spec.ts` and `org-admin-modules.spec.ts` (below) needed updating: both had explicitly, correctly scoped themselves to "no real module exists yet" and named exactly this rebuild as the trigger to revisit.

**Two Playwright specs updated to match the now-real Compliance module, per their own explicit "revisit once Phase 5 ships a real module" docstrings — not a Phase 12 feature change, an overdue one from Phase 1/2/5 becoming due the moment the container above was rebuilt.** `module-contributed-roles.spec.ts`'s two tests previously asserted "exactly N core role checkboxes, nothing extra" (the correct assertion for a registry with zero modules); now asserts a real fourth (`"Compliance Manager (Compliance)"`, org-scoped) and fifth (`"Compliance Officer"`, project-scoped, no module-name suffix per Phase 2's own established difference between the two surfaces) option is present alongside the fixed core set, and that granting/revoking a core role still works (this is what caught finding (1) above). `org-admin-modules.spec.ts` previously asserted the Modules section's *empty* state; now asserts the Compliance row renders, entitled and enabled by default, and its `ToggleSwitch` actually flips (toggled off then back on, leaving the org's own enablement state as found, per this repo's test-idempotency rule).

**Backend.** None — this phase is frontend-only, per its own spec, and no gap was found requiring even a small backend addition (the org-scoped read/write surface Phases 6/11 already built is sufficient for every screen this phase needed).

**Frontend.** `frontend/src/modules/compliance/` (new): `types.ts` (module-local DTO interfaces mirroring `schemas.py`'s org-router shapes — kept local rather than added to the central `frontend/src/api/types.ts`, a deliberate judgment call: this is the first genuine Tier A installed module, and its own, large [15+ shapes] response-type surface fits the "installed module owns its own code" principle better than growing the one shared file every other feature's types already live in; the one exception is `ComplianceStandardVersionStatus` and its `COMPLIANCE_STANDARD_VERSION_STATUS_LABEL` map, which live in `api/types.ts` because this repo's binding label-map rule, CLAUDE.md/style guide Principle 12, names that file specifically), `api.ts` (request functions for every org-router endpoint this phase's UI calls, plus `buildRequirementTree`), `ComplianceAdminPanel.tsx` (the `Tabs`-based entry point `OrgAdminPage.tsx` imports directly), `StandardsPanel.tsx` (standards `DirectoryTable`/`FilterPanel`/create `Modal`/detail `SidePanel`/version lifecycle), `VersionWorkspace.tsx` (the version drill-down: publish/retire via `ConfirmDialog`, "Compare versions"), `RequirementTree.tsx` (the client-assembled tree, required-action editor, per-node CRUD), `RequirementMappingsModal.tsx` (§19 mapping CRUD from one requirement's own row), `VersionDiffModal.tsx` (§27 diff viewer, read-only), `ActionTypesPanel.tsx`/`MappingTypesPanel.tsx` (`DefinitionList`-based vocabularies). `frontend/src/pages/OrgAdminPage.tsx` (new `"compliance"` group). `frontend/src/components/DefinitionList.tsx` (`renderExtra` slot, additive). `frontend/src/api/types.ts` (`ComplianceStandardVersionStatus`/its label map). `frontend/src/i18n/strings.ts` (`orgAdmin.groupCompliance`).

**Tests.** `frontend/src/modules/compliance/ComplianceAdminPanel.stories.tsx` (new, 7 stories + light/dark theme variants): standards list + create, standard detail → version workspace → add-requirement round trip (portalled `Modal`/`SidePanel` content queried via `within(document.body)`, not `canvas` — confirmed necessary by a first failing run, the same convention `OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx`'s own modal assertions already establish), the action-types and mapping-types tabs (including the new `implies_equivalence` toggle calling `api.patch` with both fields), and the module-disabled error state. `frontend/src/components/DefinitionList.stories.tsx` gained `WithRenderExtra` (a boolean-checkbox harness proving the new slot's contract independent of any Compliance-specific consumer). `tests/playwright/tests/e2e-workflows/compliance-standards-management.spec.ts` (new) — logs in as the already-seeded `orgAdminAlphaBeta` persona (not a dedicated `compliance_manager` persona: `require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_manager")` composes with `OrgRole.ORG_ADMIN` by Phase 2's own design, so no new seed persona/grant was needed), creates a dynamically-named action type, standard, and draft version (per this repo's test-idempotency rule — no shared seed fixture is touched), adds a requirement and a required action, then publishes the version and confirms mutating controls disappear. Run twice back-to-back against a live `tests/container` stack to confirm idempotency; both runs green. `module-contributed-roles.spec.ts`/`org-admin-modules.spec.ts` (updated, see above) both green after the `grantOrgRole` fix. A broader regression pass (`multi-org-admin`, `org-admin-manage-users-modal`, `org-admin-nav-link`, `org-admin-project-statuses-and-link-types`, `role-display-collapsing`, `single-org-admin` — every nearby spec exercising `OrgAdminPage`'s role-granting or resource-menu machinery) run clean, confirming the `grantOrgRole` fix regressed nothing.

`tsc -b --noEmit`, `eslint .` (repo-wide, zero new warnings/errors), and `npm run build` all clean. `vitest run --project=storybook` run in full (73 files, 652 tests) — all green; three pre-existing, unrelated `Layout.stories.tsx` unhandled-rejection log lines noted but not fixed (a `/enabled-modules` path its own mock never covered, from Phase 3 — zero test failures result, cosmetic console noise only from an async effect racing test teardown; flagged here rather than silently patched, since fixing it would be undocumented scope creep on a file this phase never otherwise touches). No backend tests were run (no backend files were changed this phase) beyond the direct `curl` verification against the rebuilt container that confirmed finding (1)'s root cause before writing the fix. No `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` changes — per this plan's own repeatedly-stated precedent, seeding compliance data remains Phase 15's job, and this phase's own Playwright spec seeds its own dynamic fixtures via the UI instead.

**Same-day follow-up, direct feedback: the new Playwright spec was relocated out of the flat `e2e-workflows/` bucket into a module-scoped directory, `tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/`, extending this file's own "Module system follow-up: first-party migrations/tests colocated in each module's own directory" convention (above) from backend migrations/tests to Playwright e2e specs.** `playwright.config.ts`'s `testDir: "./tests"` has no `testMatch` override and already matches recursively, so no config change was needed — only the spec's own relative import of shared `helpers.ts` (`./helpers` → `../../e2e-workflows/helpers`; `helpers.ts` itself stays in `e2e-workflows/` as shared cross-spec infrastructure, the Playwright analogue of `tests/conftest.py` staying put while module-specific backend test files moved out to `app/modules/<key>/tests/`). Re-run from its new location against the live `tests/container` stack to confirm the move itself introduced no regression: 1 passed. A future module's own e2e specs should follow the same `tests/playwright/tests/modules/<key>/` shape rather than adding to `e2e-workflows/`.

**Same-day follow-up, Storybook coverage gap closed: seven dedicated, isolated story files added, one per remaining compliance component.** A repo-wide check of every `.tsx` component/page file against its `.stories.tsx` counterpart found this module was the sole exception to this codebase's 100%-consistent "every component has its own story file" convention — `ComplianceAdminPanel.stories.tsx`'s 7 integration-style stories exercised flows through the composed panel only, leaving `StandardsPanel`, `VersionWorkspace`, `RequirementTree`, `RequirementMappingsModal`, `VersionDiffModal`, `ActionTypesPanel`, and `MappingTypesPanel` with no coverage of their own. Each of the seven new files (`frontend/src/modules/compliance/<Component>.stories.tsx`) mounts that one component directly, with its own mocked `api` responses (`spyOn(api, "get"/"post"/"patch"/"delete")`, the same stateful-mock convention `ComplianceAdminPanel.stories.tsx` established) rather than drilling down through `ComplianceAdminPanel`'s tabs — matching the isolation pattern this app's other "used-inside-a-bigger-page-but-independently-tested" components already follow (`MultiSelectDropdown.stories.tsx`, `AddToGroupControl.stories.tsx`, `ConfirmDialog.stories.tsx`). Each covers what's specific to its own component rather than re-proving what the composed file or a shared component's own stories already cover: `ActionTypesPanel`/`MappingTypesPanel` exercise their wiring to the compliance action-type/mapping-relationship-type endpoints only (`DefinitionList`'s own generic rename/reorder/delete-with-reassign mechanics stay covered by `DefinitionList.stories.tsx`); `StandardsPanel` covers search/archive-filter/create/edit/archive and the drill-into-`VersionWorkspace` transition (stopping at proving the transition happens, not `VersionWorkspace`'s own behaviour); `VersionWorkspace` covers the status-driven publish/retire/immutability-note logic and the "Compare versions" entry point (stopping at proving `VersionDiffModal` opens); `RequirementTree` covers add-root/add-child/reorder/edit/delete for requirements, lazy-loaded expand/collapse, and the full required-action add/edit/move/delete cycle, plus the read-only (`isDraft: false`) control-hiding behaviour; `RequirementMappingsModal` covers its mapping list/archive-toggle and the three-level cascading standard→version→requirement picker's create flow; `VersionDiffModal` covers all five diff categories (added/removed/modified/replaced/re-mapped) rendering from a directly-supplied diff response, an empty-diff state, switching the comparison version, and an error state. No component `.tsx` file needed changing to write any of these. While writing `StandardsPanel.stories.tsx`, found a real pre-existing bug: the standard-edit `onSave` handler spread its whole `StandardFormModal` `values` object — which still carries the create-only `reference` field, since that type is shared with the create form — into `updateStandard`'s payload, even though the edit form never renders a reference input and `updateStandard`'s own payload type doesn't declare `reference` at all; every standard edit had therefore been silently resending the standard's original reference unchanged. Initially pinned in the story rather than fixed, per the sub-agent's own remit to flag rather than modify a component file unasked. **Verified and fixed in the same session**: `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py`'s `ComplianceStandardUpdate` confirms `reference` is deliberately excluded ("immutable after creation") with no `extra: forbid`, so Pydantic's default `extra: ignore` was silently dropping the stray field rather than 422ing — a real, if inert, bug, not a false alarm, and trivial to fix. `StandardsPanel.tsx`'s edit `onSave` now destructures only `{ name, description, issuing_organisation }` from the form values before building the update payload, rather than spreading the whole object; `StandardsPanel.stories.tsx`'s `StandardDetailEditAndArchive` assertion was updated to pin the corrected (no-`reference`) payload. `npx tsc -b`, `npx eslint .` (repo-wide), and `vitest run --project=storybook` re-run after the fix (compliance module: 8 files/62 tests, all green) confirm no regression. `npx tsc -b`, `npx eslint .` (repo-wide), and `vitest run --project=storybook` (full suite, 80 files/707 tests, plus the 8 compliance-module files run in isolation) all green, including every new file's light/dark theme pair; the same three pre-existing, unrelated `Layout.stories.tsx` unhandled-rejection log lines from the original Phase 12 run were re-confirmed present in complete isolation (no compliance files loaded) and are therefore unrelated to this follow-up.
