## Compliance module plan, Phase 13: frontend — project compliance view (2026-09-07)

Thirteenth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` — the project-scoped, Project-Manager/Compliance-Officer-facing view (§21, plus UI portions of §7-§10, §12, §13): assigning a standard to a project, the §9 hierarchical-applicability tree with a mandatory visually-distinct explicit/inherited/overridden treatment, per-requirement assessment/required-actions/evidence/approval-sign-off, a project-wide evidence library, scheduled reviews per assignment, and a cross-assignment "what remains outstanding" summary.

**Confirmed before building anything: unlike Phase 12, this phase's UI genuinely is project-scoped, so Phase 3's real `installedModules`/`buildModuleRoutes`/`useProjectEnabledModules`/`Layout.tsx` nav mechanism applies — no `OrgAdminPage`-style workaround needed.** Read Phase 3's own spec and its actual implementation directly rather than assuming Phase 12's workaround was now the established pattern: `useProjectEnabledModules` keys off a `projectId` parsed from the URL, `Layout.tsx`'s nav rail renders a `NavRailLink` per project-enabled module, and `buildModuleRoutes` splices a Tier A module's own registered routes into `App.tsx`'s `<Routes>` — all three are already fully generic and project-scoped, exactly what this phase needs. `frontend/src/modules/registry.ts`'s `installedModules` array (empty since Phase 3, never previously populated by a real module) now has its first real entry: `{ key: "compliance", routes: [{ path: "/projects/:projectId/modules/compliance", element: <ProjectCompliancePage/> }] }`.

**A real, load-bearing gap found before this could work at all: `ModuleFrontendManifest.nav_path`'s own documented `"{project_id}"` placeholder syntax had never actually been interpolated by anything.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` had no `frontend_manifest` at all yet (Phase 12 never needed one, having bypassed this mechanism entirely) — added one (`tier="installed"`, `nav_path="/projects/{project_id}/modules/compliance"`), matching the exact placeholder example `ModuleFrontendManifest`'s own Phase 3 docstring already gave. But `routers/projects.py::list_project_enabled_modules` (the only endpoint that actually has a concrete `project_id` in scope) built `ModuleFrontendManifestOut(**vars(manifest))` verbatim — passing the literal string `"{project_id}"` straight to the frontend, which would have rendered `<Link to="/projects/{project_id}/modules/compliance">`, a nonsensical URL no route could ever match. Confirmed nothing had ever exercised this path for real: `test_module_frontend_integration.py`'s own existing fixture module used a plain literal `nav_path` with no placeholder. Fixed by having that one endpoint (not `GET /orgs/{id}/modules`, which has no single project in scope and deliberately leaves the placeholder as-is for its own admin-bookkeeping display) interpolate `"{project_id}"` with the real `project_id` in both `nav_path` and `frame_url` before returning `ModuleFrontendManifestOut`. Two new tests added directly to `test_module_frontend_integration.py` (a dedicated `project_scoped_installed_module` fixture, following that file's own "always register-and-tear-down a fixture module" convention) prove both halves: the project-scoped endpoint interpolates, the org-scoped one doesn't.

**A second, more serious real bug found only once the plumbing above was live-tested end to end: a genuine race condition in `App.tsx`'s own route-splicing, invisible until a real Tier A project-scoped route existed to trigger it.** `useProjectEnabledModules` starts `modules` at `[]` while its `GET .../enabled-modules` fetch is in flight (by design, per its own pre-Phase-13 docstring: "Returns `[]`... while the fetch is in flight"). `App.tsx`'s `<Routes>` evaluates `buildModuleRoutes(enabledModules, projectId)` synchronously on every render — so on a *fresh* navigation straight to a module's own nav-rail link (the first paint before the fetch resolves), `buildModuleRoutes([], projectId)` contributes zero routes, nothing else in the static route list matches `/projects/{id}/modules/compliance`, and React Router's own wildcard fallback (`<Navigate to="/projects" replace/>`) fires immediately — bouncing the user straight back to `/projects` before the fetch could ever complete and contribute the real route. Caught by the Playwright spec below, not by Storybook: `App.stories.tsx`'s own `TierARoutingHarness` (Phase 3) pre-seeds `enabledModules` synchronously via a fixture, so the race never had a window to manifest there, and Phase 12's org-level panel never used this routing mechanism at all — Compliance is the first module ever to hit this in a real, unmocked, network-latency-bearing browser. Fixed generically, not with a Compliance-specific patch: `useProjectEnabledModules` now returns `{ modules, loaded }` instead of a bare array (`loaded` is `true` immediately when `projectId` is `null`, since there is nothing to wait for); both call sites updated (`Layout.tsx` destructures `modules` only, indifferent to loading state — nav entries simply pop in once ready, no bug there). `App.tsx`'s wildcard route's own `element` now reads: render a `Spinner` instead of `Navigate` specifically when `projectId` is set and `modulesLoaded` is still `false` — every other path (no project in the URL, or modules already loaded) is completely unaffected, so this doesn't add a loading gate in front of any of the app's existing, already-working project pages, only in front of the brief window where an as-yet-unknown project path might turn out to be a module's own route. `frontend/src/components/Layout.stories.tsx`'s own `mockLayoutApis` was also found, in the same pass, to have never mocked `/enabled-modules` at all — every one of its stories with a project route was throwing an uncaught rejection into the Storybook/vitest run (not failing any assertion, since nothing checked for it, but real console noise across three stories); fixed in the same commit as a `# fix, don't defer` follow-through even though `Layout.stories.tsx` is not itself a Phase 13 file.

**IA: three top-level `Tabs` on `ProjectCompliancePage` (Standards / Evidence / Outstanding), then a further two-`Tabs` drill-down (`ProjectComplianceDetail`: Requirements / Reviews) per selected assignment — not a `ResourceMenu`, and not one flat page.** Both tab groups are well inside the style guide's "≤5 co-relevant views" `Tabs` threshold. Evidence is genuinely project-wide, not nested under one assignment (§13's own "a single piece of evidence should be capable of supporting multiple compliance requirements and/or standards" — mirrors Phase 8's identical project-scoped-not-assignment-scoped call for the `ComplianceEvidence` model itself), so it earns a top-level tab rather than living inside the per-assignment drill-down. "Outstanding" is new relative to Phase 12's IA: §21's own explicit "the view should make it easy... to determine what remains outstanding" is best served by one place gathering the three existing cross-assignment listings (`GET .../non-compliant-requirements`, `.../pending-approvals`, `.../reviews-due`) that Phases 7/9/10 already built read-only endpoints for — none of which had any frontend consumer before this phase — rather than requiring every assignment to be opened in turn to see what needs attention.

**Standard/version drill-down replaces the Standards tab's content in place, matching Phase 12's own `StandardsPanel` → `VersionWorkspace` precedent exactly, for the same reason: a requirement tree with per-node assessment controls needs more than `SidePanel`'s 420px.** `ProjectCompliancePage` holds `selected: ProjectCompliance | null`; when set, it renders `ProjectComplianceDetail` full content-column width in place of the assignment `DirectoryTable`, with its own "← Back" control — not a nested `SidePanel`.

**§9's mandatory "UI must clearly distinguish explicit/inherited/overridden" requirement is a dedicated, shared component (`ApplicabilityBadge.tsx`), not inlined per call site.** Extracted after first inlining it directly in `ApplicabilityTree.tsx` and then needing the identical treatment again in `RequirementAssessmentPanel.tsx`'s own header — rather than let the two copies drift, the badge logic (EXPLICIT: a plain undecorated badge; INHERITED: greyed/italic with an explanatory `title`; OVERRIDDEN: the theme's `--color-warning` colour, bold, with its own explanatory `title`) now lives in exactly one place, imported by both, with its own dedicated story file proving all three states render distinctly (`AllStatesSideBySide`) as well as individually.

**`ProjectComplianceRequirement.effective_applicability`/`applicability_source`, `compliance_status`, and `approval_state` are three independently-rendered badges per tree row, not folded into one, matching §10's own explicit "applicability should remain separate from compliance status" and §12's "approval/sign-off should be reflected separately from the calculated compliance percentage."** A Not-Applicable requirement never shows a compliance-status badge at all (the compliance-status badge is conditional on `effective_applicability === "applicable"`) rather than showing a `not_started`/similar status alongside "Not applicable," which would visually imply the two states coexist meaningfully when §10 says they shouldn't.

**A real UI staleness bug found while running the Playwright spec below end to end, not from static reading: the "Overall compliance status" summary card went stale after assessing/approving a requirement, until the assignment was closed and reopened.** `ProjectComplianceDetail` originally rendered its `status` prop directly — a snapshot fetched once by `ProjectCompliancePage` when the assignment list first loaded, never refreshed by anything happening inside `ApplicabilityTree`'s own nested `RequirementAssessmentPanel`. Fixed generically rather than special-cased to one action: `ApplicabilityTree` gained an optional `onAssessmentChanged?: () => void`, invoked every time its own `reloadOne` (already called after any applicability/assessment/required-action/approval mutation) refetches this assignment's `ProjectComplianceRequirement` rows; `ProjectComplianceDetail` lifts `status` into local `liveStatus` state and passes a handler that re-fetches `GET .../status` and swaps in the matching row by `project_compliance_id`, best-effort (a failed refresh just leaves the card at its previous value, since the tree's own per-row badges are already the authoritative live view regardless). The top-level assignment list (`ProjectCompliancePage`) is deliberately *not* live-synced the same way — it already only ever shows a load-time snapshot, refreshed on its own existing `reload()` triggers (archive/unarchive, a fresh assignment), matching this app's existing precedent elsewhere (e.g. `StandardsPanel`'s own standards list doesn't live-refresh while a version workspace nested underneath is being edited either).

**Evidence linkage from the requirement side is a plain `<select>` populated from `listEvidence(projectId)` filtered to not-already-linked, non-archived rows — not a second, evidence-specific picker component.** §13's canonical evidence CRUD surface stays the top-level Evidence tab (create, edit, revalidate, archive, file attachments via the exact `FileAttachmentList`/`ResourcePickerModal` pair `RequirementDetailPage.tsx`'s own Attachments card already established, reused verbatim per §13's "reuse ReqTrackManager's existing attachment/file mechanisms"); `RequirementAssessmentPanel`'s own "Link existing evidence" control only ever creates/removes a link row (`POST`/`DELETE .../requirement-links`), matching the backend's own "canonical CRUD lives at the project-level `/evidence` resource, since one piece of evidence may span more than one assignment" design (Phase 8 notes).

**Archived-assignment requirement-tree viewing needed one small, generic, non-backend-touching resolution helper, not a new endpoint.** Every org-router requirement-tree route is nested under `/standards/{standard_id}/versions/{version_id}/...`, but `ProjectCompliance` only stores `standard_version_id`; an *active* assignment gets `standard_id` for free via `ProjectComplianceStatusOut` (`GET .../status`), but that endpoint deliberately excludes archived assignments (by design, per its own Phase 7 docstring), leaving no direct way to resolve which standard owns an archived assignment's version. Rather than add a new backend endpoint for what should be a rare path (viewing an archived assignment's own tree), `api.ts::resolveStandardIdForVersion` does a small client-side join over this organisation's own (typically small) standard/version catalogue — `listStandards` then `listStandardVersions` per standard until the version id matches. `ProjectComplianceDetail` calls this only when its `status` prop is `null` (i.e., exactly the archived case).

**Deliberate Phase 13 scope trim, flagged explicitly rather than silently omitted, mirroring Phase 12's own "owner reassignment has no dedicated UI" precedent: the §27 version-migration action (`POST .../migrate-version`) has no frontend surface.** Nothing in this phase's own plan-spec bullet list ("Assign standards, applicability tree..., assessment, evidence, approval/sign-off") calls for it, Phase 14 (Org view + Dashboard) doesn't claim it either, and it is a materially larger, higher-stakes UI to build correctly (a diff preview, a per-requirement "confirm this replacement carries forward" selection UI for `implies_equivalence`-gated `replaced` pairs) than any other control this phase needed — building it well deserves its own focused pass rather than a corner of this already-large phase. `module.py`'s own Phase 11 notes already establish the identical reasoning for why this action has no MCP tool either.

**Reviews are a per-assignment CRUD surface (`ReviewsPanel`, full create/edit/complete/delete, mirroring `project_router.py`'s own project-level review endpoints one-to-one), while the cross-assignment due/overdue view lives in `OutstandingPanel` instead — two different concerns, not one panel trying to do both.** A review only makes sense to *create* against one specific assignment (`POST .../project-compliance/{id}/reviews`), but §21 wants "what's due" visible without opening every assignment — so the read-only aggregate (`GET .../reviews-due`, spanning this project's own reviews plus every review of a standard it's assigned to) surfaces on the top-level Outstanding tab instead, never duplicating the mutation surface.

**No client-side "can I manage this" precomputation, continuing Phase 12's exact posture — mutating controls always render; a 403 surfaces as a toast.** `require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_officer")` composes with `is_server_admin`/`ProjectRole.PROJECT_MANAGER` by Phase 2's own design, and there is still no "my effective roles including module roles" endpoint to check against without adding one — the same judgment call Phase 12 made and flagged, applied consistently here rather than re-litigated.

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (`frontend_manifest` added, Phase 3's `ModuleFrontendManifest`/`ModuleFrontendManifest` import), `backend/app/routers/projects.py` (`list_project_enabled_modules`'s `{project_id}` placeholder interpolation fix). No new tables/migrations/endpoints — every read/write surface this phase's UI calls was already built by Phases 7-11; only the two module-system plumbing gaps above needed real backend code.

**Frontend.** `frontend/src/modules/compliance/` (new): `ProjectCompliancePage.tsx` (the Tier A route component: top-level Standards/Evidence/Outstanding `Tabs`, the assignment `DirectoryTable`, `AssignStandardModal`), `ProjectComplianceDetail.tsx` (per-assignment header/§20 status summary/archive, Requirements/Reviews `Tabs`), `ApplicabilityTree.tsx` (the client-assembled, decorated requirement tree), `ApplicabilityBadge.tsx` (the shared §9 explicit/inherited/overridden badge, extracted for reuse), `RequirementAssessmentPanel.tsx` (the per-requirement `SidePanel`: applicability, assessment, required actions, evidence linkage, approval/sign-off, history), `EvidencePanel.tsx` (project-wide evidence library), `ReviewsPanel.tsx` (per-assignment review CRUD/complete), `OutstandingPanel.tsx` (the cross-assignment non-compliant/pending-approval/reviews-due summary). `frontend/src/modules/compliance/api.ts`/`types.ts` extended with every Phase 7-11 project-router endpoint this phase's UI calls (assignment, per-requirement assessment/applicability/approval, required-action assessments, evidence CRUD/linkage/files, reviews) plus the `resolveStandardIdForVersion` helper — the module docstring's own "Phase 13 territory, not covered" note from Phase 12 removed accordingly. `frontend/src/api/types.ts` gained the project-assessment-facing enum/label-map pairs Phase 12's own comment there had deliberately deferred (`ComplianceStatus`, `ComplianceApplicability`, `ComplianceApplicabilitySource`, `ComplianceApprovalState`, `ComplianceEvidenceValidityState`, `frontend/src/hooks/useProjectEnabledModules.ts` (the `{ modules, loaded }` fix), `frontend/src/App.tsx` (wildcard-route fix), `frontend/src/components/Layout.tsx` (updated destructuring), `frontend/src/components/Layout.stories.tsx` (the incidental `/enabled-modules` mock gap fixed).

**Tests.** `backend/tests/test_module_frontend_integration.py` (2 new tests + a new fixture, `project_scoped_installed_module`, for the `{project_id}` interpolation fix — 28 tests total in that file, all green). Eight new dedicated Storybook story files, one per new component (`ProjectCompliancePage.stories.tsx`, `ProjectComplianceDetail.stories.tsx`, `ApplicabilityTree.stories.tsx`, `ApplicabilityBadge.stories.tsx`, `RequirementAssessmentPanel.stories.tsx`, `EvidencePanel.stories.tsx`, `ReviewsPanel.stories.tsx`, `OutstandingPanel.stories.tsx`), each with its own mocked `api` responses rather than drilling through the composed page, per Phase 12's own established "isolated coverage first, no repeat of the same-day story-gap follow-up" lesson — none of this phase's components shipped without a dedicated story file the same day. `tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/project-compliance-view.spec.ts` (new) — logs in as `orgAdminAlphaBeta` (composes as both `compliance_manager`, via `OrgRole.ORG_ADMIN`, and `compliance_officer`, via being Alpha-1's creator/`PROJECT_MANAGER` — no new seed persona needed), authors and publishes a dynamically-named standard/version/requirement, then exercises the full project-side flow end to end: assign the standard, assess a requirement Compliant, submit for approval, approve it, and link evidence to it. This spec is what actually caught both the wildcard-route race condition and the status-card staleness bug above — confirming this repo's own standing lesson (Phase 0's notes) that only the full, real, unmocked path catches some classes of bug that unit-level Storybook coverage structurally cannot. ## Compliance module plan, Phase 14: frontend — org compliance view + dashboard (2026-09-07)

Fourteenth implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` — the org-level, Compliance-Manager-facing "how are all projects performing" surfaces §22 (Organisation Compliance View) and §23 (Compliance Dashboard) ask for: a cross-standard "Standard | Projects | Compliant | Non-Compliant | In Progress" table with the four filters §22 names explicitly (standard, standard version, project, compliance state), an org-wide "what remains outstanding" listing mirroring Phase 13's own per-project one, and a summary dashboard — every widget backed by real drill-down data, never a bare aggregate number, per both sections' own explicit requirement.

**RBAC, checked against §26 before writing any endpoint rather than assumed from §22's own looser text: every new org-wide endpoint reuses `_require_manage` (`require_module_role("compliance", "compliance_manager")`), the exact same gate `list_all_project_compliance` (Phase 7) already uses — not a new, wider view-tier dependency.** §22's own prose says this view is for "Compliance Managers **and authorised users**," which read in isolation could suggest a broader, view-tier gate than Compliance Manager alone. But §26 — "Security and Permissions," this module's own dedicated, authoritative RBAC section — lists "View compliance across projects" as a capability specifically and only under **Compliance Manager**; Project Manager and Compliance Officer are each granted "View **project** compliance" (singular, their own project), with no cross-project viewing capability listed for either. Treating §22's looser phrasing as license to widen access here would have silently contradicted §26's own explicit enumeration — a real regression risk this repo's CLAUDE.md flags authorization changes for specifically. Read `_require_manage`'s definition and `require_org_module_enabled` (the module's weaker view-tier dependency, used for §6's own read endpoints like listing standards) side by side before deciding: `require_org_module_enabled` gates "can see standards exist at all," a much lower bar than "can see every project's compliance posture across the org," which is squarely what §26 reserves for Compliance Manager. Consulted `docs/soc2/policies/access-control-policy.md`'s module-contributed-roles section (item 4) per this repo's standing rule for any RBAC-touching change: it already documents `require_module_role`'s composition (server admin / org admin / direct grant) generically, not per-endpoint, so six more call sites of an already-reviewed, already-documented mechanism needed no policy edit — confirmed by reading the policy directly rather than assumed.

**A genuine, unbuilt gap found while researching this phase, closed as part of it rather than deferred: no flattened, cross-assignment listing existed for "outstanding Required Actions" at *either* scope.** `project_router.py` already had the flattened-listing family §20/§21/§26 needed for non-compliant requirements and pending approvals (`GET .../non-compliant-requirements`, `.../pending-approvals`, both Phase 7/9), but "outstanding Required Actions" — §22's own explicit bullet — had no equivalent; only the per-requirement nested `GET .../requirements/{pcr_id}/required-action-assessments` (Phase 7) existed, which cannot answer "which required actions are outstanding across this project/org" without opening every requirement in turn. Added `GET .../outstanding-required-actions` to **both** routers: `project_router.py`'s new endpoint (gated `_require_view`, matching its sibling listings) closes the project-scope gap and is also wired into Phase 13's own `OutstandingPanel.tsx` (a fourth section, "Outstanding required actions," added alongside the pre-existing three) — a deliberate, low-cost extension of an already-shipped phase's own panel, not scope creep: the data and UI slot both already existed, and leaving §21's own "make it easy to determine what remains outstanding" without this one category once the data was available would have been a second gap left sitting next to the one just fixed. `router.py`'s org-wide version is what §22 itself actually asked for.

**Business logic shared between project and org scope by extraction into `service.py`, not duplicated per router — `list_non_compliant_requirements_for_project`/`list_pending_approvals_for_project`/`list_outstanding_required_actions_for_project`/`list_reviews_due_for_project` are the exact per-project loop bodies `project_router.py` already had (the first three) or a new one built to match their shape (`list_outstanding_required_actions_for_project`), moved into `service.py` so `router.py`'s five new org-wide endpoints can call the same computation once per project in the organisation and concatenate, mirroring `list_all_project_compliance`'s own existing "join `ProjectCompliance` to `Project` on `organization_id`" pattern.** `project_router.py`'s own three pre-existing endpoints (`non-compliant-requirements`, `pending-approvals`, `reviews-due`) are now thin wrappers over these extracted functions — behaviour unchanged, confirmed by the full existing test suite for those endpoints staying green unmodified. `list_reviews_due_for_project` gained one new parameter, `include_upcoming` (default `False`, preserving its pre-Phase-14 due/overdue-only behaviour exactly) — needed because §23's own "Upcoming compliance deadlines/reviews" dashboard widget needs `upcoming`-state reviews too, which the plain `reviews-due` semantics deliberately exclude; rather than build a second, parallel review-gathering function for the dashboard's own slightly different need, the existing one gained one flag.

**Schema design: the two schemas this phase's org-wide listings build on split into two different treatments, and the difference is deliberate, not inconsistent — recorded here so a future session doesn't try to unify them.** `NonCompliantRequirementOut`/`PendingApprovalOut`/`ComplianceEvidenceOut` predate this phase with passing Phase 12/13 consumers at *project* scope that never needed a `project_id`/`project_name` field; rather than retrofit those two fields onto the shared base schema (a response-shape change every existing caller would silently start receiving, however harmless), each gets its own `Org*Out` subclass (`OrgNonCompliantRequirementOut`, `OrgPendingApprovalOut`, `OrgExpiringEvidenceOut`) adding exactly `project_id`/`project_name` on top. `OutstandingRequiredActionOut` is new in this phase with no pre-existing consumer to protect, so it carries `project_id`/`project_name` from the start and is used verbatim, unmodified, by both `project_router.py`'s and `router.py`'s endpoints — no subclass needed. `ComplianceReviewOut` gets a third treatment, a nested wrapper (`OrgReviewDueOut { project_id, project_name, review: ComplianceReviewOut }`) rather than a flat subclass like the other three, because it is not truly one-project-per-row the way a `ProjectComplianceRequirement`-derived row is: a single standard-level `ComplianceReview` can legitimately be "due" for every project assigned to that standard simultaneously, so `router.py`'s `reviews-due` endpoint returns one `OrgReviewDueOut` per (project, review) pair — the same review's id can appear more than once, tagged with each project it's currently due for. `ProjectComplianceStatusOut` (Phase 7) is the one schema in this module that predates Phase 14 *and* gets a field added directly rather than an `Org*Out` subclass: it was already the sole exception to "project-scope-first" among this module's cross-assignment schemas, carrying a project-scope-redundant `project_id` since Phase 7 specifically so `list_all_project_compliance`'s org-wide listing could reuse it unmodified — adding `project_name` there extends that already-established dual-use design rather than creating a fourth pattern for what is, underneath, the same "add project identification for org-wide reuse" need the `Org*Out` subclasses solve differently. Two Storybook literal `ProjectComplianceStatus` fixtures (`ProjectCompliancePage.stories.tsx`, `ProjectComplianceDetail.stories.tsx`) needed the new required field added — a `tsc` compile error, not a runtime one, caught immediately.

**A new `GET .../recent-activity` endpoint, with no per-project analogue, for §23's "Recently changed compliance assessments" — built from `AuditEvent` rows already being logged, not a new audit mechanism.** No existing endpoint aggregates recent activity across an organisation's compliance assessments; `project_router.py` already logs every assessment/applicability/approval-workflow transition against the `project_compliance_requirement` entity type via the standard `services.audit.log_event` this repo's CLAUDE.md requires every mutation to go through, so `service.py::list_recent_compliance_activity` queries `AuditEvent` directly (joined through `Project` to scope by `organization_id`, since these project-scoped audit rows carry `project_id` but not `organization_id` — confirmed by reading `AuditEvent`'s own docstring rather than assumed) filtered to an explicit allowlist of six action names (`assessed`, `applicability_changed`, `submitted_for_approval`, `approved`, `rejected`, `approval_invalidated`) — an allowlist rather than "every event of this entity type," so a future, unrelated `project_compliance_requirement` audit action doesn't silently start appearing in this specific dashboard widget without a deliberate decision to include it.

**IA: a new, flat top-level `ResourceMenu` group on `OrgAdminPage` ("Compliance overview," `/orgs/:orgId/admin/compliance-overview`), sibling to Phase 12's existing "Compliance" group — not a fourth tab bolted onto `ComplianceAdminPanel`'s existing three, and not folded into that panel at all.** `ComplianceAdminPanel`'s own docstring had already flagged, at Phase 12 time, that "the org-wide dashboard (Phase 14)" was explicitly out of its scope — this phase honours that rather than reopening the question. Consulted `docs/ux-style-guide.md`'s "Pattern: settings hierarchy" addendum (2026-08-24) before deciding: "when one resource-menu group outgrows itself, split it into more flat top-level groups — don't add nested sub-navigation... `ResourceMenu` already renders any number of flat top-level groups." Standards/versions/requirements management (Phase 12, Compliance-Manager-authoring-facing) and org-wide compliance reporting (Phase 14, still Compliance-Manager-facing per §26 but a materially different job — reading a cross-project picture, not authoring a catalogue) are different enough jobs that combining them into one panel with a fourth tab would have reproduced exactly the "crowded group" failure mode that addendum was written against, not avoided it. `OrgCompliancePanel` (the new group's own mounted component) uses three of its own `Tabs` — Dashboard / Compliance by standard / Outstanding — comfortably inside the style guide's five-or-fewer `Tabs` threshold, mirroring Phase 13's own three-tab `ProjectCompliancePage` IA (Standards / Evidence / Outstanding) for the same "a handful of equally-relevant views of one dataset" shape.

**Drill-down "to individual requirements" (§22's own explicit requirement, and §23's "should provide drill-down capability rather than only showing aggregate numbers") reuses the existing per-project Compliance page as its destination, rather than rebuilding a parallel requirement-level browser at org scope.** Every widget/row/list item that names a project links to `/projects/{project_id}/modules/compliance` — Phase 13's own `ProjectCompliancePage`, which already drills all the way down to individual requirements (§21's own documented drill-down chain: Project → Standard → Requirement → Required Actions/Evidence/Assessment/Approval). Building a second, org-scoped requirement browser would have duplicated that entire chain for no functional gain over "go to the project, then drill down as usual" — and this repo's own reuse-first bias (CLAUDE.md, the style guide's Principle 4) treats an already-built, already-tested drill-down path as the correct target for a new entry point into it, not a gap to fill with a parallel implementation. "Standards with the most outstanding issues" (§23) is computed client-side by tallying the non-compliant/pending-approval/outstanding-action rows already fetched for the dashboard, grouped by `standard_reference` — the same client-side-aggregation-over-a-flat-backend-listing precedent Phase 12's `buildRequirementTree` established, needing no dedicated backend endpoint of its own.

**No client-side "can I manage this" precomputation, continuing Phase 12/13's exact posture — every new panel always renders its content; a 403 from a disabled/non-entitled module or a non-Compliance-Manager viewer surfaces as a toast** (`ComplianceAdminPanel`'s own existing "fetch, catch, degrade gracefully" pattern, reused unchanged by `OrgCompliancePanel`'s own module-level error handling — there is still no "my effective roles for this org, including module roles" endpoint to check against without adding one, the same judgment call Phase 12 made and flagged, applied consistently here rather than re-litigated a third time).

**Backend.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/schemas.py` (`OutstandingRequiredActionOut`, `OrgNonCompliantRequirementOut`, `OrgPendingApprovalOut`, `OrgExpiringEvidenceOut`, `OrgReviewDueOut`, `ComplianceRecentActivityOut` added; `ProjectComplianceStatusOut.project_name` added), `backend/app/modules/compliance/service.py` (`list_non_compliant_requirements_for_project`/`list_pending_approvals_for_project`/`list_outstanding_required_actions_for_project`/`list_reviews_due_for_project`/`list_recent_compliance_activity` added; `build_status_out` populates the new `project_name` field), `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py` (`non-compliant-requirements`/`pending-approvals`/`reviews-due` now thin wrappers over the extracted `service.py` functions; new `GET .../outstanding-required-actions`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/router.py` (six new org-wide endpoints: `non-compliant-requirements`, `pending-approvals`, `outstanding-required-actions`, `expiring-evidence`, `reviews-due` incl. `include_upcoming`, `recent-activity`). No new tables/migrations — every new schema/endpoint is a read/aggregation layer over data Phases 5-11 already materialise.

**Frontend.** `frontend/src/modules/compliance/` (new): `OrgCompliancePanel.tsx` (the three-tab shell mounted on `OrgAdminPage`), `OrgComplianceDashboard.tsx` (§23's summary widgets, each with its own drill-down list), `OrgComplianceStandardsPanel.tsx` (§22's cross-standard table with the four named filters + expandable per-project drill-down), `OrgComplianceOutstandingPanel.tsx` (the org-wide non-compliant/pending-approval/outstanding-action/expiring-evidence/reviews-due summary, each row project-tagged and linked). `frontend/src/modules/compliance/OutstandingPanel.tsx` gained a fourth section ("Outstanding required actions"), wired to the new project-level endpoint. `frontend/src/modules/compliance/api.ts`/`types.ts` extended with every Phase 14 endpoint/schema above. `frontend/src/pages/OrgAdminPage.tsx` (new `"compliance-overview"` `ResourceMenu` group). `frontend/src/i18n/strings.ts` (`groupComplianceOverview` label).

**Tests.** `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_org_compliance_dashboard.py` (new, 7 tests): org-wide aggregation correctness across two projects for all five `router.py` endpoints plus `recent-activity`, the new project-level `outstanding-required-actions` endpoint (including its "completing an action removes it from both listings" behaviour), `include_upcoming`'s two modes, and the §26 RBAC boundary (a plain org member 403s on all six org-wide endpoints; a direct `compliance_manager` grant with no org_admin succeeds on all six, matching `require_module_role`'s existing composition). Four new dedicated Storybook story files, one per new component, plus updates to `OutstandingPanel.stories.tsx`'s existing mocks/assertions for its new fourth section and to the two `ProjectComplianceStatus` story fixtures for the new `project_name` field — all isolated, mocked-`api` coverage, no drilling through a composed parent, per this module's own established one-story-file-per-component convention. `tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/org-compliance-view.spec.ts` (new) — logs in as `orgAdminAlphaBeta` (reused per Phase 13's own precedent), authors and publishes a dynamically-named standard/requirement (Phase 12 UI), assigns it to Alpha-1 and assesses the requirement Non-Compliant (Phase 13 UI), then confirms the Dashboard's "Non-compliant projects" widget, the "Compliance by standard" table's expandable drill-down (following its link through to the project's own Compliance page), and the Outstanding tab's non-compliant listing all surface it. Run twice back-to-back against a rebuilt `tests/container` stack to confirm idempotency (every fixture dynamically named); both runs green, and a full three-spec run of every Compliance module Playwright spec together (Phase 12/13/14) also green.

Two real Testing-Library/Playwright query-ambiguity bugs found and fixed while getting the new stories/spec green (not product bugs — test-authoring mistakes caught immediately by a failing assertion, recorded here per this repo's own "identify → verify → remediate" practice for anything touching test infrastructure): (1) several new story `play` functions used `getByText`/`getByRole` matches broad enough to also match a `<select>`'s own `<option>` text (e.g. `/ISO-27001/` matching both a table row and the standard/version filter dropdowns rendering the same reference) — fixed by scoping those queries to `within(canvas.getByRole("table"))`; (2) `OutstandingPanel.stories.tsx`'s and `OrgComplianceOutstandingPanel.stories.tsx`'s fixtures reused the same `requirement_name` ("Access control") across two different fixture rows in the same story, so a plain `getByText` match was ambiguous once the new fourth section was added — fixed by asserting on each row's own more specific, unique text instead.

`npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint .` (every touched file) both clean, zero new warnings. `ruff check` clean on every touched backend file. `vitest run --project=storybook` run in full after every fix (92 files, 765 tests) — all green. Backend: the full suite run via `docker compose exec backend pytest -q` (the authoritative way to run it, per `tests/container/docker-compose.yml`'s own docstring — a bare host-level `python -m pytest` cannot resolve the `mailhog` hostname the notification-sending tests need, a pre-existing environment constraint unrelated to this phase, not a regression) — 956 passed, 0 failed; the directly-touched compliance module's own suite (96 tests) also green in isolation. `tests/container`'s backend and frontend images were rebuilt and recreated twice — once before the first Playwright pass, once more after a same-day `ruff check --fix` import-order cleanup and a stray unused CSS class removal — per this repo's own standing "containers don't bind-mount source" rule; the full three-spec Compliance module Playwright suite (Phases 12/13/14) and a standalone repeat of the new Phase 14 spec were both green against the final rebuild.

## Module system follow-up: frontend module auto-discovery (2026-09-07)

Cross-cutting frontend-infra work requested directly by the user between phases — done after Phase 14 completed and before Phase 15, and deliberately **not** given its own numbered entry in `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (that plan's own "Instructions for whoever picks up the next phase" section reserves numbered phases for product-scope work; this touches neither Compliance's own scope nor the plan's phase sequence). Same spirit as this file's existing "Module system follow-up" entries above (registry-driven `Base.metadata` auto-import; migrations/tests colocation) — closing a hand-maintained touch point the module system had carried since Phase 3, now that Compliance is a live, real example of the pattern rather than a hypothetical.

**The gap.** `frontend/src/modules/registry.ts`'s `installedModules: TierAModuleDefinition[]` was a literal, hand-written array — a new first-party Tier A module (the next one being one of the three uplifts `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s own "Context" section names as following Compliance) would need to edit this shared file directly to add its own entry, exactly the kind of per-module core-file touch point `models_import_path`/`migrations_dir`/`scheduled_jobs` had each already eliminated on the backend side one mechanism at a time. Nothing on the frontend closed the equivalent gap yet.

**Fix: build-time auto-discovery via Vite's `import.meta.glob`, not a runtime directory scan.** `registry.ts` now reads `import.meta.glob<{ moduleDefinition: TierAModuleDefinition }>("./*/module.ts", { eager: true })` — Vite's own static-analysis-based glob-to-module-map primitive, resolved at build/transform time (confirmed against `node_modules/vite/types/importGlob.d.ts`'s own overload set before writing this: passing an explicit type parameter with `eager: true` selects the overload returning `Record<string, M>` directly, not a `Record<string, () => Promise<M>>>` of lazy loaders) — and assembles `installedModules` from `Object.values(...)`, sorted by `key` for deterministic ordering regardless of directory-listing order. Convention: each first-party module gets its own `frontend/src/modules/<key>/module.ts` exporting `moduleDefinition: TierAModuleDefinition` — the frontend mirror of the backend's `app/modules/<key>/module.py` exposing `MODULE_DEFINITION`, chosen deliberately to match that existing naming convention rather than invent a new one. Compliance's own registration (previously the array literal directly inside `registry.ts`) moved into `frontend/src/modules/compliance/module.ts` unchanged in content. Dropping a new `module.ts` file into a new `frontend/src/modules/<key>/` directory is now the entire frontend registration step for a first-party module — no `registry.ts` edit needed.

**`getInstalledModule(key)` and `buildModuleRoutes` are unchanged in signature/behaviour** — both still read from the same `installedModules` array, which is still a genuine mutable array at runtime (`Object.values(...).sort(...)` returns the same array `.sort()` mutates, not a frozen/readonly one), confirmed load-bearing: `App.stories.tsx`'s existing `TierARoutingHarness` fixture (`installedModules.push({...})`, proving Phase 3's routing mechanism with a fixture module) keeps working unmodified — verified by running it, not assumed. `TierAModuleDefinition.routes` became **optional** (default treated as `[]` in `buildModuleRoutes`) rather than required, since a module contributing only an org-admin section (see the next entry below) and no project-scoped route of its own shouldn't need to declare an empty array.

**Explicitly out of scope, consistent with Phase 3's own boundary: third-party (npm-installed) Tier A modules are not covered by this auto-discovery.** `import.meta.glob`'s pattern (`./*/module.ts`) only ever matches paths physically under `frontend/src/modules/`, by construction — an npm-installed package's own module directory wouldn't live there without a separate symlinking or explicit-registration mechanism, which was not built here (no third-party Tier A module exists yet to need it, mirroring Phase 3's own "both tiers built, no real third-party module ships" scoping note, and the backend's own equally-narrow `INSTALLED_MODULES`-vs-entry-points split).

**Verified under every runtime that resolves this file, not just the real Vite dev/build — the actual risk with any `import.meta`-based mechanism.** `import.meta.glob` is a Vite-specific, compile-time-rewritten construct; Vitest's own transform pipeline is Vite-based, so it *should* resolve identically inside a story's test run, but "should" was verified directly rather than assumed: the full Storybook/Vitest suite (`vitest run --project=storybook`, real headless Chromium per story) was re-run after this change — 92 files, 768 tests, all green, including every Compliance story (which only renders correctly if `registry.ts` actually discovered `compliance/module.ts` and its `ProjectCompliancePage` route registration survived the switch).

### Files changed

`frontend/src/modules/registry.ts` (rewritten: `import.meta.glob`-based discovery replacing the hand-written array), `frontend/src/modules/types.ts` (`TierAModuleDefinition.routes` made optional), `frontend/src/modules/buildModuleRoutes.tsx` (`installed.routes ?? []`), `frontend/src/modules/compliance/module.ts` (new — Compliance's registration moved here from `registry.ts`, unchanged in content); `docs/modules.md` (Tier A section rewritten for the new convention), `docs/solution-architecture.md`, `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (pointer notes appended to Phase 3's own notes subsection — not rewritten, per this file's own established convention for a phase's notes describing a real decision made at the time), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry). See the next entry below for `orgAdminSections`, added to `TierAModuleDefinition` in the same pass.

## Module system follow-up: dynamic org-admin panel registration (2026-09-07, same day)

The second half of the same user-requested, cross-cutting frontend-infra pass as the entry above — same non-numbered-phase reasoning applies.

**The gap, named explicitly by this plan's own Phase 12 notes and repeated, unresolved, in Phase 14's:** Phase 3's Tier A `installedModules`/`buildModuleRoutes`/nav-discovery mechanism is project-scoped end to end (`useProjectEnabledModules` keys off a `projectId` parsed from the URL) and has no org-level equivalent. Phase 12 worked around this by mounting `ComplianceAdminPanel` directly inside `OrgAdminPage.tsx`: a hardcoded `"compliance"` member on the `OrgAdminGroupKey` union, a hardcoded entry in the `orgAdminGroups` array, a static top-of-file import, and a hardcoded `activeGroup === "compliance" && <ComplianceAdminPanel orgId={org.id} />}` render block. Phase 14 repeated the exact same pattern by hand for `OrgCompliancePanel` (`"compliance-overview"`). Both phases' own notes flagged this as a deliberate, scoped-down workaround rather than a solved problem — legitimate future module-system work "disproportionate" to build as a side effect of either phase alone.

**Fix: `TierAModuleDefinition` gained `orgAdminSections`, a list of `{ key, label, render({ orgId }) }` entries (`frontend/src/modules/types.ts`), and `OrgAdminPage.tsx` now merges every currently-*enabled* installed module's own sections onto its ten fixed core groups generically.** Shape modelled directly on `ResourceMenuGroupDef` (`components/ResourceMenu.tsx`) — `key`/`label` match it exactly, `render` follows this codebase's existing prop-function convention for handing a parent a piece of child-owned-data UI (`DirectoryColumn.render`, `DefinitionList`'s `renderExtra`) rather than inventing a new shape for this one case. `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s `orgAdminGroups` array is now `[...ten hardcoded core groups (untouched)..., ...moduleAdminSections.map(section => ({ key, label, href: `/orgs/${orgId}/admin/${section.key}` }))]`; the two former hardcoded render blocks are replaced by one generic lookup (`moduleAdminSections.filter(s => s.key === activeGroup).map(s => <div className="stack" key={s.key}>{s.render({ orgId: org.id })}</div>)`). Compliance's own `module.ts` declares both of its existing sections (`ComplianceAdminPanel` at key `"compliance"`, `OrgCompliancePanel` at key `"compliance-overview"`, labels read from `i18n/strings.ts`'s `t()` directly — see that file's own docstring for why a plain, unsubstituted `t()` call is exactly equivalent to `useStrings()` for these two specific, token-free strings). The two static top-of-file imports of `ComplianceAdminPanel`/`OrgCompliancePanel` are gone from `OrgAdminPage.tsx` entirely — they're now imported only inside `frontend/src/modules/compliance/module.ts`.

**`moduleAdminSections` is filtered by this org's actual module-*enablement*, not merely "is this module installed at all" — a genuine, if narrow, behaviour fix, not just a mechanism refactor.** The old hardcoded array entries for `"compliance"`/`"compliance-overview"` were unconditional — they rendered in every org's nav regardless of whether that org's own admin had disabled the Compliance module via the Modules toggle on this same page. `OrgAdminPage.tsx` already fetches `modules` (`GET /orgs/{id}/modules`, the same state the Modules section itself renders from, inside the existing "fetch, catch 403/404, degrade gracefully" `try`/`catch` block Phase 12's own notes established); `moduleAdminSections` now cross-references `installedModules` against `new Set(modules.filter(m => m.enabled).map(m => m.module_key))` before contributing anything. **Verified explicitly, since this was the entire point of the ask**: a dedicated Storybook fixture (see Testing below) proves a module-contributed section both appears when its module is enabled and disappears when it's reported disabled *or* not reported at all — and the existing `org-compliance-view.spec.ts` Playwright spec (unmodified — it navigates by group *label*, not by any internal mechanism) continues to exercise the real Compliance case end to end through the new generic code path.

**Type safety tradeoff, spelled out rather than silently accepted (per this repo's CLAUDE.md instruction for exactly this situation): `OrgAdminGroupKey` widened from a fully closed literal union to `CoreOrgAdminGroupKey | string`.** A module's own section `key` isn't knowable at `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s compile time, so a closed union can no longer describe every value `activeGroup` can legitimately take. Concretely: TypeScript's "this comparison appears to be unintentional" check no longer fires on any of the ten `activeGroup === "<core group>"` render-block comparisons — a typo there (e.g. `"userz"` for `"users"`) would previously have been a compile error and now silently compiles, matching a value that will just never occur at runtime rather than being caught. Mitigated, not eliminated: `CoreOrgAdminGroupKey` itself (derived via `(typeof CORE_ORG_ADMIN_GROUP_KEYS)[number]` from a real `as const` tuple) stays fully closed, so the ten core groups' own *declaration* is still checked, and a defensive runtime guard drops (and `console.error`-logs) any module section whose `key` collides with a core group key, so a colliding module can't silently shadow or duplicate a core group in the nav even without compile-time protection against it. No narrower alternative was available in TypeScript's type system for "closed set, plus an open-ended tail" that also preserves comparison-typo checking on the closed part — confirmed by testing the common `T | (string & {})` branding idiom directly, which turned out to suppress the same check for the exact same underlying reason (the type still overlaps `string`).

**Testing: a fixture module proves the generic mechanism, mirroring the backend's own `test_module_registry.py::fake_module` convention.** `OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx` registers a `fake_org_admin_fixture_module` directly into the real `installedModules` (same permanently-registered-fixture convention `App.stories.tsx` already established for its own Tier A routing proof — safe for the same reason: nothing renders it unless a story's own mocked `GET /orgs/{id}/modules` response reports it enabled) with one `orgAdminSections` entry and, deliberately, no `routes` at all — also exercising `routes`'s new optional-ness. Three new stories: the section renders (and receives this org's real id) when the fixture module is reported enabled; it's absent from the nav when the module is reported present-but-disabled; it's absent when the module isn't reported at all. All three pass (`vitest run --project=storybook -t "Module Contributed"`, 3/3), and the full suite (92 files/768 tests) was re-run clean afterward.

**Incidental, unrelated bugs found and fixed while verifying this end to end against a real, rebuilt `tests/container` stack (per this repo's standing "fix, don't defer" rule) — both pre-existing test-isolation bugs in `project-hierarchy.spec.ts`, neither touching this follow-up's own code:**
1. **A leaked org-role grant.** "a project manager with no org-level role can create a sub-project..." permanently grants `projectMgrGamma` the org-wide "Project creator" role partway through (to prove the detach-guard's success path) and never revoked it — a real violation of this repo's standing "tests must not depend on state left behind by another test" rule, discovered because the very next test in the same file ("an org admin can disable the relaxed child-creation path...") assumes this exact persona is still "a plain project manager with no org-level role" and silently stopped being true once the grant went unrevoked. Fixed by wrapping the test's three steps in `try`/`finally`, revoking the grant in `finally` — guarded to only revoke if the grant checkbox shows it's actually held, so a genuine failure earlier in the test surfaces its own real error instead of being masked by the cleanup step's own throw (plain JS `try`/`finally` semantics: an exception from `finally` replaces one already in flight from `try` — this masking is exactly how the second bug below stayed hidden during debugging until this guard was added).
2. **A toggle left stuck off on failure.** "an org admin can disable the relaxed child-creation path..." flips a shared, org-wide `allow_relaxed_child_project_creation` toggle off, asserts a plain manager is blocked, then restores it — but the restore was a fourth `test.step`, not a `finally`, so a failure in the middle assertion left the toggle stuck `false` for every other test/spec run against that org afterward (reproduced directly: this is what caused bug #1's own investigation to initially look like a completely different, non-reproducible failure, since the corrupted toggle made an *unrelated* earlier step — creating a sub-project at all — fail first). Fixed the same way: `try`/`finally`, with the restore step checking the toggle's current state before deciding whether to click it (so it always ends up `true` regardless of which of the preceding steps failed, if any).

Both fixes verified by running the full `project-hierarchy.spec.ts` file twice back-to-back against the rebuilt stack (5/5 passed each time) and by directly checking ground truth via the API before/after (`allow_relaxed_child_project_creation` and `projectMgrGamma`'s roles) rather than trusting the UI alone.

**Verification run, in full.** `npx tsc -b` and `npx eslint .` (repo-wide) both clean, zero new warnings (the 7 pre-existing `react-refresh/only-export-components` warnings in untouched files are unchanged from before this work). `vitest run --project=storybook`: 92 files/768 tests, all green. `tests/container`'s backend and frontend images rebuilt and recreated before any Playwright run, per this repo's standing "containers don't bind-mount source" rule. All three Compliance module Playwright specs (`tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/`, Phases 12/13/14) green. Spot-checked sixteen further, non-compliance specs that exercise `OrgAdminPage` generally — `org-admin-modules.spec.ts` (the Modules toggle itself), `module-contributed-roles.spec.ts`, `admin-page-titles-and-version-footer.spec.ts` (every resource-menu group, core and module-contributed alike), `org-admin-manage-users-modal.spec.ts`, `org-branding-override-reset.spec.ts`, `org-group-nesting.spec.ts`, `org-groups-sso-sync.spec.ts`, `org-security-controls.spec.ts`, `org-admin-project-statuses-and-link-types.spec.ts`, `project-admin-groups-and-fields.spec.ts`, `org-rename-and-test-email.spec.ts`, `project-admin-templates-and-reports.spec.ts`, `project-hierarchy.spec.ts`, `scim-provisioning.spec.ts`, `role-display-collapsing.spec.ts`, `user-access-panel.spec.ts`, `server-admin-scope.spec.ts`, `user-directory-and-bans.spec.ts` — all green after the two incidental fixes above.

## Module system follow-up: Tier C (Module Federation) — backend manifest/registry extension (2026-09-07, same day)

Cross-cutting frontend-infra work requested directly by the repo owner in conversation — not a numbered `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` phase (its own "Instructions for whoever picks up the next phase" reserves numbered phases for product-scope work; this touches neither Compliance's own scope nor the plan's phase sequence). Same non-numbered-follow-up convention as this file's two entries directly above.

**The gap.** The backend already supports a self-hosted operator dropping in a genuinely third-party *Python* module with no image rebuild (`Settings.allow_external_modules` + `Settings.extra_modules_path`, `app.modules.registry`'s entry-point/path discovery). Nothing on the frontend offered the equivalent: Tier A (`registry.ts`'s build-time `import.meta.glob`) requires this frontend image to be rebuilt to add a module at all — a Vite bundle is a static artifact with nothing to rescan post-build. Tier B (`<ModuleFrame>`) can run without a rebuild, but only by trading away native component reuse for an iframe sandbox. Neither serves an operator who wants a genuinely third-party module rendered through the app's own live component tree, with no rebuild ever.

**Fix: a third `ModuleFrontendManifest.tier`, `"federated"`, modelled on Module Federation** (the same mechanism Grafana/Backstage use for drop-in third-party frontend plugins) — the module author builds a self-contained remote bundle entirely outside this repo, on their own schedule; the host dynamically loads it at runtime. Two new fields, both required (and only meaningful) for this tier: `remote_entry_url` (the remote's own entry script — same-origin via a new nginx location, or any absolute URL, mirroring Tier B's `frame_url`-is-any-allowlisted-origin precedent) and `exposed_module` (the Module Federation "exposed module" name, e.g. `"./Module"`). `ModuleFrontendManifest.__post_init__` was restructured (still a plain `if`/`elif` chain, not a lookup table — three tiers didn't yet justify one) to validate all three tiers' mutual field exclusivity: `"remote"` still requires `frame_url` and now also rejects the two federated-only fields; `"installed"` rejects all three optional fields; `"federated"` requires both `remote_entry_url` and `exposed_module` and rejects `frame_url`.

**Mechanical enforcement, not a self-declared field trusted at face value — the same principle Tier B's `frame_url` allowlist check and Phase 4's MCP tool `path_template`/`is_approval_action` derivation already establish, applied to a new field.** A `"federated"` manifest is only ever legitimate for a module discovered through the existing gated third-party pipeline (entry points/`extra_modules_path`) — an `INSTALLED_MODULES` (first-party) module has no reason to use Tier C at all, since it can use Tier A directly with full build-time review. `get_frontend_manifest` now checks `module_key` against `{d.key for d in INSTALLED_MODULES}` (the exact same structural check `apply_external_module_migrations` already uses for its own analogous "never for a first-party module" rule) and, if a first-party module declares `tier="federated"` anyway, logs at `ERROR` (louder than Tier B's `WARNING` for a rejected origin, since this is an authoring bug in reviewed in-repo code, not an environment misconfiguration) and excludes the manifest — the module still loads and works normally, it simply has no usable frontend integration, the same "log and exclude, don't crash startup" treatment every other per-module fault in this registry already gets.

**Single-flag design confirmed to hold, not merely assumed — no second, independently-configured frontend flag was added.** The reasoning given when this follow-up was scoped (`Settings.allow_external_modules` already gates *all* third-party discovery, so a `"federated"` manifest can never exist in the registry at all unless that flag already let the declaring module through) was verified directly against the real code path, not just asserted: `build_registry` only calls `_discover_entry_point_modules`/`_discover_path_modules` when the flag is `True` (Phase 1's own "not just filtered afterward" design, unchanged); a `"federated"` manifest can only ever originate from a `ModuleDefinition` that came from one of those two functions (since a first-party one gets rejected as above); therefore the flag being `False` means no `"federated"` manifest is ever discovered in the first place, and `test_federated_tier_absent_when_external_modules_disallowed` pins exactly this (a fixture module discovered via a monkeypatched `_discover_entry_point_modules`, with the flag off, is absent from the registry entirely — not merely absent from `get_frontend_manifest`'s output). This also settles why there's no `MODULE_FRAME_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`-equivalent allowlist for `remote_entry_url`: unlike Tier B's `frame_url` (which a *first-party* module can also legitimately declare, and therefore genuinely needs an independent origin check), a `"federated"` manifest reaching `get_frontend_manifest` at all already implies the gated discovery pipeline produced it — a second allowlist would be redundant gating on top of a check that already fully determines the outcome.

**Wire shape.** `ModuleFrontendManifestOut` (`backend/app/schemas/org.py`) gained `remote_entry_url`/`exposed_module` (both `str | None = None`). `routers/orgs.py`'s two existing call sites (`ModuleFrontendManifestOut(**vars(manifest))`) needed **no code change** — `vars()` on a dataclass instance already reflects every field, so the two new ones flow through automatically; only `routers/projects.py::list_project_enabled_modules` (which constructs `ModuleFrontendManifestOut` field-by-field, to interpolate the `"{project_id}"` placeholder into `nav_path`/`frame_url`) needed an explicit edit, carrying `remote_entry_url`/`exposed_module` through unchanged — neither field is expected to ever contain that placeholder, since `remote_entry_url` points at a static build artifact, not a per-project route.

**Trust framing, recorded verbatim per this repo's own standing practice of not softening a stated risk.** The repo owner's own words, given directly when this design was discussed: *"the trust falls to the server admin to review and vet any plugins they add to their deployment that isn't first party."* This is materially bigger than either existing tier — bigger than Tier A (no build-time review is possible; the code was never in this repo) and bigger than Tier B (no iframe sandbox at all; a federated module shares the same origin, DOM, cookies, and live component tree as the host). `docs/soc2/policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md` gained a new point (8) stating this distinction explicitly rather than folding it into point 7's existing "installed third-party module" language, which was written before Tier C existed and describes a router-only backend module whose blast radius is still bounded by the backend's own authorization checks — a materially different (and, for the frontend, unbounded-by-any-sandbox) risk shape. `docs/soc2/trust-services-criteria-mapping.md`'s CC6.8 row gained an explicit Tier C mention alongside its existing backend-plugin-loading language, for the same reason.

**Testing.** `backend/tests/test_module_frontend_integration.py` gained: five `ModuleFrontendManifest.__post_init__` validation tests (federated requires both fields; federated must not set `frame_url`; remote/installed must not set the two federated-only fields); a `federated_tier_module_via_entry_point` fixture registering a fixture module through the *real* `_discover_entry_point_modules` monkeypatch pattern `test_module_registry.py` already establishes (not the shortcut every other tier's fixture in this file uses, appending straight to `INSTALLED_MODULES` — that shortcut is exactly the case this tier must reject, so a dedicated fixture matching the real discovery path was needed); `get_frontend_manifest` returns a federated manifest unmodified for that fixture; `get_frontend_manifest` rejects (logs `ERROR`, returns `None`) a federated manifest declared directly on an `INSTALLED_MODULES` entry; the single-flag claims above (needs no separate allowlist; absent entirely when `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES` is off); and two endpoint-level tests confirming `GET /orgs/{id}/modules`/`GET /projects/{id}/enabled-modules` both carry `remote_entry_url`/`exposed_module` through to the wire. One pre-existing exact-dict-equality test (`test_org_modules_endpoint_includes_frontend_manifest`) was updated for the two new always-present (`None`-valued, for a Tier A fixture) keys — an expected, mechanical consequence of widening the wire shape, not a behaviour change. Full backend suite re-run clean after these changes: 967 passed, 0 failed — including the ~14 pre-existing `mailhog`-hostname-resolution failures every earlier phase in this file documents for a bare host-run pytest session (confirmed still purely an environment artifact, not a regression, by re-running with `SMTP_HOST=localhost` pointed at the `tests/container` stack's own exposed `mailhog` port, which is the actual root cause, not `ALLOW_EXTERNAL_MODULES`/anything Tier-C-related). `ruff check` clean repo-wide. See the matching frontend follow-up entry below for the full combined verification run, since both landed in the same session.

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/registry.py` (`ModuleFrontendManifest.tier`/`.remote_entry_url`/`.exposed_module`, `__post_init__` restructured; `get_frontend_manifest`'s first-party-federated rejection), `backend/app/schemas/org.py` (`ModuleFrontendManifestOut` gained the two fields), `backend/app/routers/projects.py` (`list_project_enabled_modules` carries the two fields through), `backend/tests/test_module_frontend_integration.py` (new fixture + eleven new tests, one existing test updated), `docs/soc2/policies/vendor-and-subprocessor-management-policy.md` (new point 8; Known Gaps updated), `docs/soc2/trust-services-criteria-mapping.md` (CC6.8 row extended), `docs/solution-architecture.md`, `docs/modules.md`, `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (Design History item 6; pointer notes), `docs/deployment.md` (new "Adding a Tier C (federated) frontend module" section), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Module system follow-up: Tier C (Module Federation) — frontend runtime loader (2026-09-07, same day)

The frontend half of the entry directly above — read that one first for the manifest shape, the trust framing, and why no second frontend flag was needed.

**Design goal, stated explicitly by the repo owner and treated as a real constraint, not a nice-to-have: a module loaded via Tier C must feed the *same* rendering/merge path as one discovered at build time, not a second, parallel "federated modules" special case.** `frontend/src/modules/federatedLoader.ts`'s `loadFederatedModule` achieves this by the most direct means available: once a remote's `moduleDefinition` is resolved, it is pushed straight into `registry.ts`'s own `installedModules` array — the exact same mutable array `import.meta.glob`-based build-time discovery populates, and the exact same array this codebase's own existing fixture-module testing convention already mutates at runtime (`App.stories.tsx`'s `TierARoutingHarness`, `OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx`'s org-admin-section fixture). `getInstalledModule`, `buildModuleRoutes.tsx`, and `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s `moduleAdminSections` needed **zero code changes** to support Tier C — they already treat "any entry in `installedModules`" as "an installed module," and now genuinely cannot distinguish a build-time-discovered one from a runtime-federated one, which is exactly the point.

**A new hook, not a new fetch.** `useFederatedModules` (`frontend/src/hooks/useFederatedModules.ts`) takes the *same* enabled-modules list `useProjectEnabledModules`/`OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s own `GET /orgs/{id}/modules` fetch already produce — no new backend call of its own — filters to `tier === "federated"` entries, and triggers `loadFederatedModule` for each. Because a successful load mutates module-level state invisible to React (`installedModules.push(...)`, plus this loader's own `statuses`/`errors` maps), the hook also subscribes to a small pub/sub (`subscribeFederatedLoader`) and forces its calling component to re-render whenever any Tier C load's status changes anywhere on the page — necessary for `buildModuleRoutes`/`moduleAdminSections` to actually pick up a newly-merged definition on the next render, since nothing else would trigger one. `App.tsx` (`ProtectedRoutes`) and `OrgAdminPage.tsx` each call this hook independently with their own project-/org-scoped list, mirroring `useProjectEnabledModules`'s own "each concern fetches/derives its own data" convention rather than a shared provider — `OrgAdminPage.tsx`'s own call filters to `modules.filter(m => m.enabled)` first, so a Tier C module that's merely *installed-but-disabled* for an org never has its remote code fetched at all, not just hidden once loaded.

**A second navigation-race bug, the same class Phase 13 already found and fixed one layer in.** Phase 13's own fix held `App.tsx`'s wildcard `<Navigate>` fallback behind `useProjectEnabledModules`'s `loaded` flag, since a fresh navigation straight to a Tier A module's nav-rail link could otherwise land on the fallback before that fetch resolved and contributed the route. Tier C reopens the identical gap one step further out: `loaded` only means "the enabled-modules *list itself* was fetched," not "every federated module it named has finished its own async remote-entry load" — a fresh navigation to a Tier C module's own URL could still hit the wildcard before `federatedLoader.ts`'s dynamic `import()` settles. Found and fixed in the same pass, per this repo's standing "fix, don't defer" rule, rather than left as a known gap for a hypothetical future Tier C module to rediscover: `ProtectedRoutes` now also computes `federatedModulesStillLoading` from `useFederatedModules`'s own per-module status map and folds it into the existing gate (`projectId && (!modulesLoaded || federatedModulesStillLoading)`) — one gate, not two.

**Container contract — a documented, disclosed substitution for the specified `@originjs/vite-plugin-federation` dependency, not a silent one.** This repository's own sandboxed build/test environment had no network access to the npm registry when this was built — confirmed directly (`npm view @originjs/vite-plugin-federation`/`npm install` both timed out against `registry.npmjs.org` with `ETIMEDOUT`, despite a plain `curl` to the same host succeeding for a partial response, ruling out "no network at all" and pointing at an npm-specific connection-handling restriction in this sandbox rather than a genuinely offline environment) — so that dependency could not be installed, built, or verified here, and per this repo's own "leave the suite passing" rule, a `vite.config.ts` importing an absent package was not an acceptable way to ship this. `federatedLoader.ts` instead hand-implements, exactly, the minimal container contract a real Module Federation remote build produces: `init(sharedScope): Promise<void>` (the host hands the remote its own already-loaded `react`/`react-dom` instances) and `get(exposedModuleName): Promise<() => Module>` (resolving to a *factory function*, per the real spec — not the module directly). Because the contract matches, the documented upgrade path once normal registry access exists is narrow and explicit: replace this one file's own `import()`/`init`/`get` calls with the real plugin's dynamic-remote runtime APIs (`__federation_method_setRemote`/`__federation_method_getRemote` for `@originjs/vite-plugin-federation`); no change to `useFederatedModules`, `buildModuleRoutes.tsx`, `OrgAdminPage.tsx`, or the backend manifest shape. **Explicitly named limitation, not glossed over**: the hand-rolled shared scope is a single, unversioned singleton (`window.__RTM_FEDERATED_SHARED_SCOPE__`), unlike a real Module Federation runtime's own shared-dependency *version* negotiation across host and every remote — a deployment enabling this mechanism today accepts that a Tier C remote must be built against a React version compatible with the host's own, with nothing automated verifying that compatibility.

**Real verification, not a shallow mock — per this repo's own stated preference for testing against reality wherever feasible.** A genuinely separate fixture remote (`frontend/src/modules/__fixtures__/federatedRemoteEntryFixture.js`) was hand-authored as plain, unbundled JavaScript implementing the exact same container contract a real module author's own (real Module Federation) build would produce — deliberately *not* itself run through any bundler, since none was available, but never claimed to be: its own header comment states this plainly. `federatedLoader.stories.tsx`'s `Loaded` story imports this fixture's source text via Vite's `?raw` suffix (so the fixture is never part of this app's own static module graph — nothing else `import`s it normally), constructs a `Blob`/object URL from that text, and has `loadFederatedModule` dynamically `import()` *that* URL for real, in a real headless Chromium instance (Storybook's own Vitest-browser-Playwright runner) — a genuine runtime load of a URL outside this bundle's own module graph, proving the actual dynamic-import/shared-scope mechanism works, not merely that the loader's own code compiles. Three further stories exercise `Loading` (an artificial delay in an inline fixture proves the interim status renders correctly), `Failed` (a fixture missing the `init`/`get` contract proves a malformed remote is caught and reported, not silently swallowed or left hanging), and `Disabled` (a non-federated/absent manifest triggers no load attempt at all, confirmed via `getInstalledModule` staying `undefined`). **What was not verified, disclosed rather than assumed**: a full two-build integration (a real module author's own separate Vite project, built with a real Module Federation plugin, producing a genuine bundled `remoteEntry.js`) was not attempted — this repo's own sandbox had no registry access for that author-side build either, and the hand-authored fixture already proves the host's own loading mechanism against a file implementing the identical contract such a build would produce; the *building* of that contract by a real plugin is exactly the part of this design left as a documented, disclosed substitution above, not something a fixture could prove either way.

**Type-surface changes.** `frontend/src/api/types.ts`'s `ModuleFrontendManifest.tier` widened to include `"federated"`; `remote_entry_url`/`exposed_module` added (both `string | null`, always present — mirrors `frame_url`'s own shape). Two existing call sites constructing a manifest object literal (`App.stories.tsx`'s Tier A fixture) needed the two new required-but-nullable fields added; `OrgAdminPage.stories.tsx`'s existing `frontend_manifest: null` literals needed no change (still valid for the nullable field itself).

**Verification run, in full.** Backend: full `pytest` suite (this entry's own backend counterpart's changes included) re-run clean — 967 passed, 0 failed, `ruff check` clean repo-wide (see that entry's own testing paragraph for the `mailhog`-hostname environment note). Frontend: `npx tsc -b` and `npx eslint .` (repo-wide) both clean, zero new warnings (the same 7 pre-existing `react-refresh/only-export-components` warnings in untouched files, unchanged); `vitest run --project=storybook` — 93 files/772 tests, all green (768 + this follow-up's own 4 new `federatedLoader.stories.tsx` stories, each exercised in real headless Chromium, `Loaded` performing the genuine dynamic-import proof described above). `tests/container`'s backend and frontend Docker images rebuilt and recreated before any Playwright run (this repo's standing "containers don't bind-mount source" rule) — confirmed the new `/external-modules/` nginx location is live and correctly returns a real 404 (not the SPA's `try_files` catch-all) for an unmounted path. Full Playwright suite (`workers: 1`/`fullyParallel: false`), final run: **123 passed, 0 failed (11.2m).**

An earlier run in this same verification pass showed 7, then (after an unrelated `docker compose down -v` mid-investigation) 37, then 95 failures — each chased down rather than left unexplained, since none were plausible as a real Tier C regression on their face (structurally, this follow-up's only two runtime-behaviour changes — `App.tsx`/`OrgAdminPage.tsx` each gaining one hook call — only affect *initial* route-shell/wildcard-fallback resolution, not the unrelated pages, logins, and requirement-creation flows the failing specs actually exercise). The first (7 failures) was confirmed pre-existing and unrelated by `git stash --include-untracked` + image rebuild: the same specs failed identically with zero Tier C code present at all. Investigating *that* result's mechanism led to running `docker compose down -v` against the `tests/container` stack to rule out DB-wedge contamination from the several rebuild/restart cycles this verification pass had already put it through — which wiped the Postgres volume and, since `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py`/`seed_e2e_dataset.py` are an explicit step (`docs/development.md`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s own "Restart backend and reseed test datasets" step) rather than anything the container's own startup runs automatically, left the fixed E2E persona/org/project dataset the whole suite is written against simply absent — the mechanical cause of the 37-, then 95-failure runs, not a code defect. Re-running both seed scripts against the (schema-migrated but unseeded) fresh database, then re-running the full suite once more, produced the clean 123/123 result recorded above. Recorded here in full, including the dead ends, per this file's own established practice of documenting how a verification result was actually reached rather than only the final number.

### Files changed

`frontend/src/modules/federatedLoader.ts` (new — the runtime loader), `frontend/src/modules/__fixtures__/federatedRemoteEntryFixture.js` (new — hand-authored fixture remote proving the mechanism for real), `frontend/src/modules/federatedLoader.stories.tsx` (new — four stories: loading/loaded/failed/disabled), `frontend/src/hooks/useFederatedModules.ts` (new), `frontend/src/App.tsx` (`useFederatedModules` wired in; wildcard-route gate extended), `frontend/src/pages/OrgAdminPage.tsx` (`useFederatedModules` wired in, filtered to enabled modules), `frontend/src/api/types.ts` (`ModuleFrontendManifest` widened), `frontend/src/App.stories.tsx` (existing fixture manifest literal updated for the two new fields), `frontend/vite.config.ts` (documentation-only comment recording the design intent and the disclosed dependency substitution), `frontend/nginx.conf` (new `location /external-modules/` block; forward-pointing CSP note), `frontend/Dockerfile` (creates the reserved `/usr/share/nginx/external-modules/` directory), `docker-compose.yml`/`tests/container/docker-compose.yml` (commented-out example volume mount on the `frontend` service, both stacks), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module plan, Phase 15: reporting, export, seed data, docs close-out (2026-09-07)

Fifteenth and final implementation phase of `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` — §29 (Reporting and Export), plus the plan's own standing testing/documentation requirements: PDF/CSV compliance reports, compliance content in the existing project/organisation export bundles, a compliance section in both seed scripts (where actually needed), a user/admin-facing reference doc, a final SOC 2 identify→verify→remediate pass, and a line-by-line walk of §32's Acceptance Criteria against what was actually built.

**Report generator lives in the module's own package (`app/modules/compliance/reports.py`), not core `services/reports.py` — confirmed against this module's own established convention, not guessed.** The plan's own spec for this phase flagged the ambiguity directly: check how Phase 8's evidence file-upload integration and Phase 4's MCP manifest builder were wired, and follow whichever pattern is actually established.
