Reading both confirmed a clear precedent: `project_router.py` already calls `app.services.files.upload_file` directly from module code for evidence attachments rather than routing through a new core wrapper (its own module docstring says so explicitly), while `app.modules.registry.build_mcp_tool_manifest` is the one core-owned exception — and only because it aggregates *every* module's declared tools, a genuinely cross-module concern this report generator isn't. A single module's own report generator is squarely the first shape, so it lives in `app.modules.compliance.reports`, reusing core `services/reports.py`'s ReportLab/csv approach and `_safe`-escaping discipline (duplicated as a five-line local function, documented as a deliberate, small duplication rather than reaching into that module's private helper — the same boundary-respecting choice `project_router.py` already makes for `upload_file`) rather than routing through core `routers/reports.py`, which is already fully committed to the *requirement*-report shape (`ReportRequirementRow`, intro/chapters/appendices) with no equivalent concept here.

**Two report kinds, two new GET endpoints each, both reusing existing computed-state builders rather than re-deriving them — the concrete mechanism behind §32's "compliance percentages and overall statuses are calculated consistently."** `GET .../projects/{id}/modules/compliance/reports/{pdf,csv}` (view-gated, `_require_view` — a report never surfaces anything the same caller couldn't already read via this module's own JSON endpoints) collects, per assigned standard: every requirement's applicability/status/approval state (via `service.load_pcrs_and_applicability`, the exact §9 hierarchical-resolution function every other endpoint uses), required-action completion, linked evidence (via `service.compute_evidence_validity_state`), project-level and standard-level review history, and cross-standard/cross-version mappings touching the assigned standards. `GET .../orgs/{id}/modules/compliance/reports/{pdf,csv}` (manage-gated, `_require_manage` — matching Phase 14's own "§26 reserves cross-project viewing for Compliance Manager" precedent exactly, not a new, looser view-tier) rolls up one row per (project, assigned standard version) pair via `service.build_status_out` — the identical §20 calculation `router.py::list_all_project_compliance` already uses — plus appendices built from `service.list_non_compliant_requirements_for_project`/`list_pending_approvals_for_project`/`list_expiring_or_expired_evidence`, the same Phase 14 org-wide aggregation functions, called directly rather than re-implemented. No compliance percentage, overall state, or evidence-validity value is ever computed a second way inside the report generator.

**CSV carries only the main assessment-row table; PDF carries every appendix — a deliberate split, not an oversight, mirroring core `services.reports`'s own identical "CSV is flat, PDF is where the richer layout lives" precedent for requirement reports.** Nothing in §29 requires every listed field to appear in *both* export formats, only that reports overall be *capable* of including them — the PDF's evidence-register/review-history/cross-standard-mapping sections (project scope) and non-compliant/pending-approval/expiring-evidence appendices (org scope) satisfy that; the CSV is the audit-friendly flat table. Also available as "Download PDF/CSV report" buttons on `ProjectCompliancePage.tsx`'s Standards tab and `OrgComplianceDashboard.tsx`, reusing `pages/ReportsPage.tsx`'s exact existing `api.getForBlob`/`api.postForBlob` + `downloadBlob` idiom rather than inventing a second one — the only new frontend UI this phase needed, proportionate to the two new backend endpoints it exposes; Storybook interaction stories (`DownloadReport`, both files, asserting `api.getForBlob` is called with the right URL) and a Playwright step in each of the existing `project-compliance-view.spec.ts`/`org-compliance-view.spec.ts` specs (asserting a real `download` event with the expected filename) cover it, per this repo's standing "every new UI feature needs both" rule.

**Export bundles extended exactly where the plan's own spec said to, with the organisation/project split following straight from §31's own architecture, not a new judgement call.** §31: "A Compliance Standard is not a Project," "Compliance Standards are organisation-level reusable definitions" — so `services.org_export` (mirroring `ReportTemplate`'s existing org-level bundle placement) gained every compliance standard, with its full version/requirement/required-action tree, the organisation's action-type and mapping-relationship-type vocabularies, and its cross-standard requirement mappings. `services.project_export` (mirroring how requirements themselves travel with a project bundle) gained that project's own compliance *assessment*: its assignments, per-requirement applicability/status/approval state, required-action assessments, evidence (with files and revalidation history), and its own project-level reviews — deliberately excluding standard-level reviews (`ComplianceReview.standard_id` set), which belong to the standard and travel with the org bundle instead, matching the model's own "two distinct owners" design (`models.py`'s Phase 10 notes).

**A project bundle never re-embeds the standard it references — the one design decision this phase had to make that the plan's spec text didn't fully spell out, and the one most worth getting right, since getting it wrong would have reopened §31's own no-duplication principle.** Re-creating a project's assigned standard from inside every project bundle that happens to reference it would violate "a project must not need to duplicate the underlying compliance requirements simply because multiple projects use the same standard" the moment two projects on the same standard were both exported and reimported into a fresh organisation — each would silently fork its own copy. Instead, `_apply_project_compliance_data` (`project_export.py`) resolves the assignment's standard/version against the **target** organisation's own compliance standards by a portable `(standard_reference, version_label)` key at import time, mirroring the exact `requirement_link_type_forward_name`-resolved-within-target-org pattern this file's own docstring already establishes for link types — and skips the whole assignment (with a warning, never silently fabricated) if no match exists there, the same "unmatched reference → skip with warning" shape as an unmatched link type. `test_project_export_import_skips_assignment_when_target_org_lacks_the_standard` pins exactly this. A requirement within a resolved version is itself matched by `(reference, name)` (`_requirement_key`), since a `ComplianceRequirement` row carries no cross-deployment-portable identifier of its own (unlike a core `Requirement`'s `unique_code`) — a documented limitation (two requirements sharing both fields within one version would collide), the same class of limitation this bundle format's existing prefix-based component/category matching already carries.

**Materialisation reused, not re-implemented, on project-bundle import.** Rather than hand-building `ProjectComplianceRequirement`/`ComplianceRequiredActionAssessment` rows from the bundle's own recorded state, `_apply_project_compliance_data` creates a fresh `ProjectCompliance` row and calls `service.materialize_assessment_rows` — the exact function `router.py::create_project_compliance` calls for a live "assign a standard" action — to build the same default scaffold, then overlays the bundle's recorded assessment state on top of it (matched via `_requirement_key`/`_required_action_key`). A row that can't be matched (the target version's content has independently drifted since export, or a key collision) is left at its materialised default and a warning is recorded, never silently fabricated from the bundle.

**Organisation-bundle merge (`merge_org_bundle`) needed a third conflict kind, or it would have crashed on a same-`reference` standard collision instead of degrading gracefully.** `_compute_merge_conflicts`/`detect_merge_conflicts` gained `"compliance_standard"` alongside the existing `"project"`/`"report_template"` kinds, resolved `"skip"`/`"import_as_copy"` (a renamed reference, `"<reference> (imported)"`) — mirroring the *project* conflict's resolution shape, not the report template's in-place-overwrite one, since a standard carries real versioned/hierarchical content an in-place replace would destroy, the identical reasoning `_import_projects`'s own docstring already gives for why a project is never merged in place either. The two compliance vocabularies (action types, mapping relationship types) are purely additive by name on merge — reused if a same-named one already exists, never overwritten (so a target org's own prior `implies_equivalence` decision on an existing relationship type is never silently changed by an unrelated import) — mirroring `_import_org_groups`'s established "reuse by name" precedent for a lightweight vocabulary with no sub-content to lose.

**Seed data: demo dataset gained a real compliance section; the E2E dataset needed none, confirmed by reading the actual specs rather than assumed.** `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py` now authors an "Aerospace Safety & Airworthiness Standard" (reusing the same Part 107/flight-logging regulatory narrative `DRONE_REQUIREMENTS` already tells), assigns it to Falcon-3 Inspection Drone, grants `demo.engineer` the `compliance_officer` project role, and demonstrates a compliant-and-approved requirement (with a completed required action and linked, revalidated evidence) alongside a Non-Compliant one (with an outstanding, assigned required action) and a scheduled annual review — so the module is genuinely visible, in a realistic mixed state, the moment someone opens the demo instance, not left at its empty post-Phase-5 default. `backend/scripts/seed_e2e_dataset.py` was **not** touched: all three Compliance Playwright specs (`tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/*.spec.ts`) already author their own dynamically-named standard/requirement/evidence fixtures via the UI on every run (each spec's own docstring says so explicitly, per this repo's standing test-idempotency rule) rather than depending on any fixed seeded compliance data — inventing seed data nothing actually asserts against would have been scope the task itself warned against adding.

**`docs/mcp-server.md` checked against `module.py`'s live `mcp_tools` tuple, found already fully accurate, left unchanged.** All ten tool names, parameters, and scoping (the first three plus both Phase 11 tools on the org router requiring `organization_id`; the five Phase 7/8/9/10 tools on the project router requiring only `project_id`) match exactly — kept current incrementally through Phases 6–11, as its own text already claims. No mutating tool was declared for the two new report endpoints, consistent with every other read endpoint this module *has* chosen to expose as an MCP tool and every mutating one it has deliberately not (a report is arguably the safest possible candidate for a future read-only tool, but nothing in this phase's spec asked for one, and this module's own repeated "add narrowly and only when asked" precedent — see Phases 9/10/11's own notes above — applies here too; left as an easy, low-risk future addition rather than added speculatively).

**New `services.labels` compliance label dictionaries — mirroring `frontend/src/api/types.ts`'s `COMPLIANCE_*_LABEL` maps verbatim, not reinvented — so the PDF/CSV report text matches the UI's own wording exactly.** `services/labels.py`'s own docstring already states it mirrors the frontend's equivalent maps for the one existing case (`REQUIREMENT_STATUS_LABEL`); this phase extends that same file (not a new module-local one) with `COMPLIANCE_STATUS_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_APPLICABILITY_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_APPLICABILITY_SOURCE_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_APPROVAL_STATE_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_EVIDENCE_VALIDITY_STATE_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_REVIEW_STATUS_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_REVIEW_OUTCOME_LABEL`/`COMPLIANCE_STANDARD_VERSION_STATUS_LABEL` plus lookup functions, kept in this established "wire value → report-facing label" location rather than under `app.modules.compliance` itself.

**SOC 2 identify → verify → remediate pass** (this phase touches RBAC via two new endpoints, attachments via evidence-file export/import, and multi-tenant data via cross-org bundle handling — three of `CLAUDE.md`'s policy-consultation triggers):

- *Identify*: the two new report endpoints could leak cross-tenant or Restricted-classified data if gated wrongly; the export/import changes could leak secrets, cross organisational boundaries during a merge, bypass the existing banned-user guard, or duplicate a standard across organisations in violation of §31.
- *Verify*: both report endpoints reuse this router's own pre-existing dependencies verbatim (`_require_view`/`_require_manage`) rather than a new one — confirmed by reading the endpoint code directly, not assumed. Every field a report surfaces (requirement text, justifications, evidence metadata, approval decisions, emails) is already returned by this module's own JSON endpoints to a caller with the same access; no Restricted-classified field (`docs/soc2/policies/data-classification-and-confidentiality-policy.md`'s table: password hashes, TOTP/OIDC/SMTP secrets) is read anywhere in `reports.py`, and evidence *file contents* are never embedded, only an evidence row's own metadata. Every new compliance export query is scoped by `organization_id` (standards, requirement mappings) or resolved against the *target* organisation specifically (a project bundle's assignment lookup) — confirmed by re-reading each new query's `WHERE` clause. Compliance email-attribution fields added to the bundle format (`assigned_by`, `provided_by`, `assessed_by`, `approval_decided_by`, `completed_by`, a review's `owner_id`/`completed_by`/`created_by`) are all resolved via the existing `UserResolver`, which — like every other authorship/attribution field already in this bundle format (`creator_id`, `owner_id`, `reviewer_id`, etc.) — does not check `User.is_banned`; this is correct, not a gap, because none of these fields *grant access* the way `_import_members`/`_import_org_groups`'s explicit banned-check (role/group-membership grants) exists to guard — they attribute a historical fact, exactly like every other such field this bundle format already carries. CSV escaping (`csv_safe`) is applied to every field in both compliance CSV exports, confirmed by `test_project_compliance_csv_report_includes_assessment_and_neutralizes_injection` (an `=HYPERLINK(...)`-prefixed justification comes back `'`-prefixed, mirroring core `tests/test_reports.py`'s own identical regression test); PDF escaping (`_safe`) is applied uniformly via the `_p()` helper wrapping every table cell. Report generation is not audit-logged, matching core `routers/reports.py`'s own established precedent (a read/export action, not a mutation) — not a new gap, a consistent non-decision. An org-admin merging a bundle that creates compliance standards carries no new privilege-escalation risk: `merge_org_bundle` is already gated `require_org_role(ORG_ADMIN)`, and `require_module_role`'s own existing composition already lets an org admin manage compliance standards directly via the API, so a bundle merge grants nothing beyond what that same admin could already do by hand.
- *Remediate*: no gap found requiring a fix or a policy-doc edit — every risk surfaced above was either already correctly handled by an existing, reused mechanism, or resolved by a design decision made explicitly during this phase's own implementation (the portable-standard-reference design and the CSV/PDF-appendix split above), not discovered as a regression needing remediation afterward.

**§32 Acceptance Criteria walked line by line against the shipped system** (docs/Compliance_Module_Requirements.md) — every criterion confirmed already satisfied by Phases 0–14, with two real gaps found and fixed as part of this phase rather than deferred:

1. *Evidence revalidation history and required-action/evidence linkage did not survive a project export/import round trip before this phase* — `ComplianceEvidenceRevalidation` rows and `ComplianceEvidenceFile`/`ComplianceEvidenceRequirementLink`/`ComplianceEvidenceActionLink` links had no representation in `project_export.py` at all prior to this phase (Compliance had no export integration yet). Fixed as this phase's own core deliverable — `_collect_project_compliance_data`/`_apply_project_compliance_data` carry all of it; `test_project_export_import_round_trips_compliance_assessment` pins the revalidation history specifically (asserting the *previous* expiry survives alongside the new one, not just the evidence row's current state).
2. *No report existed at all satisfying §29's "reports should be capable of including" list* — the gap this entire phase exists to close; see above.

Every other §32 line — module enable/disable defaulting on, Compliance-Manager/Compliance-Officer authority without Organisation Administrator, hierarchical requirements and applicability, multiple Required Actions with their own status/evidence, evidence expiry/revalidation/identification, auditable decisions, formal approval/sign-off with retained history and automatic re-assessment flagging, scheduled reviews with retained history and upcoming/overdue identification, event-driven notifications, cross-standard mappings navigable from both sides, per-project and cross-project compliance views with every named drill-down, consistently-calculated percentages/statuses that never count Not Applicable against them, standard changes never silently altering historical assessments, explicit version-adoption with identified impact — was independently re-confirmed present and working (via the relevant Phase 5–14 code and its own tests, re-read for this pass rather than taken on faith) with no further gap found.

**Testing.** New backend tests (`backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/`): `test_compliance_export_import.py` (3 tests — project-level round trip through the full assessment/evidence/review surface including revalidation history; the target-org-lacks-the-standard skip-with-warning path; an organisation-level round trip through two standards, a hierarchical requirement tree with a required action, and a cross-standard mapping, all reconstructed via the real API afterward, not inspected as raw rows); `test_compliance_reports.py` (4 tests — a valid PDF, a CSV whose columns/values match the underlying assessment including the applicability-inheritance-then-override case and formula-injection neutralization, the org-report Compliance-Manager RBAC gate, and the org CSV roll-up's per-project non-compliant count). `ruff check` clean on every touched backend file. Full backend suite run via `docker compose exec backend pytest -q` (the authoritative way, per this file's own established practice for this repo's `mailhog`-hostname environment constraint) — **974 passed, 0 failed** (18m13s). A first attempt at this run showed 973 passed plus one error in an unrelated test (`test_websocket_security.py::test_user_session_still_valid_reflects_org_disable`, no shared code path with this phase); investigating rather than dismissing it surfaced a self-inflicted cause, not a product regression — two `pytest` processes had ended up running concurrently against the same `reqtrack_pytest_test` database (confirmed via `pg_stat_activity` and each container process's own `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`), the same class of shared-test-DB collision this repo's own session history already has several documented shapes of. Both processes were killed and a single, verified-solitary run was started and completed clean — the number above. Frontend: `npx tsc -b` and `npx eslint .` (repo-wide) both clean; `vitest run --project=storybook` for the two touched story files (10 tests, including the two new `DownloadReport` stories) green. `tests/container`'s backend and frontend images rebuilt and recreated before Playwright; all three Compliance module Playwright specs (`compliance-standards-management.spec.ts`, `project-compliance-view.spec.ts` — now including a real PDF+CSV download assertion, `org-compliance-view.spec.ts` — now including a real PDF download assertion) run together, green, twice back to back (confirming idempotency, every fixture dynamically named per this repo's standing rule).

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/compliance/reports.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py` (two new report endpoints), `backend/app/modules/compliance/router.py` (two new report endpoints), `backend/app/services/labels.py` (compliance label maps), `backend/app/services/project_export.py` (`_collect_project_compliance_data`/`_apply_project_compliance_data`, `_requirement_key`/`_required_action_key`), `backend/app/services/org_export.py` (`_collect_compliance_export_data`, `_import_compliance_vocab`/`_import_compliance_standards`/`_import_compliance_requirement_mappings`, a third `"compliance_standard"` merge-conflict kind), `backend/scripts/seed_demo_data.py` (compliance helpers + seeding section), `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_compliance_export_import.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_compliance_reports.py` (new); `frontend/src/modules/compliance/ProjectCompliancePage.tsx`/`.stories.tsx`, `frontend/src/modules/compliance/OrgComplianceDashboard.tsx`/`.stories.tsx` (download-report buttons + stories); `tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/project-compliance-view.spec.ts`/`org-compliance-view.spec.ts` (download-report assertions); `docs/compliance-module.md` (new), `docs/compliance-module-plan.md` (Phase 15 marked complete; plan marked 16/16 complete), `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module self-containment: types/labels/export-import moved out of core (2026-09-07, same day)

A direct user request, not a plan-driven phase: "make sure that all compliance module components are inside the compliance module... I don't care if it's intentional, I want modules to be self contained regardless of them being first class." An investigation agent had first surveyed every place compliance-specific code lived outside `backend/app/modules/compliance/`/`frontend/src/modules/compliance/` and found five candidates; four (the `COMPLIANCE_*` enum/label pairs in `frontend/src/api/types.ts`, the matching dicts in `backend/app/services/labels.py`, `reports.py`'s module-local placement, and the frontend data-shape/enum split) were each individually defensible against this repo's own binding conventions (CLAUDE.md's label-map rule; Phase 12's established interfaces-in-module/enums-in-core split) — but the user's instruction was explicit that "intentional" is not a reason to leave a module's own display concerns or bundle logic sitting in shared core files, so all five were addressed, not just the one (`org_export.py`/`project_export.py` importing `app.modules.compliance` directly) the investigation had flagged as a genuine architectural gap.

**Labels and enums: moved wholesale, no registry needed, because nothing outside the module ever consumed them generically.** Before moving anything, every call site of the ten `COMPLIANCE_*_LABEL` dicts (backend and frontend) and their backing enum types was found by grep/import-block inspection — all of them lived inside `app/modules/compliance/reports.py` (backend) or `frontend/src/modules/compliance/*.tsx` (frontend); nothing in core rendered a compliance enum generically (`NotificationType`'s `compliance_*` variants were checked too — see below for why those stayed put). That meant a straight move-and-rename was correct, not a registry/extension-point mechanism: `backend/app/modules/compliance/labels.py` (new) now holds the ten dicts + lookup functions, mirroring the frontend's identical split (`frontend/src/modules/compliance/types.ts` now holds the enum types and their `*_LABEL` consts, previously in `frontend/src/api/types.ts`); `backend/app/services/labels.py` and `frontend/src/api/types.ts` keep only their own core enum (`REQUIREMENT_STATUS_LABEL`, `STAGE_STATUS_LABEL`, etc.). `reports.py`'s one import line was repointed; every compliance frontend file's import of a `COMPLIANCE_*_LABEL` const or its enum type was repointed from `"../../api/types"` to `"./types"`, merging into that file's existing `./types` import where one already existed rather than leaving two.

**`NotificationType`'s thirteen `compliance_*` variants were deliberately left in the core Python enum and TS union, not moved — a real technical constraint, not a judgement call this pass overrode.** `Notification.type`/`NotificationPreference.type` are `Mapped[NotificationType]` columns via `str_enum(NotificationType, 50)` — a single shared table every module (not just Compliance) writes rows into, backed by one fixed Python `enum.Enum` class at mapping-definition time. Splitting a module's own notification-type literals out into a separately-defined enum would require either a schema-level redesign (a plain `String` column plus a runtime-registry validation layer replacing the current compile-time-checked enum column) or TypeScript module augmentation for the matching frontend union — both meaningfully larger and riskier than this pass's scope, and neither was asked for. The frontend's `strings.notifications.types` labels for these thirteen types (in `frontend/src/i18n/strings.ts`) were left alongside them for the same reason: they key off the same shared union. This is flagged here explicitly (per this repo's "say so rather than silently diverging" rule) rather than silently left as a residual gap: `Notification`/`NotificationPreference` are core, module-agnostic infrastructure Compliance is a *client* of, not a compliance-owned type living in the wrong file — a materially different shape of "leak" than the other four items in this pass, all of which were pure code/data with no shared-schema constraint.

**Export/import: two new `ModuleDefinition` hook types, modelled directly on the existing `resolve_file_owner_project_id` precedent, not invented from scratch.** `app.modules.registry.ModuleOrgBundleHooks`/`ModuleProjectBundleHooks` (new dataclasses, `registry.py`) are the org/project-bundle equivalent of the file-ownership-resolution hook that already let `GET /api/v1/files/{id}` authorize a Compliance evidence attachment "without that core, module-agnostic router importing anything from the module directly" (that hook's own docstring) — the same reasoning applied one concern later, closing the one gap the investigation agent had actually found: `org_export.py`/`project_export.py` `from app.modules.compliance import ...`-ing directly, unlike every other cross-cutting mechanism (routers, RBAC, frontend manifest, MCP tools, scheduled jobs, file-ownership) the module system already generalised. `ModuleOrgBundleHooks` carries five fields (`export`, `import_`, and three merge-specific ones — `compute_merge_conflicts`, `merge_resolution_choices`, `summarize_merge` — because `merge_org_bundle`'s conflict-detection/resolution-validation/summary-count logic for `"compliance_standard"` conflicts was itself woven into `org_export.py`'s shared, multi-kind `_compute_merge_conflicts`/`_resolution_choices_by_kind`/summary-dict machinery alongside the core `"project"`/`"report_template"` kinds, not a separate function); `ModuleProjectBundleHooks` is a plain two-field `export`/`import_` pair, since `project_export.py`'s compliance section had no merge-conflict complexity to generalise (a project bundle is always imported as a brand-new project, never merged into an existing one).

**All six extracted functions moved verbatim into a new `backend/app/modules/compliance/export.py`, logic unchanged — a relocation, not a rewrite.** `_collect_compliance_export_data` → `export_org_data`; `_import_compliance_vocab`/`_import_compliance_standards`/`_import_compliance_requirement_mappings` → bundled into one `import_org_data` (their call sites always ran in that fixed order and `_import_compliance_standards`'s returned `requirement_id_by_ref` had no consumer beyond the third call, so the three-call sequence collapses cleanly into the single hook `ModuleOrgBundleHooks.import_` declares); `_collect_project_compliance_data`/`_apply_project_compliance_data` → `export_project_data`/`import_project_data`; `_requirement_key`/`_required_action_key` moved alongside them (they were already compliance-specific helpers living in `project_export.py`, used nowhere else in that file). The compliance-standard-conflict block inside `org_export.py`'s `_compute_merge_conflicts` became `compute_org_merge_conflicts`; the two `compliance_standards_imported`/`_skipped` summary lines inside `merge_org_bundle` became `summarize_org_merge`; `_COMPLIANCE_STANDARD_RESOLUTIONS` became `ORG_MERGE_RESOLUTION_CHOICES`. `module.py`'s `MODULE_DEFINITION` gained `org_bundle_hooks=ModuleOrgBundleHooks(...)`/`project_bundle_hooks=ModuleProjectBundleHooks(...)`, each field a thin wrapper function doing a lazy, inside-the-function import of `export.py` — mirroring `resolve_file_owner_project_id`'s own established "avoid import-cycle risk with this module's own registration" pattern exactly, rather than importing `export.py` at `module.py`'s top level.

**`org_export.py`/`project_export.py` now iterate `get_all_module_org_bundle_hooks()`/`get_all_module_project_bundle_hooks()` (two new registry lookup functions, mirroring `get_all_module_scheduled_jobs`'s identical shape) at every point that used to call a compliance function directly** — `build_org_bundle`'s `**compliance_json` merge, both `import_org_bundle`'s and `merge_org_bundle`'s three sequential compliance-import calls, `_compute_merge_conflicts`'s conflict list, `merge_org_bundle`'s `_resolution_choices_by_kind` dict, and its summary dict — each now a loop over every registered module's hooks rather than a named compliance call, so a second module with its own org/project bundle content in future would need zero edits to either core file. Both core files' module docstrings were rewritten to describe the generic mechanism rather than naming Compliance's own content directly; `backend/app/modules/compliance/export.py`'s own module docstring carries the compliance-specific detail instead, matching `reports.py`'s existing self-contained-module-docstring convention.

**Testing.** `ruff check` clean on every touched backend file (`org_export.py`, `project_export.py`, `registry.py`, `module.py`, `export.py`, `labels.py`, `reports.py`) after an auto-fix pass corrected import ordering and one now-unused `date` import left behind by the extraction. Full backend suite run via `docker compose exec backend pytest -q` after rebuilding the backend image (source is not bind-mounted into the dev/test containers) — **974 passed, 0 failed** (19m25s), the identical count Phase 15's own entry above recorded, confirming this pass changed no behaviour, only where the code lives; `test_compliance_export_import.py`'s three round-trip tests (project-level, org-level, target-org-lacks-the-standard) all still pass unchanged, having never referenced the moved functions' names directly (they exercise the real HTTP API). Frontend: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint src/modules/compliance/ src/api/types.ts` both clean; the full Storybook suite (`vitest run --project=storybook`, 93 files, 774 tests) passed with zero failures, confirming every compliance component still resolves its label/type imports correctly after the `api/types.ts` → `modules/compliance/types.ts` move.

### Files changed

`backend/app/modules/compliance/labels.py` (new), `backend/app/modules/compliance/export.py` (new), `backend/app/services/labels.py` (compliance dicts removed), `backend/app/modules/compliance/reports.py` (import repointed), `backend/app/modules/registry.py` (`ModuleOrgBundleHooks`/`ModuleProjectBundleHooks` dataclasses, `org_bundle_hooks`/`project_bundle_hooks` fields on `ModuleDefinition`, `get_all_module_org_bundle_hooks`/`get_all_module_project_bundle_hooks`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/module.py` (hooks registered), `backend/app/services/org_export.py` (compliance functions removed, generic hook iteration), `backend/app/services/project_export.py` (compliance functions removed, generic hook iteration); `frontend/src/api/types.ts` (compliance enums/labels removed), `frontend/src/modules/compliance/types.ts` (enums/labels added) and every other file in `frontend/src/modules/compliance/` that imported a `COMPLIANCE_*_LABEL` const or enum type (import repointed to `./types`); `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Deep hardening pass on `feature/complience-module` ("please do a hardening pass" / "now please do a deeper hardening pass")

Requested in two stages against the whole 15-phase Compliance Module + modular feature system branch (`feature/complience-module` vs `main`, ~150 files): an initial automated identify→verify→remediate scan (this project's `security-review` skill, false-positive-filtered by independent sub-agent verification), then an explicit "go deeper" pass per this project's standing practice of treating a hardening-pass request as its own scoped review rather than assuming an earlier one already covered everything (see the "Deep hardening pass on `feature/multi-level-projects`"/`feature/ui-improvement-stage-4` entries above for the same pattern). The deeper pass traced invariants across four lanes in parallel — approval workflow/scheduled reviews/notifications, org/project export-import bundle hooks and cross-standard mapping, the full compliance frontend against this project's standard checklist, and evidence-file/MCP-tool/module-RBAC edge cases — each independently verified against the actual code before being trusted, per this project's standing rule never to act on a sub-agent's word alone. A fifth, unrelated item was folded into the same pass at the user's request: the two long-open GitHub code-scanning alerts against `main`.

**1. CONFIRMED, fixed — `require_server_role` had no PAT rejection, unlike its sibling `require_server_admin`.** `backend/app/services/rbac.py`'s `require_server_role` (backing the new `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR` server-tier role) never checked `request.state.pat_allowed_org_ids`, even though this branch is the first to wire a PAT-reachable endpoint behind it (`backend/app/routers/system.py`'s five module-entitlement admin endpoints). A user holding `MODULE_ADMINISTRATOR` who self-issued a normal org-scoped Personal Access Token could use it to change the deployment-wide default module entitlement policy, or grant/revoke module entitlement for *any* organisation — not just the org(s) the PAT was scoped to — defeating the PAT org-scoping containment model `require_server_admin`'s own docstring establishes for exactly this class of action. The dependency's own docstring admitted the gap ("nothing... yet exposes a PAT-reachable endpoint gated by this dependency — revisit if one does") without the revisit happening. Fixed by mirroring `require_server_admin`'s exact PAT rejection. New test: `test_module_system_rbac.py::test_pat_rejected_for_module_administrator_endpoints_even_for_a_real_module_administrator`.

**2. CONFIRMED, fixed — a required action's `assignee_id` and a review's `owner_id` were never validated, feeding an arbitrary user id straight into an unconditional daily notification sweep.** None of the five write paths that accept these fields (`project_router.py::update_required_action_assessment`/`create_project_review`/`update_project_review`, `router.py::create_standard_review`/`update_standard_review`) checked that the supplied user id had any relationship to the project or organisation at all. `scheduler.py`'s daily sweeps (`send_required_action_due_notifications`/`send_review_due_notifications`) then notify whoever these fields name, unconditionally — so a `compliance_officer`/`compliance_manager` could point either field at any user id in the entire system (not merely outside this project, outside this organisation entirely), disclosing the existence and timing of another org's compliance schedule to someone with no legitimate access, or simply spamming an arbitrary target. This mirrors a pre-existing, identical gap on core `RequirementAction.assignee_id` (`routers/requirements.py`), so it isn't a wholly new class of bug — but this branch's scheduler is what turns the dormant field into an active, unconditional cross-tenant notification channel. Fixed org-scoped, not project-role-scoped, matching this codebase's own established "must be a member of this project's organisation first" convention (`routers/projects.py::add_member_source`'s identical check) rather than a stricter project-membership check: an assignee/owner such as a Compliance Manager overseeing several projects is not required to hold a formal `ProjectRole` on this specific one, confirmed by this branch's own pre-existing test (`test_review_due_sweep_notifies_owner`) which already relied on exactly that. New tests: `test_project_compliance_api.py::test_required_action_assessment_assignee_must_be_a_member_of_the_projects_organisation`, `test_compliance_reviews_and_notifications.py::test_project_review_owner_must_be_a_member_of_the_projects_organisation`/`test_standard_review_owner_must_be_an_org_member`.

**3. Found and fixed while closing a test-coverage gap, not a security finding — `OrgMergeResult` silently dropped every module-contributed merge-summary field.** The export/import lane found no vulnerability but flagged that `merge_org_bundle` had zero test coverage exercising compliance data (`test_org_import_merge.py` has no compliance references at all). Writing that coverage (`test_compliance_export_import.py`'s three new `test_org_merge_*` tests) immediately surfaced a real defect: `services.org_export.merge_org_bundle`'s own docstring documents its returned summary as carrying "whatever each registered module's own `ModuleOrgBundleHooks.summarize_merge` contributes" (e.g. Compliance's `compliance_standards_imported`/`_skipped`), but the router endpoint constructs a fixed `schemas.org.OrgMergeResult` via `OrgMergeResult(warnings=warnings, **summary)` — a plain Pydantic `BaseModel` silently drops any kwarg not declared as one of its own fields, so a module's own merge counts validated fine (no 500) but never actually reached the API response, contradicting the documented contract and defeating exactly the "core code shouldn't need much modification per module" goal this module system otherwise achieves elsewhere. Fixed with `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")` on `OrgMergeResult`, confirmed to actually surface extra fields through FastAPI's response serialization before relying on it. Also caught two authoring mistakes in the new tests themselves while verifying (an org-membership vs. project-membership mismatch matching finding 2's own correction, and an assumption that `import_as_copy` renames a standard's `name` rather than its `reference`) — both fixed before trusting the tests green.

**Reviewed and found adequate, no changes needed:**
- *Approval workflow* (`service.py`'s `advance_approval_state_on_assessment`/`invalidate_approval_if_in_flight`, `project_router.py`'s `submit-for-approval`/`approve`/`reject`): every transition checks current state first (409 otherwise); no path double-approves, approves-after-reject, or bypasses the check. Self-approval (the same `compliance_officer`/`PROJECT_MANAGER` may assess, submit, and approve their own work) is deliberate and documented (§11/§26 name "Approve/sign off compliance" as the same capability as assessing, with no distinct approver role), not a finding.
- *Scheduled review/notification sweeps*: recipients always resolved from the review's own project/org, never a global list; notification content is generic title/date-only, no cross-org field values embedded; no manual "trigger review now" endpoint bypasses the sweep's own scoping.
- *Cross-standard mapping/version impact* (Phase 11/12): `create_requirement_mapping` validates both requirements and the relationship type against the caller's own organisation; `migrate_project_compliance_version` constrains a replacement version to the same standard as the original.
- *Org/project export-import bundle hooks* (beyond finding 3): every cross-reference in a bundle is resolved by portable ref/key scoped to the target org/project, never a raw bundle-supplied database id; merge-conflict resolution values are validated against the same core-plus-module-contributed allowed set before any hook's `import_` runs.
- *Evidence file download, MCP tool proxying, module-RBAC edge cases*: `resolve_evidence_file_project_id` resolves to the evidence's real owning project, correctly re-authorized by `download_file`; `mcp-server/server.py` forwards the caller's own token fresh on every call with no cross-call session-context caching; `require_module_role` checks `is_module_enabled` before any admin-override or explicit-grant check, so disabling a module for an org correctly revokes access for a user already holding an explicit `UserModuleRole`.
- *Compliance frontend* (~25 files plus the Module Federation loader): every closed enum has a matching label map used consistently; every destructive/elevated action's confirmation dialog names its target; no reload-clobbers-unsaved-edit race or stale-closure bug found; Module Federation's lack of a `remote_entry_url` origin allowlist is a considered, documented, backend-gated omission (`registry.py`'s own docstring), not a new gap. Two label-map misses were found and fixed regardless (below).

**4. Fixed, style/consistency (this project's binding label-map rule, not a security finding) — two raw backend action strings rendered unmapped.** `RequirementAssessmentPanel.tsx`'s requirement-history list and `OrgComplianceDashboard.tsx`'s recent-activity list both rendered `ComplianceAuditEvent`/`ComplianceRecentActivity`'s `action` field directly (one completely raw with underscores, one via an inline `.replace(/_/g, " ")` reimplementing half of an existing helper) instead of routing through `frontend/src/api/types.ts`'s existing `activityActionLabel()`. Fixed both call sites to import and use it.

**5. Fixed, unrelated to this branch but folded in at the user's request — two long-open GitHub code-scanning alerts (`py/path-injection`, #5/#6) against `backend/app/storage_backends/local.py`.** An earlier "security uplift" pass (see the "Security uplift" entry below) claimed to fix "all 7 code-scanning alerts at the source" by rewriting the path-confinement guard into a `_path_for` helper using CodeQL's documented-safe `os.path.realpath`+`startswith` idiom — this genuinely closed the alert at the construction site itself (#4), but left two flow-through alerts open at `save()`'s actual filesystem sinks (`path.parent.mkdir(...)`/`path.write_bytes(...)`), confirmed still open as of a `main` commit dated after that "fix all 7" one. Root cause: CodeQL's Python taint-tracking does not treat a check performed inside a called helper method as a sanitizing barrier for the *caller's* later use of the returned value — its own documented-safe example performs the check and the filesystem access in the same function, which this codebase's fix did not. Fixed by inlining the confinement check directly into `save()` itself, immediately before its two filesystem calls, rather than relying solely on the helper (`read`/`delete` were never flagged — CodeQL's query models writes, not reads/deletes, as the sink here — so they keep using the shared helper). Confirmed no behaviour change: existing `test_local_storage_backend.py` (6 tests) still passes unchanged.

**Verified.** Backend: `ruff check app` clean. Full backend suite (`tests/` + `app/modules/compliance/tests/`) run host-level against the dedicated `reqtrack_pytest_test` database — **954 passed, 0 failed**, with 27 deliberately deselected (14 pre-existing failures unrelated to this branch, confirmed by direct reproduction to be a host-level-only artifact: `aiosmtplib.errors.SMTPConnectError: ... mailhog ...`, a Docker-internal hostname unreachable from a host-level pytest run, not resolvable via `tests/container`'s stack from this environment; plus a handful more from the same email-dependent files). `test_project_hierarchy.py`'s transient 5-error showing in one earlier combined run was independently confirmed to be self-inflicted same-session test-DB pollution, not a regression: it passed 52/52 in isolation. Frontend: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` clean on both changed files.

### Files changed

`backend/app/services/rbac.py` (`require_server_role` PAT rejection); `backend/tests/test_module_system_rbac.py` (new test); `backend/app/modules/compliance/router.py` (`_require_org_member_or_none`, wired into `create_standard_review`/`update_standard_review`), `backend/app/modules/compliance/project_router.py` (`_require_project_member_or_none`, wired into `update_required_action_assessment`/`create_project_review`/`update_project_review`); `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_project_compliance_api.py`, `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_compliance_reviews_and_notifications.py` (new tests); `backend/app/schemas/org.py` (`OrgMergeResult` gains `extra="allow"`); `backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_compliance_export_import.py` (three new merge tests); `frontend/src/modules/compliance/RequirementAssessmentPanel.tsx`, `frontend/src/modules/compliance/OrgComplianceDashboard.tsx` (route `action` through `activityActionLabel()`); `backend/app/storage_backends/local.py` (confinement guard inlined into `save()`), `backend/app/services/files.py` (stale docstring reference to the renamed helper fixed); `docs/decisions.md` (this entry).

## Compliance module, human review follow-ups (Phases 17-19 planned)

The first human walkthrough of the shipped Compliance Module (16/16 phases, plus the hardening pass above) surfaced a batch of UX feedback — a mix of real bugs and two genuine IA gaps: Standards/Action Types/Mapping Types were three clicks deep inside Org Admin with no first-class identity, and there was no org-wide dashboard-style page at all outside that. Two items in the original feedback turned out to already be handled or non-issues on investigation: the "Add required action" button's disabled-state tooltip already existed (`RequirementTree.tsx:301-311`, a plain `title` attribute — correct per this codebase's own convention, since `Tooltip` is reserved for icon-only controls and this button has a visible label); and the greyed-out state itself was confirmed to have a real root cause — no `ComplianceActionTypeDefinition` ships by default for a fresh org (now Phase 17c).

Recorded here are the design decisions behind `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s new Phases 17-19, reached via a planning session that surfaced three points needing explicit user sign-off before implementation, each revised once from the first cut:

**Standards get a nav-rail section; Action Types/Mapping Types get a `ResourceMenu`.** The user's own framing — "I see these as effectively a special type of project" — was taken literally for a single `ComplianceStandard` entity (own top-level nav tab, cross-org list like Projects, and a `Layout.tsx` left-nav *section* triggered by `standardId` in the URL, exactly mirroring how `projectId` triggers today's Project section), but Action Types and Mapping Types are confirmed org-wide shared vocabularies (`ComplianceAdminPanel.tsx`'s `actionTypes`/`api.ts`'s `listActionTypes(orgId)` — no `standardId` anywhere in that path), not per-standard data. A nav-rail section is reserved for an actual project-like *entity*; a fixed pair of org-wide settings screens is exactly the "one page, persistent side menu of a handful of named sections" shape this codebase already has a component for (`ResourceMenu`, used by `ProjectAdminPage.tsx`/`OrgAdminPage.tsx`/`ServerManagementPage.tsx`) — reusing it here rather than `Tabs` (`OrgCompliancePanel`'s current choice) is a direct instance of the style guide's "use the existing shared component" rule, raised explicitly by the user mid-review rather than found independently.

**"Organisation Overview" is a real full page, not a widget bolted onto an existing one, and it now carries general org stats, not just compliance.** The first-cut plan folded a compliance summary into `ProjectListPage.tsx` and skipped a standalone org overview entirely; the user corrected this twice. First: it must be "another full page similar to the projects page... at the same level in the tree, not within the projects page" — i.e. its own top-level nav-rail tab (`/org-overview` → `/orgs/:orgId/overview`, reusing `/orgs`'s existing single-org/multi-org auto-redirect convention), not a section grafted onto Projects. Second, after the plan already had this page hosting only the relocated `OrgCompliancePanel` content: the user asked for a stats header too — project count, requirement count, org member count, total uploaded file size — making the page generally useful even to orgs with compliance switched off. This changes the tab's own visibility rule: unlike the Compliance Standards tab (gated on a new nav-visibility check, since it's genuinely niche), Organisation Overview is shown unconditionally to any org member, same precedent as the always-shown Projects link, since every org has projects/requirements/members/files regardless of compliance status.

**Every Organisation Overview stat is scoped to what the caller can actually see — except an org admin, who gets real org-wide totals.** The user's exact correction: "a user can't see the number of all projects if they themselves can't see them all," followed immediately by "an org admin is the exception and should see the raw proper totals." The design settled on reusing `_accessible_project_ids` (`backend/app/routers/projects.py:147` — the same visibility computation `list_projects` already uses: direct/group/org-wide roles plus hierarchical inheritance) for a plain member's project/requirement/file counts, with a branch for `is_server_admin`/`OrgRole.ORG_ADMIN` on that org returning unfiltered org-wide counts instead. Org member count needed no such branch at all — `list_org_users`'s existing permission (`require_org_role(ORG_ADMIN, PROJECT_CREATOR, MEMBER)`, i.e. any role) already lets any member see the full list, so scoping it further would only be inventing a restriction nothing else in the product enforces.

**Full cross-org aggregation was chosen over an org-scoped-only tab for Compliance Standards**, matching the user's explicit "like Projects" framing over the smaller-lift alternative, at the cost of two new backend endpoints that don't exist yet: an org-oblivious `GET /api/v1/compliance/standards/{standard_id}` (so `/standards/:standardId` can work without org in the URL, mirroring how a project's own id already resolves to its org) and the nav-visibility check above. No backend cross-org standards-listing endpoint was added on top of that — the list page fans out `listStandards(orgId)` per org client-side instead, since orgs-per-user is small (unlike total project count), making new backend fan-out infrastructure unwarranted for this.

**Phase 17 complete as of this entry** (all five sub-items — see `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s own Phase 17 checklist for the final per-item account). Phases 18-19 remain fully specified but not started.

**Worth recording: shipping the Phase 17c default action types broke ~83 of the ~110 compliance backend tests**, not from anything wrong with the seeding itself but because the entire compliance test suite's shared setup helpers had converged, independently and by habit, on the same generic placeholder name real users would also reach for — `_create_action_type`'s own default parameter in `test_compliance_standards_api.py` was literally `name="Test"`, and `test_project_compliance_api.py::_setup_published_standard_with_tree` (imported by 7 other test files as their standard "give me a published standard with a full requirement tree" fixture) passed `name="Test"` explicitly; a third, ORM-direct literal in `test_compliance_data_model.py` used the same string. Once every organisation started with a real `ComplianceActionTypeDefinition` row named "Test" from creation, all three collided on the model's own `(organization_id, name)` uniqueness constraint. This is the exact same class of "test fixtures unintentionally shadow a soon-to-exist product default" risk this codebase has hit before (see `seed_demo_data.py`'s own `create_compliance_action_type` calls this same phase's 17c retired for an identical reason) — worth checking for on any future "ship a new default row" change: grep the test suite for the literal default name *before* picking one, not after. Fixed by renaming all three to `"Verification"` (confirmed unused anywhere else in the suite) plus correcting one explicit `sort_order` assertion that had assumed its action type was the org's first ever (now the third, at index 2). Caught and fully reconciled in the same session, not left as a follow-up.

This entry documents the reasoning the plan's phase specs were built on; update the plan doc's own Status table as each phase/sub-item actually lands, per its standing "Instructions for whoever picks up the next phase" convention — don't let this entry drift out of sync with what's actually true of the code.

## Phase 18 complete — "Compliance Standards" as a first-class, cross-org, project-like nav entity

Implemented per the "human review follow-ups" entry above's design decisions. Records what was actually built, one real deviation from the picked-up spec (a genuine architecture-boundary mistake caught and corrected mid-implementation, not a design change), and verification results.

**Backend: a third, generic `ModuleDefinition.get_global_router` kind, not a one-off route.** `nav-visibility` and `standards/{standard_id}` both genuinely have no single org/project id to key a path off — `get_router()` (org-scoped) and `get_project_router()` (project-scoped, Phase 7) both assumed one. Rather than bolt either endpoint onto an existing router with a fake path parameter, `backend/app/modules/registry.py` gained `get_global_router: Callable[[], APIRouter | None] | None = None` — a third optional field, mounted by `backend/app/main.py`'s existing mount loop exactly like the other two (`for _module_router in (get_router(), get_project_router(), get_global_router())`), and included in `build_mcp_tool_manifest`'s router-prefix validation alongside the other two (no MCP tool declared against it yet — Phase 18 doesn't need one). `backend/app/modules/compliance/global_router.py` (new file, `/api/v1/compliance` prefix) holds both endpoints. `backend/app/services/rbac.py` gained `require_org_access_and_module_enabled(db, current_user, organization_id, module_key, request=None)` — a plain callable, non-dependency-factory sibling of `require_org_module_enabled`, for exactly this "resolve org from something else, not a path parameter" shape: `standards/{id}` looks the standard up first, then calls this to get the same 404-not-403 posture (member of a different org / module disabled there both read as "not found," never confirming the standard's existence to a caller who can't see its org). `nav-visibility` reuses the existing `service.py::get_effective_compliance_managers` helper (already computes "org admin ∪ direct `compliance_manager` grant" per org) rather than reimplementing that union, adding only the `is_server_admin` and "org has ≥1 non-archived standard" branches the formula also needs. A third small addition, in the spirit of the spec but not literally named by it: `router.py` gained `GET .../standards/{id}/history` (org-scoped, `_require_view`-gated), mirroring `project_router.py::get_requirement_history`'s exact shape against `compliance_standard`-entity audit events — needed to serve the Standard workspace's "History" section, which the spec names as a required nav-rail section without specifying how it's backed; adding it to the *existing* org router (organization_id is already known once inside the workspace) rather than the new global router keeps the global router limited to the two genuinely id-less endpoints.

**Frontend: a real course-correction, not a footnote.** The first implementation pass hardcoded compliance-specific knowledge directly into `Layout.tsx` — a `useComplianceNavVisibility()` Context imported from `modules/compliance/`, an inline `/^\/standards\/(?!settings\/)([^/]+)/` regex, and a literal "Standard" section — the exact "module coupled into a core file" mistake `docs/compliance-module-plan.md`'s own "Design history" section records as *already rejected twice* during the module system's original design (draft 2/3's rejection points). Caught via review before this phase was reported done, not found later. Fixed by generalizing `frontend/src/modules/types.ts`'s `TierAModuleDefinition` with two more optional, `orgAdminSections`-shaped fields: `globalNavItems` (`{key, render: ({railCollapsed}) => ReactNode}`, for a top-level nav-rail link — each item owns its own visibility and may render nothing) and `standaloneWorkspaces` (`{key, matchPath: RegExp, render: ({entityId, railCollapsed}) => ReactNode}`, for a "Standard"-shaped left-nav section — `Layout.tsx` tests every installed module's `matchPath` against the current pathname and renders the first match's own section). `Layout.tsx` now only does `installedModules.flatMap(m => m.globalNavItems ?? []).map(...)` and the equivalent for `standaloneWorkspaces` — zero compliance-specific code, symmetrical with how it already treats `orgAdminSections`. `NavRailLink` (previously private to `Layout.tsx`) is now exported so a module's own render functions can build visually-consistent links. Compliance's own contributions live in three new files under `frontend/src/modules/compliance/`: `ComplianceGlobalNavLink.tsx` (the "Compliance Standards" link, gated on its own visibility hook), `StandardNavSection.tsx` (the "Standard" section — Overview/Versions/History links), and `useComplianceNavVisibility.ts`. The last of these replaced an original `ComplianceNavVisibilityContext`/`Provider` design (deleted) that would have required `Layout.tsx` to mount a compliance-owned `<Provider>` in its own tree — instead it's a self-contained hook backed by a tiny module-level `useSyncExternalStore` store, keyed to the current session's user id (so a different user logging in on the same tab never inherits a stale cached value) with a `refreshComplianceNavVisibility()` export called after the two actions inside the compliance module itself that can flip it (`StandardListPage.tsx` creating an org's first standard; `StandardWorkspacePage.tsx` archiving/unarchiving one). A core page performing an action that could also flip it (`OrgAdminPage.tsx` toggling the module's enablement, or granting/revoking `compliance_manager`) does **not** call this refresh — doing so would reintroduce the same core-imports-a-specific-module coupling; visibility there converges on the next full page load instead, a deliberate, documented trade-off, not an oversight.

**A second instance of the identical mistake was caught in the same review, on the routing side rather than the nav side.** `App.tsx` — a core file — directly imported `StandardListPage`/`StandardWorkspacePage`/`ComplianceSettingsPage` and hardcoded three `/standards*` `<Route>` entries for them, reasoning correctly that `buildModuleRoutes` (project-scoped, gated on a project's own currently-enabled-modules list) doesn't fit a cross-org, always-present surface — but drawing the wrong conclusion from that correct diagnosis (hardcode it into `App.tsx` instead of extending the registration schema). The three page components themselves also lived under `frontend/src/pages/` — the core pages directory — despite importing extensively from `modules/compliance/` (`api`, `useComplianceNavVisibility`, `StandardFormModal`, `StandardVersionsSection`, `ActionTypesPanel`, `MappingTypesPanel`, `types`), unlike the existing, correct precedent (`modules/compliance/module.ts`'s pre-Phase-18 `routes` array points at `ProjectCompliancePage`, which itself lives inside `modules/compliance/`, never under `pages/`). Fixed the same way as the first instance: `TierAModuleDefinition` gained a fourth field, `globalRoutes?: TierAModuleRoute[]` (reusing `TierAModuleRoute`'s existing `{path, element}` shape — the always-mounted counterpart to the existing project-gated `routes`), and all three page components (plus their `.stories.tsx` files) were moved from `frontend/src/pages/` into `frontend/src/modules/compliance/`, registered via `module.ts`'s new `globalRoutes` array. `App.tsx` now only does `installedModules.flatMap(m => m.globalRoutes ?? []).map(...)` spread into `<Routes>` — no compliance import, no hardcoded `/standards*` path, anywhere in `App.tsx`. Two genuinely different things stayed correctly distinguished throughout this correction: a **core file** (`App.tsx`, `Layout.tsx`) must never import a specific module's own components, but a module's own page components (wherever they live) importing the rest of that same module freely is not the violation — `modules/compliance/ProjectOverviewPage`-adjacent case is `pages/ProjectOverviewPage.tsx` itself, a genuinely core-owned page that imports compliance code directly for its own summary tile (confirmed pre-existing, predating this phase — see below), which is a different, already-accepted pattern this phase didn't need to (and didn't) touch.

**Confirmed pre-existing, not introduced by this phase, and deliberately left untouched (flagged as known debt instead):** `frontend/src/pages/ProjectOverviewPage.tsx` (imports `../modules/compliance/api`/`types` directly, for its own compliance-status summary tile) and, on the backend, `backend/app/routers/orgs.py`/`projects.py`/`backend/app/services/bootstrap.py` (each a lazy inline `from app.modules.compliance...` import, for org-creation seeding / bundle-export type checks / bootstrap seeding respectively) — `git diff`/`git log` against each confirms none was touched by this phase's changes (all last modified in or before the Phase 17 commit). Same category of violation as the two caught and fixed above, but out of this phase's scope to fix; reported to the user as separate known debt rather than silently left unmentioned.

**`StandardsPanel.tsx`/`ComplianceAdminPanel.tsx` fully retired, not layered under.** Split into: `StandardFormModal.tsx` (extracted create/edit dialog, now also handling the create-time multi-org picker `StandardListPage.tsx` needs, mirroring `ProjectListPage.tsx`'s own "New project" org-picker-as-first-field shape exactly); `StandardVersionsSection.tsx` (extracted version list + `VersionWorkspace` drill-in, reused as-is per the spec); `StandardListPage.tsx` (`/standards`, cross-org fan-out — no cross-org listing endpoint exists, so it fetches `GET /orgs?mine=true` then calls `listStandards(orgId)` per org via `Promise.allSettled`, dropping a 404'd org silently); `StandardWorkspacePage.tsx` (`/standards/:standardId[/versions|/history]`, resolving org via the new global endpoint then threading it through unchanged to every existing org-scoped call); `ComplianceSettingsPage.tsx` (`/standards/settings/:orgId[/actionTypes|mappingTypes]`, a `ResourceMenu` page hosting `ActionTypesPanel`/`MappingTypesPanel` near-unchanged). `module.ts`'s `orgAdminSections` lost its `"compliance"` entry (the `"compliance-overview"` entry is untouched — Phase 19's). `OrgAdminPage.tsx` needed **zero edits** for this removal: it already derives its `ResourceMenu` groups from `installedModules`' declared sections, so dropping one from `module.ts` was sufficient — direct evidence the earlier org-admin-sections generalisation (`docs/decisions.md`'s "Module system follow-up: dynamic org-admin panel registration" entry) is doing its job.

**A pre-existing `.side-grid` order bug was not carried forward.** `StandardsPanel.tsx` (now deleted) rendered its `FilterPanel` *before* its `DirectoryTable` inside `.side-grid` — backwards from every other list page in this codebase (`theme.css`'s own comment: "list/detail content first, filters second" is the documented, mobile-reordering-dependent convention `ProjectListPage.tsx` follows correctly). `StandardListPage.tsx` uses the correct order from the start, per this repo's fix-don't-defer rule; `OrgComplianceStandardsPanel.tsx` (a different, still-live Phase 14 component with the same bug, found in the same pass) was corrected too.

**Tests.** Backend: 9 new permission-boundary tests (`backend/app/modules/compliance/tests/test_compliance_nav_visibility_and_standard_lookup.py`) — nav-visibility false for a plain member with no role/standards, true in isolation for a `compliance_manager` grant / `org_admin` / `is_server_admin`, false for a user with zero org memberships anywhere (via a direct `UserOrgRole` removal — no API path exists to add an *existing* user to a second org, only to create a brand-new one, confirmed while writing the server-admin-isolation test); `standards/{id}` 404s for a member of a different org, 404s when the owning org's module is disabled, 200s with the right `organization_id` for a real member, 404s for a nonexistent id. Full backend suite run twice across this phase's two review passes: 977 passed/14 failed, then (after the `App.tsx` correction, unrelated backend-wise) 963 passed/16 failed/16 errors — the *specific* failing files differ between the two runs (invites/OIDC the first time; `test_org_lifecycle.py`/`test_org_pending_invites.py`/`test_org_rename_and_test_email.py` the second) and none is ever compliance-related, which is itself the signature of this repo's already-documented cross-test/DB-state flakiness rather than a real regression — confirmed directly, not assumed: all three second-run failing files pass cleanly (36/36) run in isolation. Ruff clean on every changed backend file both times. Frontend: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm run lint`, and `npm run build` all clean after both passes; new Storybook coverage for every new page-level and extracted component (`StandardFormModal`, `StandardVersionsSection`, `ComplianceGlobalNavLink`, `StandardNavSection`, `StandardListPage`, `StandardWorkspacePage`, `ComplianceSettingsPage`) — full suite 98 files / 780 tests passed both before and after the `App.tsx`/file-relocation correction (identical file/test counts, confirming the move lost or duplicated nothing), with the same one pre-existing, unrelated unhandled-rejection warning in `ProjectOverviewPage.stories.tsx`'s `LoadError` story both times (confirmed to predate this phase). Playwright: `compliance-standards-management.spec.ts` rewritten for the new IA (tab visibility on/off using the `orphan` persona — zero org memberships, so nav-visibility is vacuously false regardless of how many standards Alpha/Beta accumulate across this suite's own runs — one-step standard+version creation, Standard workspace Overview→Versions→History navigation, and `ComplianceSettingsPage`'s `ResourceMenu` group switch); `project-compliance-view.spec.ts`/`org-compliance-view.spec.ts` had their now-defunct org-admin "Compliance" tab setup steps replaced with the new `/standards` flow (a shared `createStandardWithVersion` helper, `tests/playwright/tests/modules/compliance/helpers.ts`), the rest of each spec (Phase 13/14 behaviour) unchanged. **Not executed in this session**: this sandboxed environment has no running Docker Compose stack (`docker compose ps` fails on a missing `MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD`, and no seeded `tests/container` database exists here) — the rewritten specs are believed correct by construction (same interactions the passing pre-Phase-18 specs already used, reached through a different, statically-verified route) but have not been run live; whoever next has the stack up should run them before trusting this phase fully closed end-to-end.
